chapters.guideHtml:
From an averaging matrix to a picture

Put the numbers 11 and ii at two positions. A row that gives them equal weight produces (1+i)/2(1+i)/2, halfway along the segment joining them. Now put a complex number vjv_j at each of nn positions. Row ii of a matrix AA gives the weights with which we average them to obtain (Av)i(Av)_i. We call the matrix row-stochastic when every weight is nonnegative and the weights in each row add to one.

An eigenvector vv gives us a particularly simple way of doing all these averages. We can multiply each old value by the same complex number λ\lambda and obtain its new value. Which multipliers can occur if we have only nn positions? The set of all such individual eigenvalues is Θn\Theta_n. We can choose a different matrix for each λ\lambda.

Throughout this construction vv is a column of values. A row of probabilities evolves by multiplication on the other side, μT↦μTA\mu^T\mapsto\mu^TA. We will use both conventions when we fill the region along a ray.

How far from zero can λ\lambda be? Choose a coordinate viv_i farthest from zero. Row ii takes a weighted average of coordinates, each at distance at most |vi||v_i|. Applying the triangle inequality to this row gives

|λ||vi|=|∑jaijvj|≤∑jaij|vj|≤|vi|.|\lambda|\,|v_i|=\left|\sum_j a_{ij}v_j\right|\le\sum_j a_{ij}|v_j|\le |v_i|.

Our chosen coordinate is nonzero because vv is an eigenvector. Dividing the inequality by |vi||v_i| gives |λ|≤1|\lambda|\le1. We can reach the point 11 on the unit circle. Every entry of A𝟏A\mathbf1 is a weighted average of ones, so A𝟏=𝟏A\mathbf1=\mathbf1. Which other points in the disk can we reach?

Mark v1,…,vnv_1,\ldots,v_n in the complex plane. What points could a row send us to if we were free to choose its weights? A row can produce any sum ∑jcjvj\sum_j c_jv_j with cj≥0c_j\ge0 and ∑jcj=1\sum_j c_j=1. Such a sum is a convex combination of the coordinates. The set of all these sums is their convex hull,

P=conv⁡{v1,…,vn}.P=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}.

Take a finite set of at least two distinct points in the complex plane. In this walkthrough we call its convex hull a polygon. If the points do not all lie on a line, the polygon includes the whole region inside its sides. If all the points lie on one line, the polygon is the segment between the two outermost points. You can move the weights to trace the segment from 11 to ii. Why exclude a single point? If we could choose P={0}P=\{0\}, then λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P would hold for every complex number, even for λ=2\lambda=2, which our matrix bound has already ruled out.

The eigenvector equation puts each image λvi\lambda v_i in PP. The hull of these images is λP\lambda P, the original hull multiplied by λ\lambda. Since PP contains every average of points in PP, it contains that image hull too. Multiplying by λ=ρeiθ\lambda=\rho e^{i\theta} rotates every point through θ\theta and scales its distance from zero by ρ\rho. The matrix equation has given us the containment λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P.

A point of PP is a vertex if we cannot draw a segment in PP that extends past that point in both directions. In a triangle the three corners have this property. Every vertex of the hull comes from one of our coordinates, although a coordinate can also lie on a side, lie inside, or repeat an earlier coordinate. There are therefore at most nn vertices.

We can already settle order two. Write the two averaging rows as (1−a,a)(1-a,a) and (b,1−b)(b,1-b), with 0≤a,b≤10\le a,b\le1. Subtract their outputs on a column xx:

(Ax)1−(Ax)2=(1−a−b)(x1−x2). (Ax)_1-(Ax)_2=(1-a-b)(x_1-x_2).

On constant columns the multiplier is one. On an eigenvector with unequal entries, dividing by x1−x2x_1-x_2 gives the real multiplier 1−a−b1-a-b. Indeed the characteristic polynomial is (z−1)(z−(1−a−b))(z-1)(z-(1-a-b)). Taking a=ba=b from zero to one gives every value in [−1,1][-1,1]. At a=b=1/2a=b=1/2 the entries become equal in one step. At a=b=1a=b=1 the two entries exchange places. For three or more positions a new possibility appears. The hull of the values can enclose area, and the common multiplier can rotate it through an angle other than a half-turn.

An exact four-point picture

Place the four numbers 1,i,−1,−i1,i,-1,-i around the unit circle in this order and collect them in the column vv. The matrix CC reads the next entry in the list, starting again at 11 after −i-i. Thus Cv=(i,−1,−i,1)T=ivCv=(i,-1,-i,1)^T=iv. To average an entry with its neighbour, give equal weight to leaving the list in place and shifting it. With II the identity matrix, this gives

A=(1/21/20001/21/20001/21/21/2001/2). A=\begin{pmatrix} 1/2&1/2&0&0\\ 0&1/2&1/2&0\\ 0&0&1/2&1/2\\ 1/2&0&0&1/2 \end{pmatrix}.

For the entry at 11 we get

(Av)1=12(1)+12(i)=1+i2. (Av)_1=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(i)=\frac{1+i}{2}.

The point (1+i)/2(1+i)/2 is halfway from 11 to ii. The next row averages ii and −1-1. Its output is ii times the first midpoint, since both inputs have been multiplied by ii. The same quarter turn takes us from each row to the next. All four midpoints are therefore obtained from their starting vertices by the same multiplier. In matrix form we have

Av=1+i2v=λv,λ=1+i2=12eiπ/4. Av=\frac{1+i}{2}v=\lambda v,\qquad \lambda=\frac{1+i}{2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}e^{i\pi/4}.

How much contraction did this particular diamond require? The image of 11 at radius rr and angle π/4\pi/4 has coordinates (r/2,r/2)(r/\sqrt2,r/\sqrt2). The line through 11 and ii has equation x+y=1x+y=1, so containment at that vertex requires 2r≤1\sqrt2\,r\le1. The other vertices give the same inequality by quarter-turn symmetry. Thus r=1/2r=1/\sqrt2 is exactly the largest radius for this diamond at this angle. To determine the largest radius in Θ4\Theta_4, we still have to allow the polygon itself to vary.

Join the four midpoints in the drawing. The smaller square is λP\lambda P. Each stochastic row could choose any point on its side. The eigenvector equation ties the four choices to one rotation and one scale.

Why the translation works in both directions

Now start with the picture. We have a polygon PP with vertices w1,…,wkw_1,\ldots,w_k, and we know that λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P. Where can we get the entries of a matrix? The point λwi\lambda w_i lies in the hull of the vertices, so we can choose weights aija_{ij} for which

λwi=∑j=1kaijwj,aij≥0,∑jaij=1.\lambda w_i=\sum_{j=1}^k a_{ij}w_j,\qquad a_{ij}\ge0,\quad\sum_j a_{ij}=1.

Use the weights for λwi\lambda w_i as row ii of AA. The row sums are one, and reading the displayed equations down the rows gives Aw=λwAw=\lambda w for w=(w1,…,wk)Tw=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)^T. At least one vertex differs from zero, so ww is an eigenvector. If we need n>kn>k states, add n−kn-k states that each stay where they are. The enlarged matrix has diagonal blocks AA and In−kI_{n-k}, and extending ww by zeros gives the same eigenvalue.

Together the two constructions give the following criterion for every n≥2n\ge2.

λ∈Θn⇔there is a polygon P with at most n vertices and λP⊆P.\lambda\in\Theta_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{there is a polygon }P\text{ with at most }n\text{ vertices and }\lambda P\subseteq P.

One case in the construction from a matrix deserves a check. If every coordinate of vv is the same number cc, then c≠0c\ne0, and each row returns cc. Hence λc=c\lambda c=c and λ=1\lambda=1. For this eigenvalue the segment [0,1][0,1] supplies the polygon in the criterion. At order one the only stochastic matrix is (1)(1), so Θ1={1}\Theta_1=\{1\}.

In a drawing we only have to check the kk points λwj\lambda w_j. To see why, choose any x∈Px\in P and write it as a convex combination x=∑jcjwjx=\sum_j c_jw_j. Its image λx=∑jcj(λwj)\lambda x=\sum_j c_j(\lambda w_j) uses the same weights. As soon as the vertex images lie in PP, every such average lies there as well. This lets us check containment again after moving a vertex.

To describe the boundary, we will rotate about zero and measure distance along a ray. We first need to know where zero lies in an invariant polygon.

Why zero is inside a nonreal invariant polygon

Consider a nonreal eigenvalue λ\lambda. Multiplication by λ\lambda turns a segment through an angle different from a multiple of π\pi. Its image then lies on a line with a different direction and cannot fit in the original segment. Our polygon therefore has interior. Where is zero in relation to its sides?

Choose w∈Pw\in P. By containment, w,λw,λ2w,…w,\lambda w,\lambda^2w,\ldots all belong to PP. If |λ|<1|\lambda|<1, their distances from zero tend to zero. The polygon is closed, so it contains their limit. If |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, average the first kk points instead. Their average is w(1−λk)/(k(1−λ))w(1-\lambda^k)/(k(1-\lambda)). Its numerator stays bounded and 1−λ≠01-\lambda\ne0, so it also tends to zero. Each average belongs to PP by convexity.

Could zero be on a side or at a corner? There would then be a line through zero with all of PP in one closed half-plane. Follow the directions of any w≠0w\ne0 in PP. If the rotation repeats after mm steps, the mm unit vectors in these directions sum to zero by the geometric sum formula. Take components perpendicular to the line, choosing the positive direction into the half-plane. These components are all nonnegative and their sum is zero. Each one would have to vanish, putting all the directions on the line. Yet two successive directions form an angle different from a multiple of π\pi. If the rotation never repeats, its directions enter every open arc, including one on the other side of the line. In both cases we get a contradiction. Thus zero lies in the interior, and we can order the vertices by their angles around it.

Why an irrational rotation visits every open arc

Write the rotation angle as 2πα2\pi\alpha with α\alpha irrational. Divide [0,1)[0,1) into MM equal intervals, and place the M+1M+1 fractional parts of 0,α,…,Mα0,\alpha,\ldots,M\alpha in them. The fractional part of xx is xx minus its integer part. One interval contains at least two points. Their difference gives a positive integer rr with rα=k+dr\alpha=k+d, where kk is an integer and 0<|d|<1/M0<|d|<1/M. Nonzero dd follows from irrationality. The positive iterates with indices 0,r,2r,…0,r,2r,\ldots have fractional parts equal to those of 0,d,2d,…0,d,2d,\ldots. The first ⌊1/|d|⌋+1\lfloor1/|d|\rfloor+1 such points step around the circle in one direction with every remaining gap at most |d||d|; here ⌊a⌋\lfloor a\rfloor means the greatest integer at most aa. Choosing MM arbitrarily large makes these points arbitrarily close to every direction. All the indices used here are nonnegative, as required for the forward orbit.

The boundary is a problem on each ray

Fix a ray on which a nonzero eigenvalue is possible, and let rr be the supremum of the possible radii there. The unit-disk bound gives r≤1r\le1. Choose realising matrices AkA_k with eigenvalues λk\lambda_k on this ray and |λk|→r|\lambda_k|\to r. Their entries are bounded by one, so a subsequence converges entry by entry. The limit AA is still stochastic. Along the same subsequence λk→λ\lambda_k\to\lambda with |λ|=r|\lambda|=r, and continuity of the determinant gives det⁡(λI−A)=0\det(\lambda I-A)=0. We can therefore choose an outermost eigenvalue on this ray. The same argument for any convergent sequence of attainable eigenvalues shows that Θn\Theta_n is closed, and hence compact.

Two operations tell us where else to look for eigenvalues. Taking complex conjugates gives Av¯=λ¯v¯A\overline v=\overline\lambda\,\overline v, since the entries of AA are real. It is therefore enough to draw the upper half of the region and reflect it. Adding a state that stays fixed preserves the old eigenvalue, so Θn⊆Θn+1\Theta_n\subseteq\Theta_{n+1}.

Return to the diamond with λ=(1+i)/2\lambda=(1+i)/2. Its first vertex goes to a side midpoint. Halve the multiplier. The image now lies halfway from zero to that midpoint, still inside the diamond. The same is true at every vertex. For any nonreal attainable λ\lambda, the polygon contains both 00 and λvj\lambda v_j, so it contains the segment between them. Hence (tλ)P⊆P(t\lambda)P\subseteq P for 0≤t≤10\le t\le1. The polygon correspondence gives a matrix at every point of that radial segment. For real eigenvalues the two-state calculation already fills [−1,1][-1,1].

We can also construct a matrix for tλt\lambda from one for λ\lambda. We want a row whose weighted average of the eigenvector coordinates is zero. Averaging against a stationary probability row πT\pi^T does just this when λ≠1\lambda\ne1. Its entries are nonnegative and sum to one, and stationarity means πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T.

Why a stationary probability row exists

Start from any probability row μT\mu^T and average the first kk rows μT,μTA,…,μTAk−1\mu^T,\mu^TA,\ldots,\mu^TA^{k-1}. The averages πkT\pi_k^T are probability rows, so a subsequence converges to a probability row πT\pi^T. Multiplying the sum by AA shifts it one term to the right. Only its ends survive subtraction:

πkTA−πkT=μTAk−μTk→0. \pi_k^TA-\pi_k^T=\frac{\mu^TA^k-\mu^T}{k}\longrightarrow0.

The numerator is the difference of two bounded probability rows. At the limit we get πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T.

Indeed, πTAv\pi^TAv equals πTv\pi^Tv by stationarity and equals λπTv\lambda\pi^Tv by the eigenvector equation. Thus πTv=0\pi^Tv=0 when λ≠1\lambda\ne1. Give weight tt to the original row and weight 1−t1-t to the stationary average in every row. The matrix

At=tA+(1−t)𝟏πTA_t=tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T

is stochastic and sends vv to tλv+(1−t)𝟏(πTv)=tλvt\lambda v+(1-t)\mathbf1(\pi^Tv)=t\lambda v. This gives radial filling for n≥2n\ge2. At order one the only point is 11.

A worked check

Try radial filling on a triangle. Write ω=e2πi/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3} and take v=(1,ω,ω2)Tv=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T. The cycle matrix A=(010001100)A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix} gives Av=(ω,ω2,1)T=ωvAv=(\omega,\omega^2,1)^T=\omega v. Its action on the triangle is a turn through 2π/32\pi/3. Now 1+ω+ω2=01+\omega+\omega^2=0, so a row giving weight 1/31/3 to each vertex sends it to the centre. Giving each row weight tt on the cycle instruction and 1−t1-t on this average gives tA+(1−t)𝟏𝟏T/3tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\mathbf1^T/3. Its eigenvalue on vv is tωt\omega for every 0≤t≤10\le t\le1.

Row checkpoint. In the square example, give the first row weights (1/4,3/4,0,0)(1/4,3/4,0,0) and leave the other three rows alone. Mark the new image of 11 on the square. Is there still one multiplier that gives all four images of the original column?

Hint

Multiply that row by (1,i,−1,−i)T(1,i,-1,-i)^T. Check the multiplier from the second row as well.

Solution

The row computes (1+3i)/4(1+3i)/4, strictly inside the side from 11 to ii and closer to ii. Its modulus is 10/4<1\sqrt{10}/4<1. This is a valid averaging instruction, but the unchanged other rows still give the old multiplier (1+i)/2(1+i)/2. Thus the one altered row does not make this same column an eigenvector for a new common multiplier. The construction of an eigenpair requires compatible averaging instructions at every vertex.

Take a nonreal outermost point on a ray and choose an invariant polygon with as few vertices as possible. Can even one vertex land strictly inside it? Topic II answers this question by changing the averaging rows.
chapters.sourceHtml:
Saturation and cyclic contacts

For n≥1n\ge1, let Θn\Theta_n be the set of eigenvalues of real row-stochastic matrices of order nn. Every such matrix has operator norm one on ℓ∞\ell^\infty, so Θn\Theta_n lies in the closed unit disk. It is compact: from any convergent sequence of these eigenvalues, compactness of the matrix set gives a convergent subsequence of corresponding matrices, and continuity of the determinant makes the limit an eigenvalue of the limiting matrix. Since the matrices are real, Θn\Theta_n is invariant under complex conjugation. Adjoining a 1×11\times1 identity block preserves all eigenvalues, giving Θn⊆Θn+1\Theta_n\subseteq\Theta_{n+1}.

For n≥2n\ge2, the invariant-polygon correspondence of Dmitriev and Dynkin [DD], §§1–2, presented in English by Swift [Swift], states that (2.1)λ∈Θn⇔λP⊆P for some non-singleton polytope P⊂ℂwith at most n vertices.\lambda\in\Theta_n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \begin{gathered} \lambda P\subseteq P\text{ for some non-singleton polytope }P\subset\mathbb C\\ \text{with at most }n\text{ vertices}. \end{gathered} Here a polytope is the convex hull of finitely many points; it may be a segment.

To prove the forward implication, choose Av=λvAv=\lambda v with v≠0v\ne0 and set P=conv⁡{v1,…,vn}P=\mathop{\mathrm{conv}}\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}. Each row of AA expresses λvi\lambda v_i as a convex combination of the coordinates of vv, so λP⊆P\lambda P\subseteq P. If PP is a singleton, all coordinates are the same nonzero number, forcing λ=1\lambda=1; any nontrivial segment then gives the required PP. Conversely, write each image of a vertex of PP as a convex combination of its vertices. These coefficients form the rows of a stochastic matrix with eigenvalue λ\lambda. If PP has fewer than nn vertices, adjoining an identity block gives order nn.

For nonreal λ\lambda, PP cannot be a segment, because λP\lambda P would be a nonparallel segment and could not lie in PP. Thus PP is a polygon. Moreover, if 0<|λ|≤10<|\lambda|\le1, then 0∈int⁡P0\in\operatorname{int}P. When |λ|<1|\lambda|<1, the iterates λkw\lambda^k w of any w∈Pw\in P converge to zero. When |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, their averages converge to zero. In both cases, invariance, convexity, and closedness give 0∈P0\in P.

If zero were on the boundary, a supporting line through it would put all iterates of a nonzero w∈Pw\in P in one closed half-plane. Their directions are obtained by successive rotations through arg⁡λ\arg\lambda. For a rotation of finite order, the rotated unit vectors sum to zero and are not collinear; for a rotation of infinite order, their directions are dense in the circle. Neither set of directions can lie in that half-plane, so zero is interior.

The sets Θn\Theta_n, n≥2n\ge2, are star-shaped about zero: if λ∈Θn\lambda\in\Theta_n, then tλ∈Θnt\lambda\in\Theta_n for every 0≤t≤10\le t\le1. To see this for λ≠1\lambda\ne1, choose Av=λvAv=\lambda v and a stationary probability row vector πT\pi^T. Since πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T, we have (λ−1)πTv=0(\lambda-1)\pi^Tv=0. Thus πTv=0\pi^Tv=0, and the stochastic matrix At=tA+(1−t)𝟏πTA_t=tA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T satisfies Atv=tλvA_tv=t\lambda v; here 𝟏\mathbf1 is the all-ones column vector. For λ=1\lambda=1, the matrix with rows (1,0)(1,0) and (1−t,t)(1-t,t) has eigenvalue tt and can be padded to order nn. Write Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) for the maximum modulus at argument θ\theta in Θn\Theta_n.

chapters.guideHtml:
An extremal eigenvalue has no room to move outward

Choose the outermost eigenvalue on a ray in Θn\Theta_n and call it ζ=ρeiθζ\zeta=\rho e^{i\theta_\zeta}. We consider the nonreal case with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and choose 0<θζ<2π0<\theta_\zeta<2\pi. Draw a polygon PP for which TP⊆PTP\subseteq P, where Tx=ζxTx=\zeta x. If the whole image TPTP lies in the interior of PP, we can increase ρ\rho a little. There are finitely many vertices, and each image has a positive distance to the boundary. Moving all of them outward by less than the smallest of these distances still gives an invariant polygon. This contradicts the choice of ζ\zeta.

Now suppose only one image lies inside. A second image may already touch a side. Enlarging both images about zero could carry the second one out of the polygon immediately. How can we use the room around the first image? We will turn that room into a choice of strictly positive coefficients in one matrix row. Subtracting a little from that row and normalising the matrix will move the eigenvalue outward.

Use NN for the least number of vertices that suffice for ζ\zeta. Topic I identifies this number with the least order of a stochastic matrix having eigenvalue ζ\zeta. A three-state realisation can be padded to order eight by adding five fixed states, so we keep NN distinct from the requested order nn. Any realisation of tζt\zeta, t>1t>1, with at most NN states could likewise be padded to nn, contradicting our original choice. This property at order NN is radial extremality. Topic XI compares the eventual formulas at NN and nn.

We will prove that in every invariant polygon with at most NN vertices each vertex image is on the boundary and every side meets TPTP. This lets us apply the theorem again after changing the polygon. Reflection replaces ζ\zeta by ζ‾\bar\zeta and its chosen argument by 2π−θζ2\pi-\theta_\zeta.

Lesson 1: watch deflation move an eigenvalue outward

Take three points at equal distances around the unit circle. If ω=e2πi/3\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}, the column v=(1,ω,ω2)Tv=(1,\omega,\omega^2)^T lists these points in order. Their sum is zero. Consider the matrix

A=16(141114411),πT=(1/3,1/3,1/3). A=\frac16\begin{pmatrix}1&4&1\\1&1&4\\4&1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \pi^T=(1/3,1/3,1/3).

In the first row, each point receives weight 1/61/6 and ω\omega receives an extra 3/63/6. The three equal contributions cancel, leaving ω/2\omega/2. In each successive row the extra weight moves to the next vertex. Thus the three averages are ω/2\omega/2, ω2/2\omega^2/2 and 1/21/2, giving Av=(ω/2)vAv=(\omega/2)v. The row sums are one, making AA stochastic. Its column sums are also one, which gives πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T for the uniform row πT\pi^T above.

How much of each average can we take away while keeping this eigenvector equation? The uniform average of our three points is zero. Take one quarter of that average out of every row, subtracting 1/121/12 from each entry of AA. This gives

B=A−14𝟏πT=112(171117711). B=A-\tfrac14\mathbf1\pi^T =\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}1&7&1\\1&1&7\\7&1&1\end{pmatrix}.

The smallest entry of AA was 1/61/6, so all entries of BB are still positive. Each row has lost a total weight of 1/41/4 and now sums to r=3/4r=3/4. On the column vv the subtraction has taken away 14𝟏(πTv)=0\tfrac14\mathbf1(\pi^Tv)=0. Hence Bv=(ω/2)vBv=(\omega/2)v. Dividing each entry by rr restores the row sums and gives

Â=Br=19(171117711),Âv=2ω3v. \widehat A=\frac{B}{r} =\frac19\begin{pmatrix}1&7&1\\1&1&7\\7&1&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \widehat Av=\frac{2\omega}{3}v.

Division by 3/43/4 changes the multiplier from ω/2\omega/2 to 2ω/32\omega/3. Its argument stays the same and its modulus increases from 1/21/2 to 2/32/3. The example therefore gives two points on the same ray, with the first strictly inside the second radius. We could make the same subtraction everywhere because all three rows were positive. If only one row is positive, we can still subtract from that row, but now the row sums differ. The next construction first makes those sums equal. If it succeeded at the outermost point of a ray, it would produce a point farther out.

The positive eigenvector needed for the general normalization

A nonnegative matrix is irreducible if its directed graph has a path from every vertex to every other, drawing an arrow i→ji\to j when aij>0a_{ij}>0. For an irreducible stochastic matrix, a stationary probability row πT\pi^T has strictly positive entries. The spectral radius of a matrix is the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues. An irreducible nonnegative matrix has positive left and right eigenvectors for that radius. In particular, once we find a strictly positive left eigenvector with eigenvalue rr, we also have a strictly positive column with eigenvalue rr. These are the precise Perron–Frobenius facts used below. They extend familiar eigenvector theory to matrices with nonnegative entries.

Derive the positive eigenvectors from stationary averages

A stationary probability row of an irreducible stochastic matrix is positive. If πj=0\pi_j=0, then 0=∑iπiaij0=\sum_i\pi_i a_{ij} forces πi=0\pi_i=0 for each predecessor ii with aij>0a_{ij}>0. Every vertex has a path to jj, so all entries of π\pi would vanish. This contradicts ∑iπi=1\sum_i\pi_i=1.

Below we have an irreducible nonnegative matrix BB and a strictly positive row with πTB=rπT\pi^TB=r\pi^T, r>0r>0. Write Pπ=diag⁡(π1,…,πN)P_\pi=\operatorname{diag}(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_N) and put Q=r−1Pπ−1BTPπQ=r^{-1}P_\pi^{-1}B^TP_\pi. Since BTπ=rπB^T\pi=r\pi, we get Q𝟏=𝟏Q\mathbf1=\mathbf1. The new matrix is stochastic and irreducible. Topic I gives it a stationary row μT\mu^T, which is positive by the argument above. From QTμ=μQ^T\mu=\mu it follows that h=Pπ−1μh=P_\pi^{-1}\mu satisfies Bh=rhBh=rh with h>0h>0. Also BB is similar to rQTrQ^T, whose spectral radius is rr by the unit-disk bound.

Why can we apply this fact to a matrix obtained from our polygon? In a graph that is not irreducible there is a vertex from which some other vertex cannot be reached. Let II be the set of vertices reachable from the starting vertex, including the starting vertex itself. No arrow leaves II. The rows indexed by II therefore give a smaller stochastic matrix, and the eigenvector equation on these rows uses only the coordinates in II. Every such coordinate is a vertex of PP, hence is nonzero because zero lies in the interior. We would have realised ζ\zeta with fewer than NN states. Thus every matrix obtained from this polygon is irreducible.

Lower one eigenvalue and preserve the others

Let row ii be positive. We want to remove a small multiple of the stationary row πT\pi^T from this one row. Left multiplication of πT\pi^T by the coordinate column eie_i places it in row ii and puts zeros in all other rows. Choose 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 small enough that each difference aij−επja_{ij}-\varepsilon\pi_j stays positive. Write

B=A−εeiπT,r=1−επi∈(0,1).B=A-\varepsilon e_i\pi^T,\qquad r=1-\varepsilon\pi_i\in(0,1).

Multiplying on the left by πT\pi^T gives πTB=πTA−ε(πTei)πT=(1−επi)πT\pi^TB=\pi^TA-\varepsilon(\pi^Te_i)\pi^T=(1-\varepsilon\pi_i)\pi^T. The subtraction kept every arrow of the graph, so BB is irreducible. The positive left eigenvector πT\pi^T now identifies rr as its spectral radius. The Perron–Frobenius theorem gives a column hh with positive entries and Bh=rhBh=rh.

Calculate a normalisation when the row sums differ

Return to the three-state matrix in Lesson 1. Subtract πT/4\pi^T/4 from the first row only. In units of 1/121/12 the new matrix is

An interior image would give exactly that forbidden row

Let x=ζvix=\zeta v_i lie inside the polygon with vertices v1,…,vNv_1,\ldots,v_N. We want a representation of xx using every vertex. Their average g=(v1+⋯+vN)/Ng=(v_1+\cdots+v_N)/N already has that property. Starting at gg, draw the line to xx and continue a little beyond xx to a point ww. Since xx is interior, we can keep ww in the polygon. Thus xx lies on the segment from gg to ww. We can check the construction on the diamond with vertices 1,i,−1,−i1,i,-1,-i. Look for weights giving the interior point (1+i)/4(1+i)/4. Its real part is the weight at 11 minus the weight at −1-1, and its imaginary part is the corresponding difference at ii and −i-i. One choice is

Lesson 2: exchange points for side inequalities

We know where the images of vertices land. To use that conclusion for a side, we would like to represent the side by a point of another polygon. Identify ℂ\mathbb C with ℝ2\mathbb R^2 and use the dot product ⟨a,x⟩\langle a,x\rangle. If uu is an outward normal to a side, its supporting line has equation ⟨u,x⟩=c\langle u,x\rangle=c with c>0c>0, since zero lies strictly on the inner side of the line. Dividing uu by cc gives a point aa for which the side equation is ⟨a,x⟩=1\langle a,x\rangle=1 and all of PP satisfies ⟨a,x⟩≤1\langle a,x\rangle\le1.

Collect all points aa whose inequality holds throughout PP. We call the set of these points the polar polygon of PP and write

P∘={a:⟨a,x⟩≤1 for every x∈P}.P^\circ=\{a:\langle a,x\rangle\le1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.

Which map on the polar corresponds to TT? To check the inequality at the image TxTx, write ⟨a,Tx⟩=⟨T*a,x⟩\langle a,Tx\rangle=\langle T^*a,x\rangle. In real coordinates T*T^* is the transpose matrix. Multiplication by ζ\zeta rotates and scales, so its transpose rotates through the opposite angle and uses the same scale. Thus T*T^* multiplies by ζ‾\bar\zeta. We will use the following correspondences.

Choose a side with outward normal aia_i scaled as above. The two endpoints determine the vertex aia_i by equality in their conditions.
Ask whether TxTx lies on this side. Check whether T*aiT^*a_i satisfies ⟨T*ai,x⟩=1\langle T^*a_i,x\rangle=1.

For the diamond P={|x|+|y|≤1}P=\{|x|+|y|\le1\}, the four vertices impose −1≤ax≤1-1\le a_x\le1 and −1≤ay≤1-1\le a_y\le1. The polar is the square [−1,1]2[-1,1]^2. Take its corner a=(1,1)a=(1,1), which represents the side x+y=1x+y=1 of the diamond. For Tz=((1+i)/2)zTz=((1+i)/2)z, multiplication by (1−i)/2(1-i)/2 sends aa to (1,0)(1,0). This polar point satisfies the inequality for the original vertex x=(1,0)x=(1,0) with equality. Indeed Tx=(1/2,1/2)Tx=(1/2,1/2) lies on the chosen side. We have read the same contact in the two pictures.

It remains to justify the use of a vertex for each side. Start with the polar inequalities. A linear functional at any convex combination of vertices gives the same combination of its values there. Checking the vertices therefore suffices:

P∘={a:⟨a,vj⟩≤1(1≤j≤N)}. P^\circ=\{a:\langle a,v_j\rangle\le1\quad(1\le j\le N)\}.

This intersection of half-planes contains a neighbourhood of zero, since each of its finitely many inequalities is strict at zero. It is also bounded. Choose r>0r>0 such that PP contains the closed disk of radius rr about zero. For each a≠0a\ne0 in the polar, the disk contains x=ra/|a|x=ra/|a|. Its inequality reads r|a|≤1r|a|\le1, which bounds the distance of every polar point from zero.

Consider the side with endpoints vi−1,viv_{i-1},v_i and normal aia_i scaled to give ⟨ai,vi−1⟩=⟨ai,vi⟩=1\langle a_i,v_{i-1}\rangle=\langle a_i,v_i\rangle=1. The endpoints are linearly independent as vectors from zero. Otherwise the side line would pass through zero, an interior point. Hence these two equations determine aia_i uniquely. Could aia_i lie strictly between two other polar points? The dot product with either endpoint would then be an average of two numbers at most one. Its value is one, so both numbers would equal one. Both polar points would solve the same two equations and would coincide with aia_i. Thus aia_i is a vertex.

Conversely, a polar vertex has two linearly independent active inequalities, meaning inequalities attaining equality there. If the active endpoint vectors spanned at most one line, a small motion perpendicular to that line in both directions would keep all active equalities, and the finitely many strict inequalities would remain strict. The point would lie inside a polar segment and would not be a vertex. Two independent active original vertices lie on the supporting line ⟨a,x⟩=1\langle a,x\rangle=1; in a polygon they are the endpoints of one side. This identifies the polar vertex as its normal. The correspondence is therefore exact, and P∘P^\circ has NN vertices.

In the drawing, follow the endpoints (1,0)(1,0) and (0,1)(0,1) of the marked side into the polar picture. Their conditions become ax≤1a_x\le1 and ay≤1a_y\le1. The two boundary lines meet at (1,1)(1,1), so their intersection records precisely the side joining the two original endpoints.

Finally, take any a∈P∘a\in P^\circ and any x∈Px\in P. Since TxTx stays in PP, we have ⟨T*a,x⟩=⟨a,Tx⟩≤1\langle T^*a,x\rangle=\langle a,Tx\rangle\le1. This holds for every xx in PP, which is exactly the condition for T*aT^*a to belong to P∘P^\circ. Thus the polar is invariant under T*T^*.

The polar construction has changed the multiplier to ζ‾\bar\zeta. A smaller matrix realising ζ‾\bar\zeta would also realise ζ\zeta, since the matrix is real. The conjugate of any point farther out on this new ray would lie farther out on the original ray. Thus ζ‾\bar\zeta has the same least order NN and the same maximality property. Apply the vertex-contact result to P∘P^\circ: for each polar vertex aa, T*aT^*a is on its boundary. A polar point satisfying all NN vertex inequalities strictly has a whole small neighbourhood satisfying them, so it is interior. Thus at least one original vertex xx satisfies ⟨T*a,x⟩=1\langle T^*a,x\rangle=1. Equivalently TxTx lies on the original side ⟨a,Tx⟩=1\langle a,Tx\rangle=1. Every side meets TPTP.

Boundary averages use one face

A supporting functional takes its maximum on a boundary face. If a convex combination with all weights positive attains that maximum, each point given positive weight attains it. A single smaller value would lower the average. Thus a boundary average lies in one common face. In a polygon, it uses either one vertex or the two endpoints of one side. A relative-interior contact means an image strictly between those endpoints.

At an interior point we can assign a little weight to every vertex. On a side all positive weight goes to its endpoints. In the next chapter we count how often both endpoints receive a positive weight.

Perron deflation forces boundary contact

The boundary-contact argument rests on a rank-one eigenvalue shift due to Brauer [Brauer] and developed further by Goddard [Goddard]. Let AA be an irreducible stochastic matrix of order nn with stationary probability row vector πT\pi^T, and suppose every entry of row ii is positive. The boundary-contact conclusions go back to Dmitriev and Dynkin [DD], §§1–2. We prove them for every polygon with NN vertices invariant under multiplication by the fixed number ζ\zeta. The extremality of ζ\zeta means that NN is the smallest vertex count for which such a polygon exists, and no tζt\zeta with t>1t>1 has an invariant polygon with at most NN vertices. Lemma 2.1. Let AA be an irreducible row-stochastic matrix with stationary probability row vector πT\pi^T. We will use an elementary fact about faces. Suppose a convex combination with strictly positive weights lies on the boundary of a polytope, taken within its affine hull. A supporting linear functional attains its maximum at this combination. Since each point used has functional value at most that maximum, equality forces every point to attain it. Thus all points used lie in one common proper face. In particular, a boundary point of a polygon can use at most two vertices with positive weights in a convex combination, and if two are used, they are adjacent.

chapters.guideHtml:
Matching the images to the sides

Mark the NN vertices of PP on its boundary, then mark the NN images of these vertices in a second colour. Topic II puts all the second marks on the boundary and guarantees that each closed side contains one or more of them. Would it follow that each side has one image? An image at a corner already touches two sides. Counting it twice would leave too few images to describe the other side contacts.

We may choose our polygon. Fix the nonreal multiplier ζ\zeta at its largest modulus on its ray in ΘN\Theta_N, where N≥4N\ge4 is its least realising order and 0<|ζ|<10<|\zeta|<1. Write T(x)=ζxT(x)=\zeta x. Our aim is to put the two kinds of marks in alternating order, allowing a vertex and an image to coincide. We first choose an invariant NN-gon in which as many images as possible are already vertices. We then test what would happen if two consecutive image marks enclosed two old corners. Their joining chord gives us a smaller polygon to compare with the one we chose.

Count interior contacts before minimising area

Take a vertex vv in the vertex set VV of PP and ask whether its image TvTv is another vertex. To count the two possible answers, put

dT(P)=|{v∈V:Tv∈V}|,bT(P)=|V|−dT(P). d_T(P)=|\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}|,\qquad b_T(P)=|V|-d_T(P).

Here |V||V| is the number of vertices. The first count, dT(P)d_T(P), includes each starting vertex whose image is a vertex. Topic II puts every image on the boundary. Each of the remaining bT(P)b_T(P) starting vertices therefore has its image strictly between the endpoints of a side.

Scale the polygon about zero until max⁡x∈P|x|=1\max_{x\in P}|x|=1. Scaling preserves invariance and both counts. Among these normalised polygons, first minimise bT(P)b_T(P). Among polygons attaining this count choose one with the smallest area. The order matters. We will move vertices while controlling the count, and use area only when a replacement also preserves the chosen scale.

Halving every vertex coordinate divides the area by four and leaves every contact of the same kind. This explains why an area comparison needs a fixed radius. It also explains what sort of smaller polygon would lead to a contradiction. A cut that preserves both the radius and the smallest possible value of bTb_T gives a better choice of polygon. A cut that creates more images inside sides gives us no such comparison.

To see that we can make both choices, take a sequence of normalised polygons with the smallest contact count and areas tending to the infimum. All NN vertices lie in the closed unit disk. After taking a subsequence we may assume each vertex coordinate converges. The convex hull of the limits still contains zero and a point of modulus one. It is still invariant, since the inclusions TP⊆PTP\subseteq P pass to the limit. A segment through zero cannot contain its image under multiplication by the nonreal number ζ\zeta, so the limiting hull has interior. Fewer than NN vertices would contradict the choice of NN.

There are only finitely many possible pairs (i,j)(i,j) with Tvi=vjTv_i=v_j. Pass to a further subsequence on which the list of equalities is fixed. Each equality persists in the limit. Thus the number of images inside sides can only fall, and it was already as small as possible. Finally, polygon area is continuous in the cyclically ordered coordinates, so the limiting polygon attains the desired area.

We want to cut off part of PP and still have a polygon with the same multiplier and vertex count. Consider a choice of QQ for which

TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=|ext⁡P|,ext⁡Q⊆V∪TV. TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\operatorname{ext}Q|=|\operatorname{ext}P|, \qquad\operatorname{ext}Q\subseteq V\cup TV.

Each is an image of an old vertex.

On the other hand, each corner added by the cut is of the form TvTv and hence gives a possible endpoint. We count how many of these paths still have their starting vertex in QQ.

Write R=V\ext⁡QR=V\setminus\operatorname{ext}Q for the lost vertices and U=ext⁡Q\VU=\operatorname{ext}Q\setminus V for the new ones. The polygons have equally many vertices, so |U|=|R||U|=|R|. If QQ also keeps a vertex of modulus one, its scale is already correct. Any proper cut would now give the same count and a smaller area, contradicting our second choice.

If a cut removes all vertices with radius one, restoring the original scale increases its area. We then have no area comparison with PP. We use the area argument only for cuts that leave a radius-one vertex in place.

List the vertices of TPTP as y1,…,yNy_1,\ldots,y_N counterclockwise. Both yjy_j and yj+1y_{j+1} lie on the boundary of the outer polygon PP. Write (yj,yj+1](y_j,y_{j+1}] for the arc along that outer boundary from one to the next, excluding its starting point and including its ending point. Imagine walking counterclockwise through the corner viv_i. The side just completed is (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i], so it counts the corner. The next side starts there and excludes it. In this way a mark right at a corner contributes to one side, just as a point at a division between two half-open intervals contributes to one interval.

To count without duplication, let rjr_j be the number of old vertices on the arc with its end included, (yj,yj+1](y_j,y_{j+1}]. ∑jrj=N,kj=rj+εj,0≤rj≤2. \sum_j r_j=N,\qquad k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j,\qquad 0\le r_j\le2.

Multiplication by ζ\zeta preserves cyclic order. Once we know which side receives the first image, each succeeding image belongs to the succeeding side. The assignment is a constant cyclic shift. For some 1≤κ<N1\le\kappa<N,

Counting vertex images

The least realizing order fixes the number of vertices. To control vertex replacement, we also count how many vertex images are not vertices. For an injective linear map TT and a polytope PP with TP⊆PTP\subseteq P and vertex set VV, define dT(P)=|{v∈V:Tv∈V}|,bT(P)=|V|−dT(P).d_T(P)=|\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}|,\qquad b_T(P)=|V|-d_T(P). Thus dT(P)d_T(P) counts vertices mapped to vertices, and bT(P)b_T(P) counts the remaining vertices. In the polygon setting just proved, every image lies on the boundary, so bT(P)b_T(P) counts the images strictly inside sides. The following theorem gives conditions under which replacing vertices cannot increase this count.

Theorem 2.3. In any dimension, let TT be an injective linear map and let P,QP,Q be polytopes satisfying TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=|ext⁡P|,ext⁡Q⊆ext⁡P∪Text⁡P.TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q|=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P|,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cup T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Then TQ⊆QTQ\subseteq Q and bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P).

Proof of Theorem 2.3

Proof. Since Q⊆PQ\subseteq P, we have TQ⊆TP⊆QTQ\subseteq TP\subseteq Q, so QQ is invariant. Write V=ext⁡PV=\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P and W=ext⁡QW=\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q. Let R=V\W,U=W\VR=V\setminus W,\qquad U=W\setminus V be the removed and new vertices. Equal vertex counts give |R|=|U||R|=|U|. Put E={v∈V:Tv∈V},E=\{v\in V:Tv\in V\}, so |E|=dT(P)|E|=d_T(P).

An old vertex lying in QQ remains a vertex of QQ: a nontrivial convex decomposition within QQ would also be one within PP. Since TV⊆QTV\subseteq Q, no removed vertex belongs to TVTV. Thus R∩TV=⌀R\cap TV=\varnothing, and each vertex in E\RE\setminus R still maps to a vertex of QQ.

Every new vertex belongs to TVTV. By injectivity, its preimage is a unique vertex of PP. Therefore S=T−1U⊆V,|S|=|U|=|R|.S=T^{-1}U\subseteq V,\qquad |S|=|U|=|R|. Also S∩E=⌀S\cap E=\varnothing, since vertices in SS map to new vertices rather than old ones. Each retained vertex in S\RS\setminus R maps to a vertex in UU and is therefore also counted by dT(Q)d_T(Q). Consequently, dT(Q)≥|E\R|+|S\R|=|E|+|R|−|E∩R|−|S∩R|≥|E|.d_T(Q)\ge |E\setminus R|+|S\setminus R| =|E|+|R|-|E\cap R|-|S\cap R| \ge |E|. The last inequality follows because E∩RE\cap R and S∩RS\cap R are disjoint subsets of RR. Since PP and QQ have equally many vertices, this gives bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P). ◻

We now return to Tz=ζzTz=\zeta z and the invariant NN-gons in (2.2). Fix their scale by requiring maxx∈P|x|=1.\max_{x\in P}|x|=1. Since TT is linear, scaling about zero preserves invariance and the vertex count. The normalized class is compact. Indeed, from any sequence of these polygons, choose a subsequence along which all NN vertex coordinates converge in the closed unit disk. Their limiting convex hull remains invariant, contains zero, and has maximum modulus one. The last two properties exclude a single point. Nonreality of ζ\zeta excludes a segment, and minimality of NN excludes a polygon with fewer vertices. Thus all NN limiting points are distinct vertices, and the limit belongs to the same normalized class.

Throughout this section, choose a normalized polygon PP by first minimizing bT(P)b_T(P) and then minimizing area among the polygons attaining that count. Such a choice exists. Any equality Tvi=vjTv_i=v_j that holds throughout a convergent sequence of vertex coordinates also holds at the limit; additional equalities may appear. Consequently, a limit of polygons minimizing bTb_T still minimizes bTb_T. These minimizers form a closed subset of the compact normalized class, and continuity of area gives an area minimizer among them. Scaling changes neither dTd_T nor bTb_T, so the chosen PP also minimizes bTb_T among all invariant NN-gons, without fixing their scale.

The two minimization conditions have separate uses. Suppose a polytope QQ satisfies TP⊆Q⊆P,|ext⁡Q|=N,ext⁡Q⊆ext⁡P∪Text⁡P.TP\subseteq Q\subseteq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q|=N,\qquad \mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q\subseteq\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cup T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Theorem 2.3 gives bT(Q)≤bT(P)b_T(Q)\le b_T(P). Since PP already minimizes this count, equality follows. If QQ also contains a vertex of PP with modulus one, it is normalized. A proper inclusion Q⊊PQ\subsetneq P would then give smaller area with the same minimum count, contradicting the choice of PP. Thus such a QQ must equal PP. The later vertex replacements need only to preserve the minimum of bTb_T.

Assigning vertex images to sides

Write [a,b]∂P[a,b]_{\partial P} for the boundary arc from aa to bb in the counterclockwise (positive) direction; parentheses indicate excluded endpoints. The half-open sides (vi−1,vi](v_{i-1},v_i] partition the boundary: each includes its ending vertex and excludes its starting vertex. Our goal is to arrange that each contains exactly one vertex of TPTP. A contact at a vertex belongs to two closed sides, and this convention assigns it to just one. If necessary, we will reflect PP in the real axis and replace ζ\zeta by ζ‾\bar\zeta to obtain the required assignment.

List the vertices y1,…,yNy_1,\ldots,y_N of TPTP counterclockwise, with indices taken modulo NN. The boundary-contact theorem puts them on ∂P\partial P and ensures that every side of PP meets TPTP. For each image edge [yj,yj+1][y_j,y_{j+1}], let QjQ_j be the intersection of PP with the closed half-plane bounded by the line through its endpoints and containing TPTP. Define kj=|ext⁡P∩[yj,yj+1]∂P|.k_j=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap[y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}|. Thus kjk_j counts the vertices of PP on this boundary arc, including any at its endpoints.

If Qj≠PQ_j\ne P, the cutting line crosses the interior of PP. Its two boundary intersections are yj,yj+1y_j,y_{j+1}, and it discards the counterclockwise open arc between them. Counting the old vertices on the closed arc and adding back the two endpoints gives TP⊆Qj⊊P,|ext⁡Qj|≤N+2−kj.TP\subseteq Q_j\subsetneq P,\qquad |\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}Q_j|\le N+2-k_j. Since TQj⊆TP⊆QjTQ_j\subseteq TP\subseteq Q_j, the cut polygon is invariant and must have at least NN vertices. Hence kj≤2k_j\le2. If kj=2k_j=2, it has exactly NN vertices, and every new vertex is one of the endpoints yj,yj+1∈Text⁡Py_j,y_{j+1}\in T\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. Theorem 2.3 therefore gives bT(Qj)=bT(P)b_T(Q_j)=b_T(P), since PP minimizes this count.

Choose a vertex v*v_* of PP with |v*|=1|v_*|=1. Since |yj|≤ρ<1|y_j|\le\rho<1, this vertex is not one of the yjy_j and lies in exactly one open boundary arc (yj,yj+1)∂P(y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P}. Any proper cut with kj=2k_j=2 must remove v*v_*. Otherwise, QjQ_j would still be normalized and minimize bTb_T, but have smaller area than PP, contradicting its choice. The arcs discarded by different cuts are disjoint, so at most one proper cut has kj=2k_j=2. If Qj=PQ_j=P, the image-edge line supports PP and the arc lies along one side. Its half-open part (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P} therefore contains at most one vertex of PP.

To count vertices with the ending endpoint included and the starting endpoint excluded, define rj=|ext⁡P∩(yj,yj+1]∂P|,εj={1,yj∈ext⁡P,0,yj∉ext⁡P.r_j=|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}|, \qquad \varepsilon_j= \begin{cases} 1,&y_j\in\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P,\\ 0,&y_j\notin\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P. \end{cases} The half-open arcs partition ∂P\partial P, so they count each vertex of PP exactly once. Also, adding the starting endpoint recovers the closed-arc count. Thus ∑jrj=N,kj=rj+εj,0≤rj≤2.\sum_j r_j=N,\qquad k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j,\qquad 0\le r_j\le2. If rj=2r_j=2, the cut must be proper, since an uncut arc contains at most one vertex in its half-open part. It then has kj=2k_j=2, so at most one rjr_j can equal two. Since there are NN arcs and their counts sum to NN, either every rj=1r_j=1, or there are unique indices s,ts,t such that rs=2,rt=0,rj=1(j∉{s,t}).r_s=2,\qquad r_t=0,\qquad r_j=1\quad(j\notin\{s,t\}).

Now suppose rs=2r_s=2 and rt=0r_t=0. Since ks=rs+εs≤2k_s=r_s+\varepsilon_s\le2, we have εs=0\varepsilon_s=0: ysy_s is not a vertex of PP. We claim that εs+1=1\varepsilon_{s+1}=1, so ys+1y_{s+1} is a vertex. Otherwise, the two vertices counted by rsr_s would both lie strictly inside the arc (ys,ys+1)∂P(y_s,y_{s+1})_{\partial P}. They are consecutive vertices of PP, and their joining side contains no vertex of TPTP.

But every side of PP meets TPTP. A linear functional defining this side would therefore attain its maximum over TPTP at a vertex of TPTP, placing an image vertex on the side, a contradiction. Thus εs=0\varepsilon_s=0 and εs+1=1\varepsilon_{s+1}=1: as the indices run around the polygon, the sequence (εj)(\varepsilon_j) changes from zero to one at ss.

We next show that any change from one to zero must occur at tt. Suppose εj=1\varepsilon_j=1 and εj+1=0\varepsilon_{j+1}=0 with j≠tj\ne t. Since εs=0\varepsilon_s=0, we also have j≠sj\ne s. Hence rj=1r_j=1 and kj=rj+εj=2k_j=r_j+\varepsilon_j=2.

This cut must be proper. If Qj=PQ_j=P, the arc would start at the vertex yjy_j and end at yj+1y_{j+1} inside the same side, before that side’s ending vertex. Excluding yjy_j would leave no vertex in (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P}, giving rj=0r_j=0, a contradiction. Thus Qj≠PQ_j\ne P. We would then have two distinct proper cuts, QjQ_j and QsQ_s, with kj=ks=2k_j=k_s=2, contradicting the fact that at most one proper cut has count two.

In a sequence of zeros and ones read cyclically, every change from zero to one is matched by a change back to zero. Since a change from one to zero can occur only at tt, there is exactly one change in each direction: from zero to one at ss, and from one to zero at tt. Now include the starting endpoint of each arc and exclude its ending endpoint. This adds εj\varepsilon_j to the count and subtracts εj+1\varepsilon_{j+1}, giving |ext⁡P∩[yj,yj+1)∂P|=rj+εj−εj+1=1for every j.|\mathop{\mathrm{ext}}P\cap[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P}| =r_j+\varepsilon_j-\varepsilon_{j+1}=1 \quad\text{for every }j.

Thus either every arc (yj,yj+1]∂P(y_j,y_{j+1}]_{\partial P} contains exactly one vertex of PP, or every arc [yj,yj+1)∂P[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P} does. In either case, call this vertex uju_j; the vertices uju_j occur in positive cyclic order. In the second case, the arc [yj,yj+1)∂P[y_j,y_{j+1})_{\partial P} contains uju_j, so yj∈(uj−1,uj].y_j\in(u_{j-1},u_j]. Each side, with its starting vertex excluded and its ending vertex included, therefore contains exactly one image vertex.

In the first case, we instead have yj+1∈[uj,uj+1)y_{j+1}\in[u_j,u_{j+1}). Reflect PP across the real axis, replacing PP by P¯\overline P and ζ\zeta by ζ¯\overline\zeta, and list the reflected vertices in positive cyclic order. Reflection reverses cyclic order, so each assigned side now excludes its starting vertex and includes its ending vertex. It preserves the extremality hypotheses (2.2), the count bTb_T, normalization, and area. We continue to write P,ζP,\zeta for the resulting polygon and complex number. The map Tz=ζzTz=\zeta z scales distances from the origin by |ζ||\zeta| and rotates by arg⁡ζ\arg\zeta.

Multiplication by ζ\zeta preserves cyclic order, so the assignment of image vertices to sides shifts every index by the same amount. chapters.guideHtml:
Move a vertex without changing the eigenvalue

At a side with an interior contact, an orbit that has so far followed vertices reaches a genuine average of two different vertices. We would like all these transitions to occur on one run of consecutive sides. The polygon chosen in Topic III gives us some freedom to arrange this. It minimises the number of images in open sides, then minimises area after scaling its largest vertex radius to one.

Write the contact on the side ending at viv_i as

ζvi−κ=ci=βivi−1+αivi,αi=1−βi>0. \zeta v_{i-\kappa}=c_i=\beta_i v_{i-1}+\alpha_i v_i, \qquad \alpha_i=1-\beta_i>0.

Suppose this contact is inside its side and the next contact is a vertex, so βi>0\beta_i>0 and βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0. Try replacing the corner viv_i by cic_i. The smaller polygon has retained the image that previously landed on this side. But the moved corner has its own image under ζ\zeta. Where does that image go? We will calculate it by changing one coordinate of the eigenvector. This gives a stochastic matrix for the smaller polygon and tells us exactly which contact has moved.

Consider the eight-state indices from Topic III, with shift κ=3\kappa=3. Suppose only sides 1 and 2 receive images between their endpoints, as in the worked octagon. Move v2v_2 to v2′=c2=β2v1+α2v2v'_2=c_2=\beta_2v_1+\alpha_2v_2. Two images explain what this move does. First, ζv7=c2=v2′\zeta v_7=c_2=v'_2, so the old contact on side 2 becomes a corner. Next, by linearity, ζv2′=β2ζv1+α2ζv2=β2v4+α2v5. \zeta v'_2=\beta_2\zeta v_1+\alpha_2\zeta v_2 =\beta_2 v_4+\alpha_2 v_5. The last equality uses the fact that sides 4 and 5 each received an image at their ending corner. Both those corners stay fixed. Hence the moved vertex now lands between v4v_4 and v5v_5. We have transferred the contact from side 2 to side 5, three places ahead. The matrix calculation explains why a transfer works at the end of any run.

Reversing stochastic factors

Taking an average of averages still gives an average of the original entries. In matrix language, if HH and SS are stochastic, then HSHS has nonnegative entries and (HS)𝟏=H(S𝟏)=H𝟏=𝟏(HS)\mathbf1=H(S\mathbf1)=H\mathbf1=\mathbf1. We can take the averages in the reverse order and reach the same conclusion about the row sums of SHSH.

The two orders generally give different matrices. But suppose that A=HSA=HS and that SS is invertible. Multiplying AA on the left by SS and on the right by S−1S^{-1} gives

A′=SH=SAS−1. A'=SH=SAS^{-1}.

Start with Av=ζvAv=\zeta v, where v=(v1,…,vN)Tv=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)^T lists the polygon vertices. Multiplication by SS gives A′(Sv)=SAv=ζ(Sv)A'(Sv)=SAv=\zeta(Sv). Thus the entries of SvSv give a new list of complex coordinates for the same multiplier. We will choose SS so that just the coordinate viv_i changes.

We need both properties of the factors here. Stochasticity lets us read the rows of A′A' as convex combinations. Invertibility makes A′A' similar to AA, and ensures that SvSv is still an eigenvector. Together they let us move a corner and continue to use ζ\zeta.

To move viv_i towards vi−1v_{i-1}, first consider the matrix EiE_i which replaces coordinate ii by coordinate i−1i-1 and leaves all the others fixed. A second application copies exactly the same entry, giving Ei2=EiE_i^2=E_i. We can move part of the way by averaging this operation with the identity. For 0≤t<10\le t<1 set

Si(t)=(1−t)I+tEi,Si(t)−1=I−tEi1−t, S_i(t)=(1-t)I+tE_i,\qquad S_i(t)^{-1}=\frac{I-tE_i}{1-t},

where II denotes the identity. Multiplying the proposed inverse by Si(t)S_i(t) and using Ei2=EiE_i^2=E_i gives II. The new iith coordinate of the vertex list is (1−t)vi+tvi−1(1-t)v_i+tv_{i-1}. We reach cic_i by choosing t=βit=\beta_i.

There are two operations in each contact equation. One takes an average of neighbouring coordinates, and one shifts the index by κ\kappa. To write them as matrices, put

(Cx)r=xr+1,(Bx)j=βjxj−1+αjxj. (Cx)_r=x_{r+1},\qquad(Bx)_j=\beta_jx_{j-1}+\alpha_jx_j.

For an arbitrary column xx with NN entries, CC reads the next coordinate and row jj of BB averages the two endpoints of side jj. In particular (CκBv)r=cr+κ=ζvr(C^\kappa Bv)_r=c_{r+\kappa}=\zeta v_r, so A=CκBA=C^\kappa B realises our multiplier. To separate the desired factor Si(βi)S_i(\beta_i) from BB, first replace row ii of BB by the row that returns xix_i unchanged. Call this matrix B̂\widehat B. We claim that

B=B̂Si(βi),H=CκB̂. B=\widehat B S_i(\beta_i),\qquad H=C^\kappa\widehat B.

To check the first identity, apply B̂Si(βi)\widehat B S_i(\beta_i) to a column xx, starting with Si(βi)xS_i(\beta_i)x. Its iith coordinate is already the average wanted in row ii of BB, and B̂\widehat B copies this entry. Row i+1i+1 is the only other row that could read the modified coordinate. Its weight on that coordinate is βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0. This verifies the factorisation and explains why we chose the end of a run.

We can now reverse the factors in A=HSi(βi)A=H S_i(\beta_i). The rows of the new stochastic matrix express every ζvj′\zeta v'_j as a convex combination of the entries of v′=Si(βi)vv'=S_i(\beta_i)v. Their hull P′P' is therefore invariant. There are NN entries and a polygon realising ζ\zeta needs at least NN vertices. Thus all NN are vertices of P′P', and the contact theorem of Topic II puts every one of their images on the boundary of P′P'.

The new corners remain in cyclic order, since viv_i moved along the preceding side. We can use the same side labels to count the contacts again.

The contact theorem controls the changed row

Put j=i+κj=i+\kappa and t=βit=\beta_i. Before reversing the factors we copied coordinate ii in B̂\widehat B. Moving Si(t)S_i(t) through the cyclic shift moves its row index from ii to jj. Indeed Si(t)Cκ=CκSj(t)S_i(t)C^\kappa=C^\kappa S_j(t). The new averaging rows therefore come from Sj(t)B̂S_j(t)\widehat B. Row jj now takes a fraction tt of the preceding row of B̂\widehat B and a fraction 1−t1-t of its own. Apply it to the new vertex list v′v'. The three possible terms are

tβ̂j−1vj−2′+(tα̂j−1+(1−t)βj)vj−1′+(1−t)αjvj′. t\widehat\beta_{j-1}v'_{j-2} +\bigl(t\widehat\alpha_{j-1}+(1-t)\beta_j\bigr)v'_{j-1} +(1-t)\alpha_jv'_j .

A hat denotes the coefficient after replacing row ii by a copying row. Since 0<t<10<t<1 and all endpoint coefficients α̂\widehat\alpha are positive, the last two vertices occur with positive weights. The sum is a boundary point by Topic II. A supporting functional reaches its maximum at this point, so each vertex with positive weight belongs to the same supporting line. The last two vertices already determine the side. Its line excludes vj−2′v'_{j-2}, so the first coefficient is zero. We can now read off the coefficient at the ending vertex, (1−t)αj=αiαj(1-t)\alpha_j=\alpha_i\alpha_j.

Only sides ii and i+κi+\kappa can have changed their coefficients. On side ii the image is now the ending vertex. On side i+κi+\kappa the weight at the ending vertex has been multiplied by αi\alpha_i. The complete update is

αi′=1,αi+κ′=αiαi+κ,αj′=αj at every other index. \alpha_i'=1,\qquad\alpha_{i+\kappa}'=\alpha_i\alpha_{i+\kappa}, \qquad\alpha_j'=\alpha_j\text{ at every other index}.

We want to follow that product through several moves. Let wj=−log⁡αjw_j=-\log\alpha_j. Since 0<αj≤10<\alpha_j\le1, this number is nonnegative, and it vanishes precisely when the image is the ending vertex. Taking logarithms gives

wi′=0,wi+κ′=wi+wi+κ. w_i'=0,\qquad w_{i+\kappa}'=w_i+w_{i+\kappa}.

For a permitted transfer in the selected polygon, take αi=1/2\alpha_i=1/2 and αi+κ=1\alpha_{i+\kappa}=1. Their new values are 11 and 1/21/2: the positive weight log⁡2\log2 moves from ii to i+κi+\kappa, while the number of positive weights stays the same. Could the target already carry positive weight? If instead αi+κ=3/4\alpha_{i+\kappa}=3/4, the new coefficient would be 3/83/8, with weight −log⁡(3/8)=−log⁡(1/2)−log⁡(3/4)-\log(3/8)=-\log(1/2)-\log(3/4). Two positive weights would merge into one, reducing the minimum contact count. Thus every permitted move in the selected polygon has a target that previously had weight zero.

Why all interior contacts form one run

Mark the indices I={i:wi>0}I=\{i:w_i>0\} and write φ=|I|\varphi=|I|. These marks are precisely the sides whose contacts lie in their interiors. If every index is marked, they already make one run around the polygon. Otherwise the final index ii of each run is marked and i+1i+1 is unmarked. At such an index the move just proved replaces a corner by a point strictly inside the preceding side. The smaller polygon still has the smallest possible count of interior contacts.

Take a vertex of modulus one in our chosen polygon. Any move at a different vertex would leave it in place. We would then have produced a smaller area at the same scale and with the same count, which is impossible. The move at a run ending removes viv_i and replaces it by cic_i of modulus at most ρ<1\rho<1. Thus the ending vertex of each run has to be the only vertex of modulus one. There can be just one such ending. Starting our numbering at the beginning of its run gives

I={1,…,φ}. I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}.

We tested each possible move on the polygon originally chosen to have smallest area. This is why we could compare the areas separately at the ends of two putative runs. For the sequence of moves below we use a different consequence which survives every move. The number of interior contacts is still the smallest possible, so a positive weight always moves to an unoccupied index.

After a transfer, a rescaling may be needed to put a vertex back at radius one. Rescaling has no effect on the number of interior contacts, so the next transfer still cannot merge two positive weights.

Let δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa), the greatest common divisor. Adding κ\kappa modulo NN runs through each residue class modulo δ\delta separately. Every class meets II, or it would consist entirely of vertex-to-vertex contacts and would give v=ζN/δvv=\zeta^{N/\delta}v. Hence φ≥δ\varphi\ge\delta.

A record in the cyclic shift

Write [a]N[a]_N for the remainder in {0,…,N−1}\{0,\ldots,N-1\} after dividing aa by NN. Suppose φ<N\varphi<N. For this calculation only, label the end of the run 00, so its other indices are N−φ+1,…,N−1N-\varphi+1,\ldots,N-1. Leave those other weights in place and move the one initially at 00. Its label after tt moves is [tκ]N[t\kappa]_N. As long as it is below N−φN-\varphi, the next label in ordinary order is empty. We can therefore make another move of κ\kappa places.

Consider the last φ\varphi labels, from N−φN-\varphi through N−1N-1. Since φ≥δ\varphi\ge\delta, at least one of these labels is a multiple of δ\delta. Repeatedly adding κ\kappa from zero visits every such multiple modulo NN, so the moving weight eventually reaches this block. All its labels except N−φN-\varphi already carry a weight. Two weights cannot merge, so the first label we reach in the block is N−φN-\varphi. Calling that first time hh, we have

[hκ]N=N−φ,[tκ]N<N−φ(0≤t<h). [h\kappa]_N=N-\varphi,\qquad[t\kappa]_N<N-\varphi\quad(0\le t<h).

Try this walk with N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3 and two positive weights. In the temporary labelling they occupy 77 and 00. The weight at 00 may move because label 11 is empty. It lands on 33. Its neighbour 44 is empty too, so it moves again, arriving at 66. This time its neighbour is the occupied label 77. The walk stops. The residues visited were 0,3,60,3,6, and 8−6=28-6=2 recovers the number of occupied sides. Topic V will read the same three integers as information about return times.

At time hh the remainder first reaches N−φN-\varphi. Every earlier remainder was smaller, which is what makes this value a record. Its distance from NN tells us exactly how many interior contacts there are. When all NN weights are positive, the initial value 00 already has the required distance NN and we take h=0h=0. In Topic V we use the times of these records to calculate how many steps separate successive visits to the marked sides.

The local operation and the global normal form

We modify the polygon by reversing the order of two matrix factors. Suppose A=HSA=HS, where H,SH,S are row-stochastic and SS is invertible. Then A′=SH=SAS−1A'=SH=SAS^{-1} is also row-stochastic and has the same eigenvalues as AA, because the matrices are similar. For the vertex list v=(v1,…,vN)Tv=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)^T, this turns Av=ζvAv=\zeta v into A′(Sv)=ζ(Sv)A'(Sv)=\zeta(Sv). We will choose SS so that SvSv replaces one vertex viv_i by a point on the preceding side [vi−1,vi][v_{i-1},v_i] and leaves the other vertices fixed.

To write the contact identities in matrix form, define CC and B(β)B(\beta) by their action on a column vector xx: (Cx)r=xr+1,(B(β)x)i=βixi−1+αixi,(Cx)_r=x_{r+1},\qquad (B(\beta)x)_i=\beta_i x_{i-1}+\alpha_i x_i, with indices modulo NN. Thus CC shifts the coordinates by one place, while row ii of B(β)B(\beta) uses the two endpoints of side ii. Both matrices are row-stochastic. Equation (2.3) becomes A=CκB(β),Av=ζv.A=C^\kappa B(\beta),\qquad Av=\zeta v. For the vertex replacement, define EiE_i by (Eix)r={xi−1,r=i,xr,r≠i.(E_i x)_r= \begin{cases} x_{i-1},&r=i,\\ x_r,&r\ne i. \end{cases} It copies coordinate i−1i-1 into coordinate ii and leaves all others fixed, so Ei2=EiE_i^2=E_i. Set Si(t)=(1−t)I+tEiS_i(t)=(1-t)I+tE_i. For 0≤t<10\le t<1, this matrix is row-stochastic and invertible, and Si(t)vS_i(t)v replaces viv_i by (1−t)vi+tvi−1(1-t)v_i+t v_{i-1}, leaving all other vertices fixed.

Since 0<αi≤10<\alpha_i\le1, the quantities wi=−log⁡αiw_i=-\log\alpha_i are nonnegative. The following lemma sets αi′=1\alpha_i'=1 and replaces αi+κ\alpha_{i+\kappa} by αiαi+κ\alpha_i\alpha_{i+\kappa}. In terms of these weights, this is wi′=0,wi+κ′=wi+wi+κ.w_i'=0,\qquad w_{i+\kappa}'=w_i+w_{i+\kappa}. Thus the weight at index ii is removed and added to the weight at index i+κi+\kappa, modulo NN. Reversing the matrix factors preserves stochasticity and the eigenvalue ζ\zeta. The boundary-contact property then forces the vertices used by each changed row to lie on a single polygon side.

Lemma 2.4. Assume βi=t>0\beta_i=t>0 and βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0. Set vi′=civ_i'=c_i and vj′=vjv_j'=v_j for j≠ij\ne i. The polygon P′=conv⁡{v1′,…,vN′}P'=\operatorname{conv}\{v_1',\ldots,v_N'\} has NN vertices and satisfies ζP′⊆P′\zeta P'\subseteq P'. Every image vertex lies on ∂P′\partial P', and every side of P′P' meets ζP′\zeta P'. The images ζvj−κ′\zeta v_{j-\kappa}' lie on the sides (vj−1′,vj′](v_{j-1}',v_j'], with new coefficients satisfying (2.5)αi′=1,αi+κ′=αiαi+κ,αj′=αj(j∉{i,i+κ}).\alpha_i'=1,\qquad \alpha_{i+\kappa}'=\alpha_i\alpha_{i+\kappa}, \qquad \alpha_j'=\alpha_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+\kappa\}). The matrices CκB(β′)C^\kappa B(\beta') and CκB(β)C^\kappa B(\beta) are similar, where βj′=1−αj′\beta_j'=1-\alpha_j'.

Proof of Lemma 2.4

Proof. Since t=βit=\beta_i and αi=1−βi>0\alpha_i=1-\beta_i>0, we have 0<t<10<t<1. Let B̂\widehat B be B(β)B(\beta) with row ii replaced by the row that copies coordinate ii. Thus β̂i=0\widehat\beta_i=0, α̂i=1\widehat\alpha_i=1, and all other coefficients are unchanged. Set S=Si(t)S=S_i(t) and H=CκB̂H=C^\kappa\widehat B. Multiplying B̂\widehat B on the right by SS restores row ii of BB. The only other row that could change is row i+1i+1, but βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0. Hence B=B̂S,A=HS,A′=SH=SAS−1.B=\widehat B S,\qquad A=HS,\qquad A'=SH=SAS^{-1}. The matrices H,SH,S are row-stochastic, and S−1=(I−tEi)/(1−t)S^{-1}=(I-tE_i)/(1-t). Thus v′=Svv'=Sv satisfies A′v′=ζv′A'v'=\zeta v', with vi′=civ_i'=c_i and all other vertices fixed. Row-stochasticity gives ζP′⊆P′\zeta P'\subseteq P'. The polygon P′P' has at most NN vertices, so minimality of NN forces it to have exactly NN. These vertices retain their cyclic order, since viv_i moves into the side [vi−1,vi][v_{i-1},v_i]. The boundary-contact property established above applies to P′P'.

Put j=i+κj=i+\kappa, with indices modulo NN. Since 1≤κ<N1\le\kappa<N, we have j≠ij\ne i. The identity Si(t)Cκ=CκSj(t)S_i(t)C^\kappa=C^\kappa S_j(t) gives A′=CκB′,B′=Sj(t)B̂.A'=C^\kappa B',\qquad B'=S_j(t)\widehat B. Only row jj of B̂\widehat B changes. Its action on a vector xx is (B′x)j=tβ̂j−1xj−2+(tα̂j−1+(1−t)βj)xj−1+(1−t)αjxj.(B'x)_j=t\widehat\beta_{j-1}x_{j-2} +\bigl(t\widehat\alpha_{j-1}+(1-t)\beta_j\bigr)x_{j-1} +(1-t)\alpha_j x_j. The coefficients of xj−1x_{j-1} and xjx_j are positive, since 0<t<10<t<1 and every α̂\widehat\alpha is positive. Applying this row to v′v' expresses the boundary point ζvj−κ′\zeta v'_{j-\kappa} as a convex combination of vertices of P′P'. By the face rule, all vertices with positive coefficients must lie on one side. The vertices vj−1′,vj′v'_{j-1},v'_j already determine that side, so the coefficient of vj−2′v'_{j-2} must vanish: a third vertex cannot lie on it. These three vertices are distinct because N≥3N\ge3. Therefore β̂j−1=0\widehat\beta_{j-1}=0. This includes the case j−1=ij-1=i, where that coefficient is zero by definition.

Row jj now uses only coordinates j−1,jj-1,j, and its coefficient at jj is (1−t)αj=αiαj(1-t)\alpha_j=\alpha_i\alpha_j. Row ii still has coefficient one at ii, and every other row is unchanged from BB. This proves (2.5) and identifies B′=B(β′)B'=B(\beta'). In every row, the coefficient at the ending vertex of the assigned side remains positive. Thus the images retain the same half-open side assignment and shift κ\kappa. Similarity of the corresponding matrices was established above. ◻

Let I={i:wi>0}={i:βi>0}.I=\{i:w_i>0\}=\{i:\beta_i>0\}. These are the indices whose image vertices lie inside their assigned sides, so |I|=bT(P)|I|=b_T(P). The lemma changes this set to (I\{i})∪{i+κ}(I\setminus\{i\})\cup\{i+\kappa\}. If i+κi+\kappa already belonged to II, two positive weights would combine at one index, decreasing bTb_T by one. This contradicts the choice of PP with minimum bTb_T. The next proposition uses the minimum-area condition to show that II consists of consecutive indices around the polygon.

Proposition 2.5. Let [r]N[r]_N denote the residue of rr in {0,…,N−1}\{0,\ldots,N-1\}. By choosing the starting vertex in the cyclic labelling, we can arrange I={1,…,φ},φ=|I|≥δ:=gcd⁡(N,κ).I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\},\qquad \varphi=|I|\ge\delta:=\gcd(N,\kappa). If φ<N\varphi<N, there is an integer h>0h>0 such that (2.6)[hκ]N=N−φ,[tκ]N<N−φ(0≤t<h).[h\kappa]_N=N-\varphi, \qquad [t\kappa]_N<N-\varphi\quad(0\le t<h). Thus [hκ]N[h\kappa]_N is a strict record: it exceeds every earlier residue. Its distance from NN is φ\varphi. For φ=N\varphi=N, take h=0h=0, whose residue is zero and whose distance from NN is NN.

Proof of Proposition 2.5

Proof. Repeatedly adding κ\kappa modulo NN visits all N/δN/\delta indices in one residue class modulo δ\delta. Each such class must meet II. Otherwise, all its contact coefficients βj\beta_j would be zero, so the identities ζvr=vr+κ\zeta v_r=v_{r+\kappa} would give vr=ζN/δvrv_r=\zeta^{N/\delta}v_r. This contradicts vr≠0v_r\ne0 and |ζ|<1|\zeta|<1. There are δ\delta classes, so |I|≥δ|I|\ge\delta.

If II contains every index, the proposition follows with φ=N\varphi=N and h=0h=0. Otherwise, consider the ending index ii of any maximal run of consecutive indices in II: i∈Ii\in I but i+1∉Ii+1\notin I. Then βi>0\beta_i>0 and βi+1=0\beta_{i+1}=0, so Lemma 2.4 applies. It replaces viv_i by cic_i, strictly inside the preceding side, and gives a proper subpolygon. Its count bTb_T cannot increase by the update formula, and cannot decrease by minimality. If necessary, rescaling restores normalization without changing this count.

Apply this replacement separately at each run’s ending index in the original polygon PP. Since |ci|≤ρ<1|c_i|\le\rho<1, any modulus-one vertex other than viv_i would remain. The new polygon would then still be normalized and minimize bTb_T, but have smaller area, contradicting the choice of PP. Thus each run’s ending vertex would have to be the unique modulus-one vertex. There can therefore be only one run. Choosing its first index as 11 gives I={1,…,φ}I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}.

To prove the record assertion, assume φ<N\varphi<N and temporarily label this run as F∪{0}F\cup\{0\}, where F={N−φ+1,…,N−1}F=\{N-\varphi+1,\ldots,N-1\}. The indices in FF carry the other positive weights wjw_j, which remain unchanged while the weight initially at index 00 is moved. Since at<N−φa_t<N-\varphi, the next index at+1a_t+1 is not in this set, so the lemma applies at ata_t. It moves the weight to at+1a_{t+1} and leaves the weights at FF fixed. If at+1∈Fa_{t+1}\in F, two positive weights would combine, decreasing bTb_T by one and contradicting minimality. Otherwise, the new positive-weight set is F∪{at+1}F\cup\{a_{t+1}\}. These later polygons need only to preserve the minimum of bTb_T; they need not minimize area.

At the first entrance into {N−φ,…,N−1}\{N-\varphi,\ldots,N-1\}, every index except N−φN-\varphi belongs to FF and is therefore forbidden. Hence ah=N−φa_h=N-\varphi, while at<N−φa_t<N-\varphi for every t<ht<h. This proves the claimed record inequalities. Returning to the original cyclic labelling does not change these displacements by multiples of κ\kappa. ◻
