Turn the contact pattern into return paths

At a vertex vjv_j there are two possibilities for the next iterate. The contact on side j+κj+\kappa either equals the vertex vj+κv_{j+\kappa} or lies between the endpoints of that side. Topic IV arranged the sides of the second kind in one block, I={1,…,φ}I=\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}. All indices on the polygon are read modulo NN.

Choose a vertex whose index belongs to II and call it a base. Add κ\kappa to its index until the next label in II occurs. Until the last step, the actual orbit under T(x)=ζxT(x)=\zeta x visits precisely the vertices in this list. At the last step it reaches a point inside the side with the new label. The vertices visited before that step form a tower. Its height counts the applications of TT needed to reach the open side.

Take the eight labels 0,…,70,\ldots,7 and mark the bases I={1,2}I=\{1,2\}. Here κ=3\kappa=3. From each marked label, keep adding three modulo eight and stop at the first marked label you meet again. The two walks in label order are

1→4→7→2,2→5→0→3→6→1. 1\to4\to7\to2,\qquad2\to5\to0\to3\to6\to1.

Starting at 11, we reach an open side on the third step. Starting at 22, we reach one on the fifth. The lists before the last arrows are (1,4,7)(1,4,7) and (2,5,0,3,6)(2,5,0,3,6), accounting for all eight vertices exactly once. On a polygon with these contacts, the last arrows give ζ3v1=c2\zeta^3v_1=c_2 and ζ5v2=c1\zeta^5v_2=c_1. For now we are deducing equations that such a polygon would satisfy. Its existence will require a separate construction.

Read the last arrow of the first list carefully. From v7v_7 the map reaches the contact on side 22, at the point c2=β2v1+α2v2c_2=\beta_2v_1+\alpha_2v_2. The label 22 tells us which side receives the image. On the earlier arrows the destination labels were outside II, so the images there were the actual vertices v4v_4 and v7v_7. This is how a list of indices produces an equation for a power of ζ\zeta.

Check the second tower. Follow 2→5→0→3→6→12\to5\to0\to3\to6\to1. At which step do we first reach a side with an interior contact? Identify the two points ζ2v2\zeta^2v_2 and ζ5v2\zeta^5v_2.

Hint

Mark 11 and 22 on the list. At a label outside this set the contact is the ending vertex of its side. At a marked label it is strictly between the endpoints.

Solution

At step two we read label 00. Its side has an endpoint contact, giving ζ2v2=v0\zeta^2v_2=v_0. Labels 33 and 66 are outside II as well. The first marked destination is 11 at step five, so ζ5v2=c1\zeta^5v_2=c_1 lies strictly between v0v_0 and v1v_1.

Compute the records before introducing the integer basis

Start at label zero and keep a tally of the total advance, three per step. Every eight places bring us once around the labels. After tt steps the number of completed turns in the labels is ⌊3t/8⌋\lfloor3t/8\rfloor, the integer quotient of 3t3t by eight. The remainder is the current label. For one period these quantities are related by

3t=8⌊3t/8⌋+[3t]8. 3t=8\lfloor3t/8\rfloor+[3t]_8.

For example, at t=3t=3 we have advanced nine places. We have completed one turn in the labels and stand at label one. As you read down the last column, mark a value whenever it exceeds every previous value. Call each such value a record, including zero as the initial record.

Time tt 3t3t Full label wraps Residue [3t]8[3t]_8
00 00 00 0
11 33 00 3
22 66 00 6
33 99 11 11
44 1212 11 44
55 1515 11 7
66 1818 22 22
77 2121 22 55
88 2424 33 00

The records are shown in bold. At time two the deficit is 8−6=28-6=2. At time five it falls to 8−7=18-7=1.

The table follows the index permutation, which continues for as many steps as we please. The geometric identity ζtv0=v[3t]8\zeta^tv_0=v_{[3t]_8} holds only while the orbit has visited vertices at every step. At a positive record time hh, put b=⌈3h/8⌉b=\lceil3h/8\rceil. It is 8b8b that gives the next multiple of eight above 3h3h. At h=2h=2, for instance, 3h=63h=6, the next multiple is 88, and b=1b=1. The difference 8b−3h=28b-3h=2 is the deficit. Thus the records at times two and five give (h,b)=(2,1)(h,b)=(2,1) and (5,2)(5,2).

There is a short way to see what the pair can tell us. From the first base we need a net gain of one label to reach the second. Three additions of 33 give 9=8+19=8+1, so three steps will do it. From the second base to the first we need a net change of −1-1. Five additions give 15=16−115=16-1, so five steps will do it. The numbers of full turns of the labels in these two calculations differ. Later, when we multiply complex contact equations, the analogous distinction for angles will tell us which argument the product has accumulated.

For this example we could inspect all eight labels to check the first returns. For general NN we need an argument that proves how long each path is and that no two paths share an intermediate vertex. The two successive records supply both facts.

Encode records with integer pairs

Return to an arbitrary NN and κ\kappa. Write at=[tκ]Na_t=[t\kappa]_N. Topic IV showed that for some record aha_h, the number of bases is its remaining distance φ=N−ah\varphi=N-a_h from NN. The residues visited from zero are exactly 0,δ,2δ,…,N−δ0,\delta,2\delta,\ldots,N-\delta, where δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa). Hence N−δN-\delta is the last record and δ\delta its distance from NN.

For a pair of integers (a,b)(a,b), count the net advance of aa steps of size κ\kappa after subtracting bb turns of NN labels. Call this number L(a,b)L(a,b), so that

L(a,b)=aκ−bN. L(a,b)=a\kappa-bN.

At a positive record time hh, choose bb so that bNbN is the first multiple of NN above hκh\kappa. Explicitly b=⌈hκ/N⌉b=\lceil h\kappa/N\rceil, obtained by rounding up. If ν\nu denotes the record deficit, then bN−hκ=νbN-h\kappa=\nu, or L(h,b)=−νL(h,b)=-\nu. The initial record has deficit NN and is represented by (h,b)=(0,1)(h,b)=(0,1), which obeys the same equation.

We need the change from one record to the next. Let V=(h,b)V=(h,b) describe a record of deficit ν\nu and V′=(h′,b′)V'=(h',b') the very next one, with smaller deficit ν′\nu'. Write their difference and the gain in the residue as

U=V′−V=(q,p),Δ=ν−ν′. U=V'-V=(q,p),\qquad\Delta=\nu-\nu'.

The record at hh falls short of bNbN by ν\nu. Between records we gain Δ\Delta places after removing pp full turns. The additional fact that these records are consecutive gives a determinant of one. We will prove the identities

qb−ph=1,qκ−pN=Δ,hκ−bN=−ν, qb-ph=1,\qquad q\kappa-pN=\Delta,\qquad h\kappa-bN=-\nu,

qν+hΔ=N,gcd⁡(Δ,ν)=δ. q\nu+h\Delta=N,\qquad\gcd(\Delta,\nu)=\delta.

Here q=h′−hq=h'-h counts the extra steps, so q>0q>0, and 0<Δ<ν0<\Delta<\nu because some deficit remains. Place UU and VV in the columns of a matrix. Its determinant qb−phqb-ph gives the signed area of their parallelogram. When it equals one, the inverse matrix has integer entries by the two-by-two inverse formula. Thus every integer pair has unique integer coordinates in the basis U,VU,V.

A single residue keeps the current label but loses the complete turns that led there. The second coordinate bb lets us put them back. The identity qν+hΔ=Nq\nu+h\Delta=N can now be read as ν\nu paths of length qq, with hh extra steps on Δ\Delta of them. These lengths add to precisely the number of polygon vertices. We still have to justify that they describe the first returns.

For a picture of the determinant argument, consider a possible pair of records at N=17N=17, κ=3\kappa=3. At times two and five the residues are 66 and 1515, with deficits 1111 and 22. Their record vectors are V=(2,1)V=(2,1) and V′=(5,1)V'=(5,1). On squared paper join them by a segment. It passes through the integer point (3,1)(3,1). That point represents time three and deficit 17−3⋅3=817-3\cdot3=8, already better than the deficit at time two. The two records cannot be consecutive.

For the general pair, consider the triangle with corners 0,V,V′0,V,V'. An integer point of the form W=ξV+ηV′W=\xi V+\eta V' with ξ,η>0\xi,\eta>0 and ξ+η≤1\xi+\eta\le1 would give the same contradiction. Its time is positive and less than h′h', and its deficit is positive and less than ν\nu, since time and deficit are linear functions of the pair. Thus consecutive records exclude such an integer point. The following argument shows that a determinant with absolute value greater than one always supplies one.

Find the extra integer point if the determinant exceeds one in absolute value

A record vector has coprime coordinates. If both were divisible by g>1g>1, dividing by gg would yield an earlier positive time with smaller deficit, contradicting the record. The initial vector (0,1)(0,1) is also coprime. Using this coprimality, an integer vector complementary to VV can be found with determinant one, by Bézout’s identity: coprime integers have an integer linear combination equal to one.

Recover Bézout’s identity by division with remainder

For integers h,bh,b not both zero, take the smallest positive integer d=hr+bsd=hr+bs obtainable with integer coefficients r,sr,s. Such a positive combination exists. Divide hh by dd with remainder 0≤z<d0\le z<d. That remainder is also an integer combination of h,bh,b, so minimality forces z=0z=0. The same argument gives d∣bd\mid b. Conversely, every common divisor of h,bh,b divides dd. Hence d=gcd⁡(h,b)d=\gcd(h,b); for a coprime pair it is one. We can therefore choose r,sr,s below with hr+bs=1hr+bs=1.

Measure the area of the parallelogram with sides V,V′V,V' by the positive integer D=−det⁡(V,V′)=(h′ν−hν′)/ND=-\det(V,V')=(h'\nu-h\nu')/N. The last equality follows by substituting bN=hκ+νbN=h\kappa+\nu and b′N=h′κ+ν′b'N=h'\kappa+\nu'. Take r,sr,s from Bézout’s identity above and set W0=(s,−r)W_0=(s,-r). Then det⁡(V,W0)=−hr−bs=−1\det(V,W_0)=-hr-bs=-1. In the integer basis V,W0V,W_0, write V′=aV+DW0V'=aV+DW_0. The second coefficient is DD by taking the determinant with VV. A common divisor of a,Da,D would divide both coordinates of V′V', so gcd⁡(a,D)=1\gcd(a,D)=1.

Suppose D>1D>1. Taking one copy of W0W_0 gives us a fraction 1/D1/D of the way towards V′V'. To place the coefficient of VV strictly between zero and one as well, choose

W=⌈aD⌉V+W0=(⌈aD⌉−aD)V+1DV′ W=\left\lceil\frac aD\right\rceil V+W_0 =\left(\left\lceil\frac aD\right\rceil-\frac aD\right)V+\frac1D V'

The first expression makes WW an integer vector. In the second expression its coefficients ξ=⌈a/D⌉−a/D\xi=\lceil a/D\rceil-a/D and η=1/D\eta=1/D both lie strictly between zero and one, since gcd⁡(a,D)=1\gcd(a,D)=1 and D>1D>1. If their sum exceeds one, use the integer vector V+V′−WV+V'-W instead. Its coefficients 1−ξ1-\xi and 1−η1-\eta are again positive and now sum to less than one. We have found an integer point in the triangle with ξ,η>0\xi,\eta>0 and ξ+η≤1\xi+\eta\le1.

Its time t=ξh+ηh′t=\xi h+\eta h' satisfies 0<t<h′0<t<h', and its deficit d=ξν+ην′d=\xi\nu+\eta\nu' satisfies 0<d<ν0<d<\nu. Since d=−L(W)d=-L(W), the residue at time tt is N−d>N−νN-d>N-\nu. If t≤ht\le h, this contradicts the record at hh. If h<t<h′h<t<h', it puts a better residue between our consecutive records. Both possibilities contradict their choice, which proves D=1D=1.

It follows that det⁡(U,V)=1\det(U,V)=1. The two equations involving LL follow from the record deficits. Expanding the determinant gives qν+hΔ=Nq\nu+h\Delta=N. Finally, because U,VU,V form an integer basis, the possible values of LL are all integer combinations of Δ,ν\Delta,\nu. By definition they are also all integer combinations of κ,N\kappa,N. Their positive greatest common divisors are therefore equal.

The tower partition is a counting proof

Assume φ>δ\varphi>\delta, so its record has a successor, and put ν=φ\nu=\varphi. Begin at a base j∈{1,…,φ}j\in\{1,\ldots,\varphi\}. Taking qq steps adds qκ=pN+Δq\kappa=pN+\Delta to the label, the same as moving forward Δ\Delta places modulo NN. If j+Δ≤φj+\Delta\le\varphi, this already gives a base. For the last Δ\Delta bases we instead take q+hq+h steps. The extra hh steps add hκ=bN−φh\kappa=bN-\varphi, putting the final label at j+Δ−φ∈{1,…,Δ}j+\Delta-\varphi\in\{1,\ldots,\Delta\}. These are candidate destinations. We still have to exclude an earlier return on either path. Writing HjH_j for the proposed height and σ(j)\sigma(j) for the destination gives

Hj={q,1≤j≤φ−Δ,q+h,φ−Δ<j≤φ, H_j=\begin{cases}q,&1\le j\le\varphi-\Delta,\\q+h,&\varphi-\Delta<j\le\varphi,\end{cases}

σ(j)={j+Δ,j≤φ−Δ,j+Δ−φ,j>φ−Δ. \sigma(j)=\begin{cases}j+\Delta,&j\le\varphi-\Delta,\\j+\Delta-\varphi,&j>\varphi-\Delta.\end{cases}

Thus the original vertex labels are read modulo NN, while σ\sigma adds Δ\Delta among the φ\varphi base labels, returning to 11 after φ\varphi.

A proposed path can end at the correct base even if it has already passed another base on the way. To rule this out, number each proposed position by (t,j)(t,j), where jj is the starting base and 0≤t<Hj0\le t<H_j is the number of steps so far. Keep these positions separate until we know which labels they carry. Counting them from the proposed heights gives

(φ−Δ)q+Δ(q+h)=qφ+hΔ=N (\varphi-\Delta)q+\Delta(q+h)=q\varphi+h\Delta=N

positions. From the last position of tower jj, take one more step and join it to the starting position of tower σ(j)\sigma(j). Within a tower the label advances by κ\kappa at each step. The congruence j+Hjκ≡σ(j)(mod⁡N)j+H_j\kappa\equiv\sigma(j)\pmod N shows that the step between towers has this same advance.

The return permutation adds Δ\Delta modulo φ\varphi. Its period is φ/δ\varphi/\delta because gcd⁡(Δ,φ)=δ\gcd(\Delta,\varphi)=\delta. Thus it visits every base in one residue class modulo δ\delta before returning. Which of them have a taller tower? The last Δ\Delta consecutive base labels give exactly Δ/δ\Delta/\delta labels from each class, since δ\delta divides Δ\Delta. Consequently its joined tower cycle contains

qφδ+hΔδ=Nδ q\frac\varphi\delta+h\frac\Delta\delta=\frac N\delta

positions. The first repeated label on a walk adding κ\kappa occurs exactly N/δN/\delta steps after the start. Indeed, mκm\kappa is divisible by NN precisely when mm is divisible by N/δN/\delta. Thus each joined cycle uses every label of its residue class once, and the distinct cycles cover distinct classes. This accounts for all NN labels with no repetitions. Each member of II already occurs as a starting position, so none can occur partway up a tower. The step at height HjH_j is therefore the first return.

For N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3 the record residues are 0,3,6,70,3,6,7, leaving deficits 8,5,2,18,5,2,1. For φ=2\varphi=2 we take V=(2,1)V=(2,1) at residue six and V′=(5,2)V'=(5,2) at residue seven. Subtracting gives (q,p)=(3,1)(q,p)=(3,1), and the deficit drops by Δ=1\Delta=1. We can check both counts directly. The determinant is 3⋅1−1⋅2=13\cdot1-1\cdot2=1. The two towers have heights q=3q=3 and q+h=5q+h=5, with qφ+hΔ=3⋅2+2=8q\varphi+h\Delta=3\cdot2+2=8 positions altogether.

Follow the two towers in the drawing as a single cycle of labels, joining the top of the first to base 22 and the top of the second to base 11. From 11 it takes eight additions of 33 modulo 88 before a label repeats. Since the eight positions already include both bases, neither base can appear a second time on an intermediate level. This proves the first in “first return” for this example.

Preserve the full turns as well as the residues

We also want the angle through which a point has actually turned. As in Topic III, list the angles Φi\Phi_i in increasing order and continue them by Φi+N=Φi+2π\Phi_{i+N}=\Phi_i+2\pi. Suppose we start at vav_a and land on a vertex for the next tt steps. Each step adds θζ\theta_\zeta to the angle and κ\kappa to the index. Adding the tt equalities from Topic III gives

Φa+tθζ=Φa+tκ. \Phi_a+t\theta_\zeta=\Phi_{a+t\kappa}.

For example, ΦN+1\Phi_{N+1} describes the same vertex direction as Φ1\Phi_1, but its value is Φ1+2π\Phi_1+2\pi. Keeping the integer index a+tκa+t\kappa preserves this extra turn. If the first t−1t-1 images are vertices and the last lies inside side a+tκa+t\kappa, the final angle is strictly between the angles of its endpoints. In that case we have

Φa+tκ−1<Φa+tθζ<Φa+tκ. \Phi_{a+t\kappa-1}<\Phi_a+t\theta_\zeta<\Phi_{a+t\kappa}.

One tower will later close the product around the polygon. From base φ\varphi its height is q+hq+h and its destination is Δ\Delta. At level hh its label is φ+hκ≡0(mod⁡N)\varphi+h\kappa\equiv0\pmod N. Since q>0q>0, this occurs before the return and the actual point is v0=vNv_0=v_N. Thus the first hh steps give ζhvφ=v0\zeta^hv_\varphi=v_0, including the possibility h=0h=0. The last qq steps give ζqv0=cΔ\zeta^qv_0=c_\Delta. Topic VII uses both equalities and their accumulated angles.

At this point a first return advances by Δ\Delta among the bases. If Δ>1\Delta>1, it passes over at least one base. Arithmetic permits this; Topic VI uses extremal polygon geometry to rule it out. The case φ=δ\varphi=\delta has no next record and is handled separately in Topic VII.

Return geometry

Arithmetic suspension

An endpoint contact, where βi+κ=0\beta_{i+\kappa}=0, gives ζvi=vi+κ\zeta v_i=v_{i+\kappa}. Start at an index j∈Ij\in I and repeatedly add κ\kappa modulo NN until the first return to II, at index kk. The intermediate destinations lie outside II, so the endpoint identities apply at each of those steps. At the final step, the destination is in II, giving ζHvj=ck\zeta^H v_j=c_k, an interior contact on the side ending at vkv_k. We call the list of indices before this return a tower, and the number of steps HH its height. The starting index is its base, and each subsequent index is another level. For example, with N=8N=8, κ=3\kappa=3, and I={1,2}I=\{1,2\}, the path 1→4→7→21\to4\to7\to2 first returns to II after three steps. Its tower consists of 1,4,71,4,7, has height 33, and closes with ζ3v1=c2\zeta^3v_1=c_2.

We also retain the integer index j+tκj+t\kappa before reducing it modulo NN. An increase by NN records a full turn in the cyclic vertex order. Combining the endpoint identities along a tower gives a power of ζ\zeta; its height and the number of turns will enter the product equation. We first determine these paths using only the index arithmetic.

The arithmetic follows the residues at=[tκ]Na_t=[t\kappa]_N. A record residue exceeds every earlier value in this sequence; the initial value a0=0a_0=0 is also a record. Its deficit ν=N−at\nu=N-a_t is its gap to NN. For N=8N=8 and κ=3\kappa=3, the sequence begins 0,3,6,1,4,7,…0,3,6,1,4,7,\ldots, with records 0,3,6,70,3,6,7 and deficits 8,5,2,18,5,2,1. The preceding proposition shows that φ\varphi is one of these deficits. We will use consecutive records to determine the tower heights and return destinations.

The calculation with record residues below reformulates Karpelevič’s analysis of Euclidean remainders [Karp], §3, Lemma 2 and Theorems III–IV. Slater studies related gaps and return times for rotations [Slater], and Hardy and Wright provide the background on Farey fractions [HardyWright], Chapter III. We prove here how the towers cover all NN indices, specifying which interval endpoints are included.

Fix 1≤κ<N1\le\kappa<N and δ=gcd⁡(N,κ)\delta=\gcd(N,\kappa). Define L:ℤ2→ℤL:\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb Z by L(a,b)=aκ−bNL(a,b)=a\kappa-bN. For each record time hh, let ν=N−[hκ]N\nu=N-[h\kappa]_N be its deficit and encode the record by V=(h,b)V=(h,b), where b={1,h=0,⌈hκ/N⌉,h>0.b=\begin{cases} 1,&h=0,\\ \lceil h\kappa/N\rceil,&h>0. \end{cases} This choice gives L(V)=−νL(V)=-\nu, including the initial record V=(0,1)V=(0,1) with ν=N\nu=N. The attainable residues are the multiples of δ\delta, whose largest value is N−δN-\delta, so the last record has deficit δ\delta.

Lemma 3.1. Let V=(h,b)V=(h,b) and V′=(h′,b′)V'=(h',b') encode two consecutive records, with deficits ν>ν′\nu>\nu'. Set U=V′−V=(q,p)U=V'-V=(q,p) and Δ=ν−ν′\Delta=\nu-\nu'. Then (3.1)det⁡(U,V)=1,L(U)=Δ,L(V)=−ν,qν+hΔ=N,gcd⁡(Δ,ν)=δ.\det(U,V)=1,\quad L(U)=\Delta,\quad L(V)=-\nu, \quad q\nu+h\Delta=N,\quad \gcd(\Delta,\nu)=\delta. Here det⁡(U,V)=qb−ph\det(U,V)=qb-ph. Thus every pair of integers can be written uniquely as an integer combination of UU and VV. In particular, q>0q>0 and 0<Δ<ν0<\Delta<\nu.

Proof of Lemma 3.1

Proof. The attainable residues are the multiples of δ\delta, so the last deficit is δ\delta. Each record vector V=(h,b)V=(h,b) is primitive, meaning gcd⁡(h,b)=1\gcd(h,b)=1. This holds for the initial vector (0,1)(0,1). Otherwise, if V=gWV=gW for an integer g>1g>1, the integer vector WW would have time h/g<hh/g<h and positive deficit ν/g<ν\nu/g<\nu. Its residue would exceed the record at time hh, a contradiction.

Since h′>hh'>h and ν>ν′>0\nu>\nu'>0, the integer D=−det⁡(V,V′)=h′ν−hν′ND=-\det(V,V')=\frac{h'\nu-h\nu'}{N} is positive. Suppose D>1D>1. Bézout’s identity says that, because gcd⁡(h,b)=1\gcd(h,b)=1, there are integers r,sr,s with hr+bs=1hr+bs=1. Set W0=(s,−r)W_0=(s,-r). Then det⁡(V,W0)=−hr−bs=−1\det(V,W_0)=-hr-bs=-1, so every integer vector has unique integer coordinates in the basis (V,W0)(V,W_0). Write V′=aV+DW0V'=aV+DW_0. Since V′V' is primitive, gcd⁡(a,D)=1\gcd(a,D)=1. Consequently W=(⌈a/D⌉−a/D)V+D−1V′=⌈a/D⌉V+W0W=\left(\lceil a/D\rceil-a/D\right)V+D^{-1}V' =\lceil a/D\rceil V+W_0 is an integer vector of the form W=αV+βV′W=\alpha V+\beta V' with 0<α,β<10<\alpha,\beta<1. If α+β>1\alpha+\beta>1, replace WW by V+V′−WV+V'-W; the new coefficients still lie in (0,1)(0,1) and have sum at most one. The time tt and deficit of WW then satisfy 0<t=αh+βh′<h′,0<−L(W)=αν+βν′<ν.0<t=\alpha h+\beta h'<h',\qquad 0<-L(W)=\alpha\nu+\beta\nu'<\nu. Thus a positive integer time before h′h' would have a residue exceeding the record at hh. This is impossible for consecutive records. Hence D=1D=1, and det⁡(U,V)=−det⁡(V,V′)=1\det(U,V)=-\det(V,V')=1.

By linearity, L(U)=L(V′)−L(V)=ΔL(U)=L(V')-L(V)=\Delta, while L(V)=−νL(V)=-\nu by definition. Expanding the determinant gives qν+hΔ=q(bN−hκ)+h(qκ−pN)=N(qb−ph)=N.q\nu+h\Delta =q(bN-h\kappa)+h(q\kappa-pN) =N(qb-ph)=N. Since U,VU,V form an integer basis, the values of LL are exactly the integer combinations of Δ\Delta and ν\nu. By its definition, they are also the integer combinations of κ\kappa and NN. Therefore gcd⁡(Δ,ν)=gcd⁡(κ,N)=δ\gcd(\Delta,\nu)=\gcd(\kappa,N)=\delta. Finally, q=h′−h>0q=h'-h>0 and Δ=ν−ν′\Delta=\nu-\nu' lies in (0,ν)(0,\nu). ◻

The identity qν+hΔ=Nq\nu+h\Delta=N can be written (ν−Δ)q+Δ(q+h)=N,(\nu-\Delta)q+\Delta(q+h)=N, suggesting ν−Δ\nu-\Delta towers of height qq and Δ\Delta towers of height q+hq+h. Why a return cannot skip a base

In the eight-vertex calculation of Topic V, base 11 returns to the side ending at base 22, and base 22 returns to the side ending at base 11. With seven bases, arithmetic alone would also allow a return that adds three to each base label. Then base 11 would return on the side ending at base 44. What property of a boundary eigenvalue rules out such a skip?

Assume N≥4N\ge4 and φ>gcd⁡(N,κ)\varphi>\gcd(N,\kappa), the case in which the record for φ\varphi has a successor. The first returns add Δ\Delta modulo φ\varphi and take qq or q+hq+h steps, with

qφ+hΔ=N,1≤Δ<φ,gcd⁡(Δ,φ)=gcd⁡(N,κ). q\varphi+h\Delta=N,\qquad1\le\Delta<\varphi, \qquad\gcd(\Delta,\varphi)=\gcd(N,\kappa).

Suppose Δ>1\Delta>1. Along the boundary there is space between a moving base and the side that receives its return. We use those intermediate vertices to adjust the side lines one at a time. Each has to pass through an already known contact. At the last side we can make the returning point fall strictly inside the polygon. Moving all the higher vertices along with their bases then preserves containment for the same map F(x)=ζxF(x)=\zeta x.

The contradiction uses the word every in Topic II. The deformed polygon still has NN vertices and is invariant under FF, so even here each vertex image has to touch the boundary. Our construction would give a vertex whose image lies in the interior.

Lesson 1: find the lines along which bases may move

Draw a line through a side of PP. All of PP lies on one side of the line. Such a line supports PP, and we can describe it by an equation ℓ(x)=c\ell(x)=c with ℓ\ell linear and ℓ(x)≤c\ell(x)\le c throughout PP. The points where equality holds form a side or a single vertex. We call these sets faces and also count PP itself as a face. Thus a point between the ends of a side belongs to two faces, that side and PP. The side is the smaller one.

Let x=(1−t)a+tbx=(1-t)a+tb lie between the distinct endpoints of a side, with 0<t<10<t<1. An affine map FF sends it to (1−t)F(a)+tF(b)(1-t)F(a)+tF(b). Suppose F(P)⊆PF(P)\subseteq P and F(x)F(x) lies on a supporting line where a linear function reaches its maximum. Both endpoints have function value at most that maximum. Their weighted average equals it, so both values equal it. Thus the whole segment [F(a),F(b)][F(a),F(b)] lies on that line. If F(x)F(x) were a corner, we could repeat the argument with its other supporting side. The two lines meet only at the corner, forcing F(a)=F(b)F(a)=F(b), which is impossible for invertible FF. More generally the image of the smallest face at xx lies in the smallest face at F(x)F(x).

Applying an invertible map to a segment with two distinct ends again gives a segment with two distinct ends. The face containing its image therefore has dimension at least one. Once a point between the ends of a side ceases to be on a side, its only possible destination is the interior. It then stays there because FF carries an open neighbourhood of the point to an open set contained in PP.

Follow the side Ei=[vi−1,vi]E_i=[v_{i-1},v_i] for rr applications of FF. If FrEiF^rE_i is still on the boundary, we can identify its starting endpoint at every earlier step. In the cyclic numbering of the vertices it is

Ftvi−1=vi−1+tκ(0≤t≤r). F^tv_{i-1}=v_{i-1+t\kappa}\quad(0\le t\le r).

At the first step, the assigned images of the two endpoints lie on successive half-open sides. For their joining segment to lie on one side, the first image has to equal their shared corner. Repeating proves the statement. A point inside the image segment, together with the supporting-functional argument, ensures that the whole next side remains on the boundary for the remaining steps.

To move a base without losing its return, first ask where the base is allowed to move. Take j≥2j\ge2 and let HjH_j be the number of steps from vjv_j to the contact on Eσ(j)E_{\sigma(j)}. All starting points that reach the line of that side after HjH_j steps lie on the line

Lj=F−Hj(aff⁡Eσ(j)). L_j=F^{-H_j}(\operatorname{aff}E_{\sigma(j)}).

Here aff⁡E\operatorname{aff}E means the full line containing the side. The entire image FHjPF^{H_j}P is on the inward side of that line, with FHjvjF^{H_j}v_j on the line. Taking preimages gives a supporting line at vjv_j. If it touched a second point of PP, it would contain one of the two sides meeting at vjv_j.

Consider first Ej+1=[vj,vj+1]E_{j+1}=[v_j,v_{j+1}]. Its starting endpoint is vjv_j. The preceding argument would keep FHjvjF^{H_j}v_j a vertex, but this is the open-side contact defining HjH_j. For Ej=[vj−1,vj]E_j=[v_{j-1},v_j], the starting endpoint is vj−1v_{j-1}. Its return time satisfies Hj−1≤HjH_{j-1}\le H_j, since the short towers come first. At time Hj−1H_{j-1} this vertex is already between the endpoints of a side and can never again be a vertex. This rules out the other incident side as well. Thus LjL_j exposes vjv_j, meaning that P∩Lj={vj}P\cap L_j=\{v_j\}.

The first lesson supplies movement lines, rather than a finished deformation. A base moved along LjL_j has its returning image on the required target line by definition of F−HjF^{-H_j}. Each neighbouring base also has a contact to preserve. The next lesson shows how successive line intersections do that.

Lesson 2: calculate one local motion before proving the general lemma

We can try the construction on the quadrilateral whose consecutive vertices are

X0=(0,0),X1=(1,0),X2=(2,1),X3=(3,3) X_0=(0,0),\quad X_1=(1,0),\quad X_2=(2,1),\quad X_3=(3,3)

Mark the midpoints C2=(3/2,1/2)C_2=(3/2,1/2) and C3=(5/2,2)C_3=(5/2,2) of its last two sides. We use this quadrilateral only to study the motion of the lines. To see that L2:y=3x/2−2L_2:y=3x/2-2 touches it only at X2X_2, evaluate y−3x/2+2y-3x/2+2 at the four vertices. The values in order are 2,1/2,0,1/22,1/2,0,1/2. Thus L2L_2 exposes X2X_2.

Move X1X_1 to X1(t)=(1−t,0)X_1(t)=(1-t,0). We want the next vertex to satisfy two conditions. It has to stay on L2L_2, and the side from X1(t)X_1(t) to it has to pass through C2C_2. A point on that second line has coordinates X1(t)+s(C2−X1(t))=(1−t+s(12+t),s2). X_1(t)+s\bigl(C_2-X_1(t)\bigr) =\left(1-t+s(\tfrac12+t),\tfrac{s}{2}\right). Substituting its coordinates in y=3x/2−2y=3x/2-2 gives s=2(1+3t)/(1+6t)s=2(1+3t)/(1+6t). At t=0t=0 we get s=2s=2, as expected since C2C_2 is the midpoint. Substitution back into the line gives

X2(t)=(2(1+5t)1+6t,1+3t1+6t). X_2(t)=\left(\frac{2(1+5t)}{1+6t},\frac{1+3t}{1+6t}\right).

Measure position on the line K=C2C3K=C_2C_3 by Y(t)=(5/2−t,2−3t/2)Y(t)=(5/2-t,2-3t/2), so that Y(0)=C3Y(0)=C_3 and Y(1)=C2Y(1)=C_2. Where does the new line from X2(t)X_2(t) to X3X_3 cross KK? Write the crossing as Y(u)Y(u). Substituting Y(u)Y(u) for a point on that new line and solving for uu gives

u(t)=t1+6t,t−u(t)=6t21+6t. u(t)=\frac{t}{1+6t},\qquad t-u(t)=\frac{6t^2}{1+6t}.

Which side of the moving line contains Y(t)Y(t)? On KK, increasing the parameter moves towards C2C_2. At t=0t=0 the point C2C_2 lies strictly on the polygon side of the final line X2X3X_2X_3. We can check the direction by taking the determinant of X3−X2=(1,2)X_3-X_2=(1,2) and C2−C3=(−1,−3/2)C_2-C_3=(-1,-3/2), which gives 1/2>01/2>0. For sufficiently small tt the same direction still points inward. The line crosses KK at Y(u(t))Y(u(t)). From that crossing to Y(t)Y(t) we move by (t−u(t))(C2−C3)(t-u(t))(C_2-C_3), so a positive difference puts Y(t)Y(t) inward. At t=0t=0 the first derivative of the difference is zero, so the actual movement is detected at second order. Starting the same projection chain at X0X_0 instead of X1X_1 corresponds to t=1t=1 and gives Z2=(12/7,4/7)Z_2=(12/7,4/7) and

Π(X0)=(33/14,25/14)=C3+(C2−C3)/7. \Pi(X_0)=(33/14,25/14)=C_3+(C_2-C_3)/7.

The coefficient 1/71/7 puts this last point strictly between C3C_3 and C2C_2. We will prove the same ordering for a chain of any length. It will give us enough information at t=1t=1 to choose a small motion near t=0t=0.

Notice which conditions the intersection enforces. For each small tt we have X2(t)∈L2X_2(t)\in L_2, and the line joining X1(t)X_1(t) to X2(t)X_2(t) passes through C2C_2. To belong to the side, C2C_2 has to lie between the two endpoints as well. At t=0t=0 it is their midpoint. Both this strict ordering and the strict turns at the corners persist for small tt, so the moving quadrilateral remains convex.

Check the motion in both directions. Take t=1/20t=1/20 and then t=−1/20t=-1/20. In each case, is Y(t)Y(t) farther towards C2C_2 than the crossing Y(u(t))Y(u(t))? What would the derivative of t−u(t)t-u(t) at zero tell us?

Hint

Compare the two coordinates by subtracting them. In 6t2/(1+6t)6t^2/(1+6t) the denominators for these choices are 13/1013/10 and 7/107/10. What sign does the numerator have?

Solution

At t=1/20t=1/20 we obtain t−u(t)=3/260t-u(t)=3/260. At t=−1/20t=-1/20 we obtain 3/1403/140. Both differences put Y(t)Y(t) on the inward side. Dividing the difference by tt gives 6t/(1+6t)6t/(1+6t), which tends to zero. The derivative alone would therefore have given no preference for either direction.

Build the general motion by intersecting lines

Take a chain of consecutive vertices X0,X1,…,Xℓ+1X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_{\ell+1} with ℓ≥2\ell\ge2. We may read the boundary in either direction. Leave at least one side of the polygon outside the chain. Mark a point CiC_i strictly between Xi−1X_{i-1} and XiX_i for each i=2,…,ℓ+1i=2,\ldots,\ell+1. At each XiX_i with 2≤i≤ℓ2\le i\le\ell, choose a line LiL_i that exposes that vertex.

The endpoints X0X_0 and Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1} stay where they are. Slide X1X_1 a little along X0X1X_0X_1. Once Xi−1(t)X_{i-1}(t) is known, the new vertex has to lie on LiL_i and its side line has to pass through CiC_i. We therefore take

Xi(t)=Li∩aff⁡(Xi−1(t),Ci),2≤i≤ℓ. X_i(t)=L_i\cap\operatorname{aff}(X_{i-1}(t),C_i),\qquad2\le i\le\ell.

At t=0t=0 each pair of lines crosses at XiX_i. The crossing is unique because CiC_i is on the side and LiL_i touches the polygon only at XiX_i. For a small change in tt the lines still cross, and their intersection depends smoothly on tt. We can therefore follow the construction to its last side. We have yet to determine on which side of that moving line the returning point will lie.

Consider one of these steps on its own. From a point with coordinate τ\tau on the first line, draw the line through the fixed contact and mark its crossing on the second line. In coordinates on the two lines this operation has the form

τ↦aτ+bdτ+e,ae−bd≠0. \tau\longmapsto\frac{a\tau+b}{d\tau+e},\qquad ae-bd\ne0.

The letters a,b,d,ea,b,d,e here are real coefficients of this particular function, not the tower parameters. The formula follows by solving two linear equations for the intersection; their common denominator is linear in the starting coordinate τ\tau. The projection centre lies off both lines. Projection back from the same centre is then its inverse. A zero denominator describes a parallel intersection, represented by a point at infinity. Adding that one direction-point to each line makes the projection invertible everywhere. This is what “projective” means in this proof: compositions of these ordinary line-intersection maps.

Why the long comparison has a definite direction

Denote the first line X0X1X_0X_1 by Λ\Lambda and the line through Cℓ,Cℓ+1C_\ell,C_{\ell+1} by KK. Starting anywhere on Λ\Lambda, project through C2C_2 onto L2L_2 and continue through CiC_i onto LiL_i. For the last projection use the fixed vertex Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1} as centre and KK as target. Write Π\Pi for the composition. Every centre lies off the two lines it connects. Indeed, each exposing line touches the polygon only at its own vertex, while CiC_i lies between vertices. Also C2C_2 lies off the first side line, and Cℓ,Cℓ+1C_\ell,C_{\ell+1} lie inside two different sides, so their line misses Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1}.

We know one value of Π\Pi immediately. A start at X1X_1 reproduces the original chain and ends at Cℓ+1C_{\ell+1}. Now start at the other marked point on Λ\Lambda, namely X0X_0. We claim that

Π(X0)∈(Cℓ+1,Cℓ). \Pi(X_0)\in(C_{\ell+1},C_\ell).

In our four-vertex calculation the point was 1/71/7 of the way from C3C_3 to C2C_2. Its precise position played no role in choosing an inward motion. We need the intersection to lie strictly between the two contacts. We can test this without computing the intersection itself. Draw the line through the final projected vertex and the fixed endpoint. If the two contacts are strictly on opposite sides of this line, their segment crosses it in its interior. The calculation below proves those signs for any chain satisfying the hypotheses.

Prove the opposite signs for a chain of any length

Choose nonnegative affine functions η0,η1\eta_0,\eta_1 on PP vanishing only at X0,Xℓ+1X_0,X_{\ell+1} respectively. Each can be obtained by adding the two side inequalities incident to its vertex. Their sum η=η0+η1\eta=\eta_0+\eta_1 is strictly positive throughout PP. With a third independent affine function ψ\psi, use coordinates

(η0(x)η(x),ψ(x)η(x)). \left(\frac{\eta_0(x)}{\eta(x)},\frac{\psi(x)}{\eta(x)}\right).

In the first coordinate t=η0/ηt=\eta_0/\eta we have 0≤t≤10\le t\le1. Equality at zero singles out X0X_0, and equality at one singles out Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1} because 1−t=η1/η1-t=\eta_1/\eta. To see what happens to a segment, take two points U,VU,V with weights 1−λ,λ1-\lambda,\lambda. Their images acquire weights proportional to (1−λ)η(U)(1-\lambda)\eta(U) and λη(V)\lambda\eta(V). These denominators are positive. Given any two image weights, dividing by the same denominators and rescaling their sum to one recovers the starting weights. Thus a whole segment goes onto a whole segment, with points strictly between its ends staying strictly between. In particular the polygon is still convex in these coordinates.

Cut this polygon by a vertical line t=τt=\tau with 0<τ<10<\tau<1. The cut is an interval by convexity. It contains an interior point since we can join an interior point to either extreme vertex and reach the required value of τ\tau while keeping a positive weight on the interior point. A small disk about that point shrinks to a smaller disk along the segment, so the cut has positive length. Only its endpoints can lie on the boundary. A supporting line through a point strictly between them would have to contain the cut, giving a vertical supporting side. Yet a vertical supporting side could only occur at t=0t=0 or t=1t=1, where the polygon has just one point. The bottom and top of the cuts therefore trace two distinct chains from X0X_0 to Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1}.

Our vertices follow one of these chains. Reflect the vertical coordinate if necessary so that they follow the bottom of each cut. Every vertical line then meets the chain just once, and the first coordinate increases as we go from X0X_0 to Xℓ+1X_{\ell+1}. Write f(t)f(t) for the height of the chain. Join the points over tt and uu by a straight segment. This segment lies in the polygon, so every point on it lies at or above the bottom of its own cut. This gives

f((1−λ)t+λu)≤(1−λ)f(t)+λf(u),0≤λ≤1. f((1-\lambda)t+\lambda u) \le(1-\lambda)f(t)+\lambda f(u),\qquad0\le\lambda\le1.

This inequality says that ff is convex. Between two successive vertices its graph is a straight side. The change of coordinates has thus given us a convex, piecewise linear function whose side slopes we can compare in the order of the chain.

Let Xi=(ti,fi)X_i=(t_i,f_i), so t0<⋯<tℓ+1t_0<\cdots<t_{\ell+1}. Denote the slope on [ti−1,ti][t_{i-1},t_i] by did_i. For 2≤i≤ℓ2\le i\le\ell the exposing line LiL_i is not vertical because tit_i lies strictly between the two horizontal extremes. Write sis_i for its slope. The inequalities we need are

We follow Karpelevič’s strategy of moving polygon vertices to exclude such returns [Karp]. The motion is built from projections between lines, each following lines through a fixed point. The required projection formulas are derived below; Coxeter [Coxeter] gives the background on these projections and their compositions.

The previous lemma supplies exposing lines along which vertices may move. After moving the first vertex slightly along its side’s line, we find each subsequent vertex by intersecting its exposing line with the line through the preceding moved vertex and a fixed side contact. We must choose the initial motion so that the closing contact moves to the inward side of the new final side: the half-plane containing the polygon’s interior.

We therefore use completed lines: each ordinary line is supplemented by the point representing its direction, so parallel lines meet at that point.

We express these projections in homogeneous coordinates. A nonzero vector X=(x,y,w)TX=(x,y,w)^T represents a point, and every nonzero scalar multiple represents the same point. When w≠0w\ne0, the ordinary point is (x/w,y/w)(x/w,y/w); vectors with w=0w=0 represent points at infinity. The part with w≠0w\ne0 is an affine chart, where we can normalize w=1w=1. A completed line has equation ηTX=0\eta^TX=0, with η\eta a nonzero column vector in ℝ3\mathbb R^3; this equation defines the two-dimensional subspace representing the line.

Let cc represent the projection centre. Suppose the source line does not contain cc and the target line ηTX=0\eta^TX=0 satisfies ηTc≠0\eta^Tc\ne0. Projection onto the target is induced by X↦(I−cηTηTc)X,X\longmapsto\left(I-\frac{c\eta^T}{\eta^Tc}\right)X, where II is the 3×33\times3 identity matrix. The result is a linear combination of X,cX,c and satisfies the target equation, so it represents the intersection of that line with the line through the original point and the centre. The map is an isomorphism between the two representing subspaces. In scalar coordinates along the lines, it has the fractional-linear form τ↦aτ+bdτ+e,ae−bd≠0,\tau\longmapsto\frac{a\tau+b}{d\tau+e},\qquad ae-bd\ne0, with real constants a,b,d,ea,b,d,e. A zero denominator represents an image at infinity. These maps and their compositions are projectivities.

An invertible 3×33\times3 matrix changes the homogeneous coordinates. Dividing the first two resulting coordinates by the third gives ordinary plane coordinates. This third coordinate is an affine function of the original point, called the denominator. On a region where it is nonzero and keeps one sign, the transformation preserves segments and their interiors, because the transformed convex combinations still have positive weights.

Lemma 3.4 shows how to move a chain so that its closing contact lies strictly inward of the final side, even when the first derivative of the signed distance vanishes. To obtain an invariant polygon, we must extend this motion to all vertices using the tower identities and keep every other returning image on its corresponding side. The next proof checks these conditions by comparing the indices of the moving bases with those of their target sides.

Theorem 3.5. For the fixed complex number ζ\zeta, assume the conclusion of Theorem 2.2 holds for every polygon QQ with at most NN vertices and ζQ⊆Q\zeta Q\subseteq Q. In particular, ζu∈∂Q\zeta u\in\partial Q for every vertex uu of every such QQ.

First choose a chain of consecutive vertices on which to apply the local motion; then extend that motion to all tower levels.

The first vertex to be moved is X1X_1. We choose between two chains, going in opposite directions around the polygon, so that the selected chain is the shorter one. Five midpoint averages show the mechanism

Thus ωq=ρqeiA\omega^q=\rho^q e^{iA} has positive imaginary part. As tt runs from zero to one, ωq−t\omega^q-t moves left at that fixed height. Its principal argument increases strictly from AA to M=Arg⁡(ωq−1)<πM=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-1)<\pi.

Our weights may equal zero but are always smaller than one, so the factor angles satisfy A≤uj<MA\le u_j<M. This also identifies their principal arguments with the positive side angles in the real turn count.

We can now hand two quantities to the next calculation. Multiplying the factors determines their product of lengths. Adding their continued angles on the polygon determines their mean as a real number. The two sixth roots in the example show why we need both.

When δ≥2\delta\ge2, we have φ=δ\varphi=\delta, so each index cycle contains exactly one interior contact. The recurrence then links each base to the preceding one; conjugating and reversing the order puts it in the same form as in the first case.

In both cases we obtain relations between successive base vertices and a relation closing the list, then multiply them to eliminate the vertices. We also add the real angular increments along the same paths, using the continued vertex arguments from (2.4). Consecutive differences of vertex arguments cancel in the sum, retaining the accumulated full turns. This real argument equality is needed to identify the intended boundary arc: the complex product alone determines an argument only modulo 2π2\pi.

The cyclic recurrence with coefficients varying from side to side already appears in Karpelevič [Karp], Theorem VI and equation (13), pp. 375–376 of the Russian original. There the coefficients are first shown to be equal, and only then are the vertices eliminated. Here we allow the coefficients to differ while deriving the product. Equality of the coefficients will follow from the later convexity argument that determines the boundary modulus.

Turning a Farey interval into one candidate radius

Consider a point on the segment from 11 to ii. If it lies on the ray making an angle of π/4\pi/4, its real and imaginary parts agree, so it is (1+i)/2(1+i)/2. Its radius is 1/21/\sqrt2. The first arc at order four has precisely this shape. On a more complicated arc we should still be able to fix a ray and solve for just one real number. Which equation takes the place of intersecting that segment with the ray?

Upper bound — still to prove. Topic IX will show that a product with the specified real winding cannot have radius beyond this candidate. Topic XI will compare candidates at different orders.

Attainment. Even after finding a radius, we still need a matrix with an eigenvalue at that point. Topic X will construct one.

The polygon supplies its data at the least order that realises a point. For the moment we can perform the following construction at any given order. We write Kn(θ)K_n(\theta) for the distance it assigns to the ray of angle θ\theta.

Fix the matrix order n≥4n\ge4. To find the equation for a ray of angle θ\theta in the upper half-plane, measure its direction in turns, x=θ/(2π)x=\theta/(2\pi). Arrange all reduced fractions in [0,1][0,1] with denominator at most nn in increasing order. This list is FnF_n. Suppose xx lies in a gap with endpoints f<gf<g in its upper-ray portion [0,1/2][0,1/2]. For any two neighbours p/q<r/sp/q<r/s of FnF_n, Topic VII gives

rq−ps=1,q+s>n. rq-ps=1,\qquad q+s>n.

Indeed, subtracting the fractions gives (rq−ps)/(qs)=1/(qs)(rq-ps)/(qs)=1/(qs). If the denominator sum q+sq+s were at most nn, the intermediate fraction (p+r)/(q+s)(p+r)/(q+s) would be available already. Its numerator and denominator are coprime since a common divisor would divide q(p+r)−p(q+s)=1q(p+r)-p(q+s)=1.

The product formula is oriented so that its left endpoint has the smaller denominator. If that is already true, set p/q=fp/q=f, r/s=gr/s=g, and y=xy=x. Otherwise set p/q=1−gp/q=1-g, r/s=1−fr/s=1-f, and y=1−xy=1-x. Reflection reverses the endpoints because conjugation gives e2πiy=e−iθe^{2\pi iy}=e^{-i\theta}. It preserves the modulus we want to determine. In both cases q<sq<s and p/q<y<r/sp/q<y<r/s. When we have reflected, y>1/2y>1/2, so the corresponding ray lies in the lower half-plane.

Using the oriented angle ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y, put

m=⌊n/q⌋,A=qϑ−2πp,B=2πr−sϑm. m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor,\qquad A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=\frac{2\pi r-s\vartheta}{m}.

There are mm factors to compare. The angle AA counts qq copies of the angular distance from the left endpoint. The angle BB counts ss copies of the distance to the right endpoint, shared equally among the mm factors. Both are positive. To see their sizes, measure the distance from the left endpoint as a fraction of the interval width. Denote that fraction by

t=y−p/qr/s−p/q∈(0,1). t=\frac{y-p/q}{r/s-p/q}\in(0,1).

Then y−p/q=t/(qs)y-p/q=t/(qs) and r/s−y=(1−t)/(qs)r/s-y=(1-t)/(qs). Substituting in the definitions gives

Both denominators in these last expressions are at least three. Indeed, q<sq<s and q+s>n≥4q+s>n\ge4 give s≥3s\ge3. For q=1q=1 we have mq=nmq=n, for q=2q=2 we have m≥2m\ge2, and for q≥3q\ge3 already mq≥3mq\ge3. Hence A+BA+B is a convex combination of 2π/s2\pi/s and 2π/(mq)2\pi/(mq), each at most 2π/32\pi/3. In particular AA, BB and A+BA+B have positive sines.

Take n=5n=5 and x=7/24x=7/24. The neighbours 1/4=6/241/4=6/24 and 1/3=8/241/3=8/24 put the smaller denominator on the right. Reflection gives y=17/24y=17/24 between 2/3=16/242/3=16/24 and 3/4=18/243/4=18/24. We read off p=2p=2, q=3q=3, r=3r=3, s=4s=4 and m=⌊5/3⌋=1m=\lfloor5/3\rfloor=1. The original angle is θ=7π/12\theta=7\pi/12, whereas the oriented angle is ϑ=17π/12\vartheta=17\pi/12. We keep K5(θ)K_5(\theta) as the radius of the original upper ray; only the coordinates used in its equation have been reflected. Although eiϑe^{i\vartheta} is in the lower half-plane, its third power has argument A=π/4A=\pi/4 after subtracting the full turns. That upper-half-plane factor is what the convexity calculation in Topic IX needs. In the drawing, follow the endpoint 1/31/3 as it becomes 2/32/3. The marked angle is halfway across the interval on either side of the drawing.

Selecting a branch requires the turn count

Write z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta} and e=s−mqe=s-mq. Recall the setting of Topic VII. There we took a nonreal eigenvalue at the greatest radius on its ray, with modulus less than one and least realising order at least four. A tower ending on a side gives a weight 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1 and a factor angle uj=Arg⁡(zq−βj)u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(z^q-\beta_j). Multiplication gives the first equality below. Counting the turns along the same paths gives the second.

ze∏j=1m(zq−βj)=∏j=1m(1−βj),eϑ+∑j=1muj=2π(r−mp). z^e\prod_{j=1}^{m}(z^q-\beta_j)=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1-\beta_j), \qquad e\vartheta+\sum_{j=1}^{m}u_j=2\pi(r-mp).

Divide the real equality by mm and collect the two terms involving ϑ\vartheta. Each of the mm factors then has the same share of the total on average, even while their weights differ.

1m∑juj=2πr−sϑm+qϑ−2πp=B+A. \frac1m\sum_j u_j =\frac{2\pi r-s\vartheta}{m}+q\vartheta-2\pi p=B+A.

For a negative ee, the first equation involves a reciprocal power of zz, so z≠0z\ne0. One can also multiply it by zmqz^{mq} to obtain zs∏j(zq−βj)=zmq∏j(1−βj)z^s\prod_j(z^q-\beta_j)=z^{mq}\prod_j(1-\beta_j). This polynomial equation holds at zero as well. Only its nonzero roots can be checked in the original product.

Why the scalar equation has exactly one answer

What radius would we obtain if all mm factors had the same weight β\beta? Put α=1−β\alpha=1-\beta and w=zqw=z^q. All the factor angles would then equal the mean A+BA+B just calculated. Taking absolute values in ze((w−β)/α)m=1z^e((w-\beta)/\alpha)^m=1 gives |w−β|=αρ−e/m|w-\beta|=\alpha\rho^{-e/m}.

Draw the triangle with vertices 00, β\beta and ww. The vector from 00 to ww makes angle AA with the positive real axis. The vector from β\beta to ww makes angle A+BA+B, so the angle inside the triangle at β\beta is π−(A+B)\pi-(A+B). The angle at ww is therefore BB. The sine rule relates their lengths. βsin⁡B=ρqsin⁡(A+B)=αρ−e/msin⁡A. \frac{\beta}{\sin B} =\frac{\rho^q}{\sin(A+B)} =\frac{\alpha\rho^{-e/m}}{\sin A}. The first equality gives β=ρqsin⁡B/sin⁡(A+B)\beta=\rho^q\sin B/\sin(A+B). The second gives α=ρq+e/msin⁡A/sin⁡(A+B)\alpha=\rho^{q+e/m}\sin A/\sin(A+B), where q+e/m=s/mq+e/m=s/m. ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B=sin⁡(A+B). \rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B=\sin(A+B).

All powers are real powers of a positive number. The left side is a continuous, strictly increasing function of ρ\rho. At zero it is zero, whereas the right side is positive. At one the left side exceeds the right side because

Vary the angle inside one Farey interval. If a sequence of angles tends to θ\theta, each corresponding radius lies in [0,1][0,1], so every subsequence has a further convergent subsequence. Taking limits in the equation shows that its limit solves the equation at θ\theta. There is just one such radius, Kn(θ)K_n(\theta). Thus the radii themselves converge to it.

A calculation to check

On the ray θ=5π/7\theta=5\pi/7 we have x=5/14x=5/14. At order seven the fractions on either side are 1/31/3 and 2/52/5, with determinant 2⋅3−1⋅5=12\cdot3-1\cdot5=1 and denominator sum eight. ρ5/2sin⁡(π/7)+ρ3sin⁡(3π/14)=sin⁡(5π/14). \rho^{5/2}\sin(\pi/7)+\rho^3\sin(3\pi/14)=\sin(5\pi/14).

Here e=5−6=−1e=5-6=-1 in the product. Its radius equation still has the two positive exponents 5/25/2 and 33.

Try two values before finding the zero to many places. At ρ=0.94\rho=0.94 the left side minus the target is approximately −0.0114-0.0114. At 0.950.95 it is about 0.01530.0153. Strict increase places the root between these two radii. Repeating the check on successively smaller intervals gives K7(5π/7)≈0.94430114K_7(5\pi/7)\approx0.94430114. In the plot, the horizontal coordinate is this trial radius.

The endpoint convention uses n≥4n\ge4. At order three the nonreal boundary approaches the point −1/2-1/2 as θ\theta tends to π\pi from below, but along the negative real ray the boundary point is −1-1. We will see both pieces of the order-three region in Topic XII.

The bound on the modulus and its attainment

The product reduction allows the coefficients βj\beta_j to vary. Its real argument identity determines the average m−1∑jujm^{-1}\sum_j u_j. For the factors normalized by 1−βj1-\beta_j, we will show that the logarithm of the modulus is a strictly convex function of the argument uju_j. Jensen’s inequality states that the average of these logarithms is at least the function’s value at the average argument. The resulting inequality gives an upper bound on |ω||\omega|, with equality precisely when the βj\beta_j are equal. We then construct stochastic matrices attaining the bound.

For fixed ω\omega, write gj=ωq−βj1−βj,uj=Arg⁡gj.g_j=\frac{\omega^q-\beta_j}{1-\beta_j},\qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}g_j. Then log⁡|gj|\log|g_j| is a strictly convex function of uju_j. This calculation and Jensen’s inequality were already used in [VGNCycle], Lemma 2.2 and Proposition 3.1 for matrices whose nonzero entries lie on a directed nn-cycle and the diagonal. Here Theorem 4.1 obtains the product and a real argument identity from an extremal invariant polygon in the general stochastic eigenvalue problem. Applying the same calculation to these identities gives a bound on |ω||\omega|, with equality precisely when all βj\beta_j agree. We include the short proof to keep the argument self-contained. The resulting equation agrees with the boundary description at a fixed argument in [KirklandLaffeySmigoc], Theorems 1.2 and 4.3; Lemma 4.4. Stochastic realization and the comparison between orders will then show that this equation describes the boundary.

Let f<gf<g be consecutive fractions in Fn∩[0,1/2]F_n\cap[0,1/2], and fix an angle θ\theta with x=θ/(2π)∈(f,g)x=\theta/(2\pi)\in(f,g). Set (p/q,r/s,y)={(f,g,x),f has the smaller denominator,(1−g,1−f,1−x),g has the smaller denominator.(p/q,r/s,y)= \begin{cases} (f,g,x),&f\text{ has the smaller denominator},\\ (1-g,1-f,1-x),&g\text{ has the smaller denominator}. \end{cases} In the chosen interval (p/q,r/s)(p/q,r/s), the lower endpoint p/qp/q has denominator qq, and the upper endpoint r/sr/s has denominator s>qs>q. In the second case, y=1−xy=1-x corresponds to complex conjugation: the angle becomes 2π−θ2\pi-\theta and the modulus is unchanged. In both cases, p/qp/q and r/sr/s are consecutive in FnF_n, with pq<y<rs,q<s,rq−ps=1.\frac pq<y<\frac rs,\qquad q<s,\qquad rq-ps=1. Define (5.1)m=⌊n/q⌋,A=2πq(y−pq),B=2πsm(rs−y).m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor,\qquad A=2\pi q\left(y-\frac pq\right),\qquad B=\frac{2\pi s}{m}\left(\frac rs-y\right). Thus AA is qq times the difference between 2πy2\pi y and the left endpoint angle, while BB is s/ms/m times the difference between the right endpoint angle and 2πy2\pi y.

Definition 5.1. Let n≥3n\ge3, and suppose θ/(2π)\theta/(2\pi) lies strictly between consecutive fractions in Fn∩[0,1/2]F_n\cap[0,1/2]. With m,A,Bm,A,B defined by (5.1), let Kn(θ)K_n(\theta) be the unique solution ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1) of (5.3)ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B=sin⁡(A+B).\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B=\sin(A+B). For n=3n=3, we use the solutions inside the Farey intervals and leave the value at θ=π\theta=\pi, the negative real direction, unspecified.

The left-hand side of (5.3) is continuous and strictly increasing for ρ≥0\rho\ge0. At ρ=0\rho=0 it is zero; at ρ=1\rho=1, its excess over the right-hand side is sin⁡A+sin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B)=4sin⁡(A/2)sin⁡(B/2)sin⁡((A+B)/2)>0.\sin A+\sin B-\sin(A+B) =4\sin(A/2)\sin(B/2)\sin((A+B)/2)>0. Dividing (5.3) by sin⁡θ\sin\theta and taking the limit gives 2ρ3+3ρ2=12\rho^3+3\rho^2=1, whose unique solution in [0,1][0,1] is 1/21/2. Since −1∈Θ3-1\in\Theta_3, the maximal modulus at θ=π\theta=\pi is 11, explaining why no continuous endpoint value is assigned there.

chapters.guideHtml:
Why equal contact weights give the largest radius

In the eight-state example the closing path gives 2ϑ+u1+u2=2π2\vartheta+u_1+u_2=2\pi. Fix ϑ=5π/7\vartheta=5\pi/7. Then the two angles can change only in opposite directions around their mean 2π/72\pi/7. What does moving them apart do to the two factor lengths? If we can answer that question on one line in the complex plane, the same argument will compare all mm factors.

Upper bound — proved here. Under the product and exact real phase hypotheses, no radius can exceed the scalar candidate. We will also identify exactly when equality holds.

Attainment. Equality will tell us which weights to choose. Topic X then uses them as entries of a stochastic matrix with the required eigenvalue.

Two operations put the comparison within reach of ordinary calculus. Divide each factor by its positive weight 1−βj1-\beta_j. Then take the logarithm of its length, so that multiplying lengths becomes adding real numbers.

Fix the interval from Topic VIII, in the orientation with q<sq<s. Thus p/q<ϑ/(2π)<r/sp/q<\vartheta/(2\pi)<r/s, and mm counts the factors. For the two endpoint angles and the closing exponent, put

A=qϑ−2πp,B=(2πr−sϑ)/m,e=s−mq, A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m,\qquad e=s-mq,

Here A,B>0A,B>0 and A+B<πA+B<\pi. Take z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta} with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, together with weights 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1 for 1≤j≤m1\le j\le m. Assume the product and the real angle sum of Topic VIII. In particular we know the number of full turns, which a polynomial equation for zz alone would leave undetermined.

All the factors start from the same complex point. Write its coordinates as

w=zq=ρqeiA=a+ib. w=z^q=\rho^qe^{iA}=a+ib.

Its height b=ρqsin⁡Ab=\rho^q\sin A is positive, and its horizontal coordinate a=ρqcos⁡Aa=\rho^q\cos A is less than one. Draw the line from 11 through ww. We will express its points using the ratio cc of the horizontal distance 1−a1-a to the height bb. For each factor put

gj=w−βj1−βj,uj=Arg⁡(w−βj),c=1−ab>0. g_j=\frac{w-\beta_j}{1-\beta_j},\qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(w-\beta_j),\qquad c=\frac{1-a}{b}>0.

Dividing by 1−βj1-\beta_j changes the length but leaves the angle uju_j unchanged. Performing this division for every factor cancels all the weights on the right of the product, leaving ze∏jgj=1z^e\prod_j g_j=1.

A line becomes a convex function

Fix ww. Where can the point g(β)g(\beta) move? Write g(β)=1+w−11−β. g(\beta)=1+\frac{w-1}{1-\beta}. At β=0\beta=0 we are at ww. Increasing β\beta moves the point farther from 11 along the straight line through 11 and ww. For example, take w=(1+i)/2w=(1+i)/2. One endpoint is g(0)=wg(0)=w, and g(1/2)=ig(1/2)=i lies farther along the same line x+y=1x+y=1. For general ww, its equation follows from a+cb=1a+cb=1.

Re⁡gj+cIm⁡gj=a−βj+cb1−βj=1. \operatorname{Re}g_j+c\operatorname{Im}g_j =\frac{a-\beta_j+cb}{1-\beta_j}=1.

Where does this line meet a ray of angle uju_j? The coordinates of the intersection are |gj|cos⁡uj|g_j|\cos u_j and |gj|sin⁡uj|g_j|\sin u_j. Substitution in the line equation introduces the function

𝒟(u)=cos⁡u+csin⁡u. \mathcal D(u)=\cos u+c\sin u.

The line equation becomes |gj|𝒟(uj)=1|g_j|\mathcal D(u_j)=1. Knowing the direction of the intersection now gives its distance from zero, namely 1/𝒟(uj)1/\mathcal D(u_j).

The ray from zero to ww has angle AA. As β\beta increases from zero to one, w−βw-\beta moves to the left at a fixed positive height, so its direction increases to M=Arg⁡(w−1)∈(A,π)M=\operatorname{Arg}(w-1)\in(A,\pi). Our factor angles satisfy A≤uj<MA\le u_j<M because βj<1\beta_j<1. The coordinates of w−1w-1 give cot⁡M=(a−1)/b=−c\cot M=(a-1)/b=-c. The sine subtraction formula then gives

𝒟(u)=sin⁡(M−u)sin⁡M>0(0<u<M). \mathcal D(u)=\frac{\sin(M-u)}{\sin M}>0 \qquad(0<u<M).

At angle uu the ray meets the line at distance 1/𝒟(u)1/\mathcal D(u) from zero. Its logarithm is therefore the real function

F(u)=−log⁡𝒟(u),0<u<M. F(u)=-\log\mathcal D(u),\qquad 0<u<M.

In particular F(uj)=log⁡|gj|F(u_j)=\log|g_j|. We want to know how two such lengths compare when their angles move apart. It suffices to determine the curvature of FF. We have F′=−𝒟′/𝒟F'=-\mathcal D'/\mathcal D, where 𝒟′=−sin⁡u+ccos⁡u\mathcal D'=-\sin u+c\cos u and 𝒟″=−𝒟\mathcal D''=-\mathcal D. The quotient rule gives

F″(u)=1+(𝒟′(u)𝒟(u))2≥1. F''(u)=1+\left(\frac{\mathcal D'(u)}{\mathcal D(u)}\right)^2\ge1.

The denominator is positive on the entire domain, so these derivatives are valid there. This proves strict convexity. For two angles, the point on the graph at their mean lies strictly below the chord whenever the angles differ. We also need to distinguish weights. For a moving upper-half-plane point X+iYX+iY, its argument derivative is (XY′−YX′)/(X2+Y2)(XY'-YX')/(X^2+Y^2). Here X=a−βX=a-\beta and Y=bY=b, so X′=−1X'=-1 and Y′=0Y'=0. Thus

ddβArg⁡(w−β)=b|w−β|2>0. \frac{d}{d\beta}\operatorname{Arg}(w-\beta) =\frac{b}{|w-\beta|^2}>0.

Thus two factors with the same direction have the same weight. We will use this when we identify the case of equality.

Prediction checkpoint. Keep the average of two unequal factor angles fixed. If both angles are replaced by that common average on the normalised line, should the product of factor sizes increase, decrease, or stay the same? Make a prediction before reading the numbers below.

Hint

At angle uu, the length is eF(u)e^{F(u)}. Taking logarithms changes the question into one about F(u1)+F(u2)F(u_1)+F(u_2). On the graph, what is the height of the midpoint of the chord between these two angles?

Solution

The product decreases. At u‾=(u1+u2)/2\bar u=(u_1+u_2)/2 the height F(u‾)F(\bar u) lies strictly below the chord midpoint when u1≠u2u_1\ne u_2. Hence 2F(u‾)<F(u1)+F(u2)2F(\bar u)<F(u_1)+F(u_2). Exponentiating compares the two products of lengths at this fixed ww. We can try the comparison numerically before imposing the eigenvalue product.

Return to w=(1+i)/2w=(1+i)/2. Read off the angles and lengths of the two factors we already placed on the line. The point ww has angle π/4\pi/4 and length 1/21/\sqrt2. The point ii has angle π/2\pi/2 and length one. Their mean angle is 3π/83\pi/8.

Hence

F(π/4)+F(π/2)2=−14log⁡2≈−0.1733, \frac{F(\pi/4)+F(\pi/2)}2=-\frac14\log2\approx-0.1733,

At the same angle the graph itself has height

F(3π/8)=−log⁡(2cos⁡(π/8))≈−0.2674. F(3\pi/8)=-\log\bigl(\sqrt2\cos(\pi/8)\bigr)\approx-0.2674.

Read the two panels from left to right. In the complex plane the middle ray meets x+y=1x+y=1 at angle 3π/83\pi/8. Its weight is 1−1/21-1/\sqrt2. On the graph at that same angle, the point on the curve lies below the midpoint of the chord. The vertical difference measures exactly how much average logarithmic length we lose by bringing the angles together. The product and turn assumptions enter in the next step.

Applying the average fixed by geometry

Let u‾=(u1+⋯+um)/m\bar u=(u_1+\cdots+u_m)/m. Each angle belongs to (0,M)(0,M), so the mean does too. To compare F(u‾)F(\bar u) with the mean height, draw the tangent at u‾\bar u. Since F″>0F''>0, its slope F′(u‾)F'(\bar u) is smaller than F′(v)F'(v) to the right of u‾\bar u and larger to the left. Integrating the slope gives

F(u)≥F(u‾)+F′(u‾)(u−u‾), F(u)\ge F(\bar u)+F'(\bar u)(u-\bar u),

Equality holds at the point of tangency. At any other uu the inequality is strict, because the derivative is strictly increasing, with the integration limits reversed when u<u‾u<\bar u. Add this tangent bound at each uju_j. The slope terms sum to F′(u‾)∑j(uj−u‾)=0F'(\bar u)\sum_j(u_j-\bar u)=0 by the definition of the mean. Dividing by mm leaves

F(u‾)≤1m∑jF(uj). F(\bar u)\le\frac1m\sum_j F(u_j).

This proves Jensen’s inequality for FF. A single angle different from u‾\bar u makes the sum strictly larger. Thus equality holds exactly when the angles are all equal. Their mean is known from the real turn count in Topic VII.

u‾=1m∑juj=2π(r−mp)−eϑm=A+B. \bar u=\frac1m\sum_j u_j =\frac{2\pi(r-mp)-e\vartheta}{m}=A+B.

On the ray at the mean angle A+BA+B, the line Re⁡g+cIm⁡g=1\operatorname{Re}g+c\operatorname{Im}g=1 meets the ray at distance 1/𝒟(A+B)1/\mathcal D(A+B). Jensen says that this distance is at most the geometric mean of the actual distances |g1|,…,|gm||g_1|,\ldots,|g_m|. The product equation tells us that mean exactly. Taking absolute values in ze∏jgj=1z^e\prod_jg_j=1 gives ∏j|gj|=ρ−e\prod_j |g_j|=\rho^{-e}, even for e<0e<0. Taking logarithms gives ∑jF(uj)=−elog⁡ρ\sum_jF(u_j)=-e\log\rho. In logarithms and then in reciprocals the same bound reads

F(A+B)≤−emlog⁡ρ,𝒟(A+B)≥ρe/m. F(A+B)\le-\frac em\log\rho, \qquad \mathcal D(A+B)\ge\rho^{e/m}.

It remains to express the bound in terms of the radius. Replace cc by (1−ρqcos⁡A)/(ρqsin⁡A)(1-\rho^q\cos A)/(\rho^q\sin A) and put the two terms in 𝒟(A+B)\mathcal D(A+B) over the same denominator. The terms multiplied by ρq\rho^q combine to sin⁡(A−(A+B))=−sin⁡B\sin(A-(A+B))=-\sin B, giving

𝒟(A+B)=sin⁡(A+B)−ρqsin⁡Bρqsin⁡A. \mathcal D(A+B) =\frac{\sin(A+B)-\rho^q\sin B}{\rho^q\sin A}.

Every factor in the denominator is positive. On multiplying through, the term ρe/mρq\rho^{e/m}\rho^q becomes ρs/m\rho^{s/m} because e=s−mqe=s-mq. We obtain

ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B≤sin⁡(A+B). \rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B\le\sin(A+B).

If ρ\rho exceeded KnK_n, strict increase of the left side would make it larger than the right. Thus ρ≤Kn\rho\le K_n. All steps from Jensen’s inequality to this bound were equalities or multiplication by positive quantities. Consequently ρ=Kn\rho=K_n precisely when all factor angles coincide. Their strict increase with β\beta makes this equivalent to β1=⋯=βm\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_m.

Changed-hypothesis checkpoint. Keep the product and the factor assumptions, but replace the real phase identity by equality only modulo 2π2\pi. A student proposes to use exactly the same Jensen calculation and conclude ρ≤Kn\rho\le K_n. Which step no longer follows? Does the convexity calculation itself fail?

Hint

Allow an unknown integer kk in eϑ+∑juj=2π(r−mp)+2πke\vartheta+\sum_j u_j=2\pi(r-mp)+2\pi k. What average does this give?

Solution

Jensen’s inequality still holds at the actual average, because every uju_j and its average lie in (0,M)(0,M). What fails is identifying that average with the known angle A+BA+B. With only the congruence, we know instead

u‾=A+B+2πkm \bar u=A+B+\frac{2\pi k}{m}

for some integer kk. Convexity still compares the product with the value at this actual mean. To evaluate the scalar bound at A+BA+B, however, we have to know k=0k=0. The product determines angles only up to full turns. Following the vertices in Topic VII is what determined that missing integer.

Return to the ray through the eight-state example

For ϑ=5π/7\vartheta=5\pi/7 in the interval (1/3,3/8)(1/3,3/8) at order eight, q=3q=3, s=8s=8, m=2m=2. Hence A=B=π/7A=B=\pi/7. Dividing the scalar bound by sin⁡(π/7)>0\sin(\pi/7)>0 gives ρ4+ρ3≤2cos⁡(π/7). \rho^4+\rho^3\le 2\cos(\pi/7). Try the radius 0.980.98 from the overview on the factor line. Here w=0.983eiπ/7≈0.8480+0.4084iw=0.98^3e^{i\pi/7}\approx0.8480+0.4084i, so c=(1−Re⁡w)/Im⁡w≈0.3723c=(1-\operatorname{Re}w)/\operatorname{Im}w\approx0.3723. At the mean angle the intersection lies at distance 1cos⁡(2π/7)+csin⁡(2π/7)≈1.0935. \frac{1}{\cos(2\pi/7)+c\sin(2\pi/7)}\approx1.0935. If two contact weights produced this radius on the eight-state arc, the geometric mean of their factor lengths would have to be ρ−e/m=1/0.98≈1.0204\rho^{-e/m}=1/0.98\approx1.0204. Even the smallest geometric mean compatible with that angle is larger. This is how a chord inequality for a fixed ww rules out a trial radius.

The closing path fixed the sum u1+u2=4π/7u_1+u_2=4\pi/7. If one of these angles exceeds 2π/72\pi/7, the other is smaller by the same amount. Strict convexity makes the displayed inequality strict. Thus a point attaining the equality radius requires u1=u2=2π/7u_1=u_2=2\pi/7, and the two averaging rows then have the same weight. We can already predict a feature of the attaining matrix before constructing it.

Check the source of strictness

For two factors we can even estimate the cost of separating their angles. Write them as u‾−h\bar u-h and u‾+h\bar u+h in (0,M)(0,M), with h≠0h\ne0. The chord joining their graph points has its midpoint at u‾\bar u. Comparing its height with the height of the curve gives

F(u‾−h)+F(u‾+h)2>F(u‾). \frac{F(\bar u-h)+F(\bar u+h)}2>F(\bar u).

One can even measure the loss. The function F(u)−u2/2F(u)-u^2/2 has nonnegative second derivative. Apply its midpoint inequality at u‾−h\bar u-h and u‾+h\bar u+h. The quadratic terms contribute [(u‾−h)2+(u‾+h)2−2u‾2]/4=h2/2[(\bar u-h)^2+(\bar u+h)^2-2\bar u^2]/4=h^2/2, so the displayed difference is at least h2/2h^2/2. These unequal arguments therefore produce a strict scalar inequality and a radius strictly below the candidate. When m=1m=1, equality of all weights is automatic; the one-factor product and the specified real phase already force the scalar equality. Topic X supplies the missing existence step by building a stochastic matrix at the equality radius.
