Building a matrix that reaches the bound

At order four we found the candidate (1+i)/2(1+i)/2. Can we produce a stochastic matrix with that eigenvalue? Let C4C_4 shift the four coordinates of a column vector one place, so that C4(1,i,−1,−i)T=i(1,i,−1,−i)TC_4(1,i,-1,-i)^T=i(1,i,-1,-i)^T. At each state, stay with probability 1/21/2 and take the next step with probability 1/21/2. The transition matrix is (I+C4)/2(I+C_4)/2. Applied to the same vector, it multiplies it by (1+i)/2(1+i)/2.

For a general arc, one row that chooses between staying and moving no longer suffices. Instead we let it choose between two return paths. Their lengths will supply the powers of zz in the product equation.

Upper bound — supplied by Topic IX. A product with the required real winding is bounded by the candidate, with equal weights precisely at equality.

Attainment. For every ray we will put the candidate point into the spectrum of an explicit stochastic matrix. Comparing the upper bound at different matrix orders remains for Topics XI and XII.

Fix an open Farey interval at order nn, in the orientation of Topic VIII. Its endpoints are p/q<r/sp/q<r/s with q<sq<s, its angle is ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y, and it gives m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor factors. Use the candidate radius ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) and put z=ρeiϑz=\rho e^{i\vartheta}. With A=qϑ−2πpA=q\vartheta-2\pi p and B=(2πr−sϑ)/mB=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m, the two lengths obtained from the triangle in Topic VIII give the row weights

α=ρs/msin⁡Asin⁡(A+B),β=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B). \alpha=\frac{\rho^{s/m}\sin A}{\sin(A+B)},\qquad \beta=\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}.

The scalar equation gives α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, and both sines in the numerators are positive. To recover the complex factor, compare zq=ρqeiAz^q=\rho^q e^{iA} with a point in direction A+BA+B. Subtracting a real β\beta leaves the height ρqsin⁡A\rho^q\sin A fixed, so the length along that direction has to be ρqsin⁡A/sin⁡(A+B)\rho^q\sin A/\sin(A+B). The horizontal difference is ρq(cosA−sin⁡Acos⁡(A+B)sin⁡(A+B))=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B)=β. \rho^q\left(\cos A-\frac{\sin A\cos(A+B)}{\sin(A+B)}\right) =\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}=\beta . Together the two coordinates give

zq−β=ρqsin⁡Asin⁡(A+B)ei(A+B)=αρq−s/mei(A+B). z^q-\beta =\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{\sin(A+B)}e^{i(A+B)} =\alpha\rho^{q-s/m}e^{i(A+B)}.

The direction of zq−βz^q-\beta is therefore A+BA+B, precisely the mean angle required in Topic IX. To see what happens to the directions when we multiply mm copies of this factor and include the closing power of zz, use

(s−mq)ϑ+m(A+B)=2π(r−mp) (s-mq)\vartheta+m(A+B)=2\pi(r-mp)

The right side is a whole number of turns, so the complex number with this argument and positive modulus is positive real. The lengths from the factor identity give zs−mq(zq−β)m=αmz^{s-mq}(z^q-\beta)^m=\alpha^m. Multiplying by zmqz^{mq} and using α=1−β\alpha=1-\beta yields the Ito equation

zs(zq−β)m=(1−β)mzmq. z^s(z^q-\beta)^m=(1-\beta)^mz^{mq}.

The transition graph

The graph can be built with a separate weight βj∈[0,1]\beta_j\in[0,1] for every block j=0,…,m−1j=0,\ldots,m-1. Write αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j. For now assume q<sq<s and s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q, and let n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. In block jj, label the qq states vj,0,…,vj,q−1v_{j,0},\ldots,v_{j,q-1}. From each state before the last, move to the next with probability one. At the last state there are two choices. The weight βj\beta_j takes us back to the start of this block. The weight αj\alpha_j takes us towards the next block, with the last connection specified below. For q=1q=1 the return to the start is a loop.

A directed arrow of weight aa from vertex uu to vertex vv means that the matrix entry MuvM_{uv} is aa, where MM denotes the transition matrix. Rows describe departure vertices. At the last vertex of a block the row sum is βj+αj=1\beta_j+\alpha_j=1. Every other vertex has a single outgoing arrow of weight one. Thus MM is row-stochastic. We use MM for the matrix to distinguish it from the scalar angle AA.

Keep track of what the graph and the polygon each label. A vertex uu of the graph is a state and indexes a row. Its complex coordinate xux_u comes from a chosen eigenvector. Distinct states can have the same coordinate, and a coordinate can lie inside the convex hull of the others. To draw row uu, attach the point xvx_v to the end of each outgoing arrow and take their weighted average. The equation λxu=∑vMuvxv\lambda x_u=\sum_v M_{uv}x_v says that this average is where multiplication by λ\lambda sends xux_u.

For instance, take a block on states 0,1,20,1,2, with the next block starting at 33. Compare the row at 00, which offers a single move, with the row at 22, which offers two.

Outgoing arrows Nonzero entries when the weights are positive What the row gives
0→10\to1 with probability one M01=1M_{01}=1 x1=λx0x_1=\lambda x_0
From 22, return to 00 with probability β0\beta_0 or move to 33 with probability α0\alpha_0. M20=β0M_{20}=\beta_0, M23=α0M_{23}=\alpha_0 λx2=β0x0+α0x3\lambda x_2=\beta_0x_0+\alpha_0x_3

Each arrow accounts for one summand. Only after summing the outgoing arrows do we know the image of the coordinate at their common starting state. Whether each coordinate is a corner of the polygon is a further question. Topic XIV will verify this for all eight states of the worked example.

Read the first two deterministic rows together. They give x2=λx1=λ2x0x_2=\lambda x_1=\lambda^2x_0. Substitute this into the branching row shown in the table to obtain

λx2=β0x0+α0x3,(λ3−β0)x0=α0x3. \lambda x_2=\beta_0x_0+\alpha_0x_3, \qquad (\lambda^3-\beta_0)x_0=\alpha_0x_3.

For a block of length qq there are q−1q-1 steps of weight one before this last row. They replace each intermediate coordinate by a power of λ\lambda times the first one, giving the factor λq−βj\lambda^q-\beta_j. On multiplying across blocks the coordinate at a shared end cancels. Where the final arrow returns decides which power of λ\lambda is still needed to close the path.

Always choose the return within a given block and we have a cycle of length qq. Its arrow weights multiply to βj\beta_j because the other weights are one. Instead choose the connection to the next block at each exit. Connecting the last state straight back to the first would give a cycle of length mqmq. We want length ss, so we adjust just that last connection.

Suppose first that s≤mqs\le mq. We need to omit d=mq−sd=mq-s steps. Since s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q we have d<qd<q, so the state v0,dv_{0,d} exists in the first block. End the final connecting arrow there. The cycle now omits exactly the states v0,0,…,v0,d−1v_{0,0},\ldots,v_{0,d-1}, none when d=0d=0. It visits ss of the mqmq states.

When s>mqs>mq, keep the return to the first state but insert s−mqs-mq new states on the way. Choose this route with the usual weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1} at the last block and give each subsequent step probability one. Now the connecting cycle visits all ss states. Together the two constructions give n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\} states.

For the example from Topic VII, q=3q=3, m=2m=2 and s=8s=8. The two blocks use six states. Send the last connecting arrow from state 55 through the two additional states 66 and 77 before returning to 00. Following the connecting arrows now uses eight steps, while taking a local return still uses three. Writing down the eigenvector rows along these routes recovers the two factors with exponent three and the extra power z2z^2 found in the closing path.

Why these cycles determine the polynomial

Expand det⁡(tI−M)\det(tI-M) by permutations. If a term selects a nondiagonal entry in row uu, its column is the next state of an arrow out of uu. A permutation uses each column once, so these moves form directed cycles with disjoint vertices. A cycle of length ℓ≥2\ell\ge2 has permutation sign (−1)ℓ−1(-1)^{\ell-1}. Its ℓ\ell entries from −M-M contribute another (−1)ℓ(-1)^\ell, leaving a single minus sign times the product of arrow weights. At a fixed vertex the diagonal entry t−Miit-M_{ii} lets us choose either tt or a loop of weight MiiM_{ii} with the same minus sign.

In block jj we can leave all its qq vertices unused, contributing tqt^q, or take its return cycle, contributing −βj-\beta_j. Different blocks use disjoint vertices, so these choices multiply. Any states outside the mm blocks still contribute tt. Thus the terms using only local cycles sum to

tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj). t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j).

The connecting ss-cycle meets every local cycle, so it can only be selected alone. Its contribution is −tn0−s∏jαj-t^{n_0-s}\prod_j\alpha_j. To exhaust the possibilities, start a simple cycle at a block’s last vertex. If its first arrow is a local return, the next q−1q-1 steps lead straight back to that vertex and the cycle is complete. Thus a cycle containing any local return is one of the local cycles. A cycle using only connecting exits has all its steps forced. It is the one of length ss. This argument includes loops when q=1q=1. Consequently

det⁡(tI−M)=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj)−tn0−s∏j=0m−1(1−βj). \det(tI-M) =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j) -t^{n_0-s}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-\beta_j).

The exponent n0−mqn_0-mq counts the states outside the blocks, while n0−sn_0-s counts those outside the connecting cycle. Both counts are nonnegative. We have therefore obtained the characteristic polynomial directly, with the correct multiplicity even at t=0t=0.

Now choose every βj\beta_j equal to the weight β\beta calculated from the scalar radius. At our point z≠0z\ne0 the Ito equation and det⁡(zI−M)=0\det(zI-M)=0 differ only by a power of zz. Hence MM has the desired eigenvalue. For these Farey endpoints, q+s>nq+s>n gives s>n−q≥(m−1)qs>n-q\ge(m-1)q, exactly the condition needed for the last connecting arrow. Also s≤ns\le n and mq≤nmq\le n. If n0<nn_0<n, adjoining an identity block supplies the remaining states and keeps zz as an eigenvalue. When the interval was reflected, complex conjugation gives the eigenvalue on the original ray because MM is real.

A six-state construction to check

Take two blocks of three states, labelled 0,1,20,1,2 and 3,4,53,4,5, and ask for a connecting cycle of length five. Inside the blocks use 0→1→20\to1\to2 and 3→4→53\to4\to5, with weight one at every step. The two exits from 22 go to 00 and 33 with weights β0\beta_0 and 1−β01-\beta_0. At 55 return to 33 with weight β1\beta_1 or go to 11 with weight 1−β11-\beta_1. This last arrow skips state 00, giving the five-cycle 1→2→3→4→5→11\to2\to3\to4\to5\to1. The two three-cycles can appear in the same determinant term. The five-cycle meets both, so its term contains neither. We obtain

det⁡(tI−M)=(t3−β0)(t3−β1)−t(1−β0)(1−β1). \det(tI-M)=(t^3-\beta_0)(t^3-\beta_1)-t(1-\beta_0)(1-\beta_1).

We can also check the five terms one at a time. Each chosen cycle contributes a minus sign, and each unused state contributes a factor tt.

no cyclet6first local cycle only−β0t3second local cycle only−β1t3both local cycles+β0β1connecting cycle only−α0α1t \begin{array}{c|c} \text{no cycle} & t^6\\ \text{first local cycle only} & -\beta_0t^3\\ \text{second local cycle only} & -\beta_1t^3\\ \text{both local cycles} & +\beta_0\beta_1\\ \text{connecting cycle only} & -\alpha_0\alpha_1t \end{array}

Selecting both local cycles gives two minus signs, hence the positive constant term. Selecting the five-cycle leaves state 00 outside it, hence its factor tt.

Can we see that extra tt in the eigenvector itself? Write xjx_j for its entries. The four arrows of weight one give x1=tx0x_1=tx_0, x2=t2x0x_2=t^2x_0, x4=tx3x_4=tx_3 and x5=t2x3x_5=t^2x_3. Only the two branching rows remain. They read

(t3−β0)x0=α0x3,(t3−β1)x3=α1x1=α1tx0. (t^3-\beta_0)x_0=\alpha_0x_3,\qquad (t^3-\beta_1)x_3=\alpha_1x_1=\alpha_1t x_0.

The final arrow enters state 11. Its coordinate is already one multiplication by tt beyond x0x_0. When 0<β0,β1<10<\beta_0,\beta_1<1, we can use these two rows to construct the vector. Set x0=1x_0=1 and take x3=(t3−β0)/α0x_3=(t^3-\beta_0)/\alpha_0 from the first equation. The second row now holds exactly when (t3−β0)(t3−β1)=α0α1t(t^3-\beta_0)(t^3-\beta_1)=\alpha_0\alpha_1t. Every root of the polynomial gives six coordinates satisfying the original rows.

For the weights β0=0.4\beta_0=0.4 and β1=0.7\beta_1=0.7 in the drawing, the product of the two connecting weights is 0.6⋅0.3=0.180.6\cdot0.3=0.18. The polynomial is t6−1.1t3−0.18t+0.28t^6-1.1t^3-0.18t+0.28. At t=1t=1 it vanishes, and the construction gives x3=(1−0.4)/0.6=1x_3=(1-0.4)/0.6=1. The four deterministic rows then give the familiar eigenvector of all ones.

Use the same graph to construct a nonconstant eigenvector

Keep the arrows in the drawing and give both local returns a common weight 0<β<10<\beta<1. Can we choose it so that t=1/4t=1/4 is an eigenvalue? With x0=1x_0=1 the two branching equations reduce to x32=tx_3^2=t. Take x3=−1/2x_3=-1/2. As the angle increases from left to right, does each weight between zero and one occur exactly once? To find out, follow the radius ρ=ρ(ϑ)\rho=\rho(\vartheta) along the interval. Allowing the block weights to differ still gives a stochastic matrix. To decide whether one of its eigenvalues reaches this particular arc, we need its factor angles as well as its characteristic equation. The construction here selects the root attaining that bound among the roots of the equal-weight matrix.

Stochastic realization of the bound

To attain the bound, we construct a matrix using the graph pattern of Johnson and Paparella [JP], Theorem 3.2. We give the construction explicitly below, verify that the matrix is row-stochastic, and derive its characteristic polynomial directly. The graph contains mm cycles of length qq, joined by connections forming a further cycle of length ss. In cycle jj, the edge returning to its starting vertex has weight βj\beta_j, while the connection to the next cycle has weight 1−βj1-\beta_j. We allow the βj\beta_j to vary independently. For the polynomial calculation, we group the determinant terms according to directed cycles with no vertices in common. Taking all βj\beta_j equal will produce a stochastic eigenvalue attaining the bound. Appendix B describes the structure of this matrix family and its limits at the Farey endpoints.

Let ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) for an angle inside a Farey interval, and put ω=ρe2πiy\omega=\rho e^{2\pi i y}, using the endpoint choice and parameters above. Choose the common weights (5.7)α=ρs/msin⁡Asin⁡(A+B),β=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B).\alpha=\frac{\rho^{s/m}\sin A}{\sin(A+B)},\qquad \beta=\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}. Both quotients are positive, and (5.3) gives α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, so α,β∈(0,1)\alpha,\beta\in(0,1). Comparing real and imaginary parts gives (5.8)ωq−β=ρqsin⁡Asin⁡(A+B)ei(A+B)=αρq−s/mei(A+B).\omega^q-\beta =\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{\sin(A+B)}e^{i(A+B)} =\alpha\rho^{q-s/m}e^{i(A+B)}. The positive coefficient in (5.8) shows that every factor ωq−β\omega^q-\beta has argument A+BA+B. Moreover, (s−mq)2πy+m(A+B)=2π(r−mp).(s-mq)2\pi y+m(A+B)=2\pi(r-mp). Raising (5.8) to the mm-th power and using this equality gives (5.9)ωs(ωq−β)m=αmωmq.\omega^s(\omega^q-\beta)^m=\alpha^m\omega^{mq}. Equation (5.9) is the Ito equation, and the displayed argument equality gives the real identity in (5.4) with all coefficients equal. If y=1−xy=1-x, conjugating ω\omega restores the original argument θ\theta.

For n≥4n\ge4, fix a Farey interval with the parameters in (5.1). We show that, as ϑ=2πy\vartheta=2\pi y increases from 2πp/q2\pi p/q to 2πr/s2\pi r/s, β(ϑ)\beta(\vartheta) decreases strictly from 11 to 00. Thus each β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) corresponds to exactly one point of this candidate arc.

Write ρ=ρ(ϑ)\rho=\rho(\vartheta) for the solution of (5.3), and define ℛ(ρ,ϑ)=ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B−sin⁡(A+B),\mathcal R(\rho,\vartheta) =\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B-\sin(A+B), where A=qϑ−2πpA=q\vartheta-2\pi p and B=(2πr−sϑ)/mB=(2\pi r-s\vartheta)/m. Its derivative with respect to ρ\rho is ℛρ=smρs/m−1sin⁡A+qρq−1sin⁡B>0.\mathcal R_\rho =\frac{s}{m}\rho^{s/m-1}\sin A+q\rho^{q-1}\sin B>0. The mean-value theorem, applied in ρ\rho and in ϑ\vartheta, together with continuity of ρ(ϑ)\rho(\vartheta), gives ρ′=−ℛϑℛρ\rho'=-\frac{\mathcal R_\vartheta}{\mathcal R_\rho} along the curve. This derivative is continuous, and repeated differentiation shows that ρ\rho is smooth. Formula (5.7) then makes β\beta smooth as well. Primes below denote derivatives with respect to ϑ\vartheta.

Set e=s−mqe=s-mq and H(ω,β)=ωe(ωq−β)m−(1−β)m.H(\omega,\beta)=\omega^e(\omega^q-\beta)^m-(1-\beta)^m. For ω≠0\omega\ne0, this is complex differentiable even if e<0e<0, and Hω=ωe−1(ωq−β)m−1(sωq−eβ).H_\omega =\omega^{e-1}(\omega^q-\beta)^{m-1} (s\omega^q-e\beta). Because Im⁡(ωq)=ρqsin⁡A>0\operatorname{Im}(\omega^q)=\rho^q\sin A>0, both ωq−β\omega^q-\beta and sωq−eβs\omega^q-e\beta are nonzero. Together with ω≠0\omega\ne0, this gives Hω≠0H_\omega\ne0. With ω(ϑ)=ρ(ϑ)eiϑ\omega(\vartheta)=\rho(\vartheta)e^{i\vartheta}, equation (5.9) gives H(ω(ϑ),β(ϑ))=0H(\omega(\vartheta),\beta(\vartheta))=0. Differentiating yields Hωω′+Hββ′=0,ω′=eiϑ(ρ′+iρ)≠0.H_\omega\omega'+H_\beta\beta'=0,\qquad \omega'=e^{i\vartheta}(\rho'+i\rho)\ne0. The last inequality follows from ρ>0\rho>0. If β′=0\beta'=0, the first identity would force Hωω′=0H_\omega\omega'=0, a contradiction. Thus β′\beta' never vanishes, and its continuity makes its sign constant on the interval.

Since s,mq≥3s,mq\ge3, the endpoint limits ρ→1\rho\to1 and (5.7) give β→1\beta\to1 at y=p/qy=p/q and β→0\beta\to0 at y=r/sy=r/s. These limits force β′<0\beta'<0. If y=1−xy=1-x, then ϑ=2π−θ\vartheta=2\pi-\theta, so increasing ϑ\vartheta means decreasing the original angle θ\theta.

Theorem 5.3 (Stochastic realization). Let m,q,sm,q,s be positive integers with s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q, and set n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. For each β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1), there is a real row-stochastic matrix of order n0n_0 having every nonzero solution λ\lambda of (5.10)λs(λq−β)m=(1−β)mλmq\lambda^s(\lambda^q-\beta)^m=(1-\beta)^m\lambda^{mq} as an eigenvalue.

More generally, for any 𝛃=(β0,…,βm−1)∈[0,1]m,αj=1−βj,\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m-1})\in[0,1]^m, \qquad \alpha_j=1-\beta_j, there is a row-stochastic matrix A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) of order n0n_0 with (5.11)det⁡(tI−A(𝛃))=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj)−tn0−s∏j=0m−1αj.\det(tI-A(\boldsymbol\beta)) =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j) -t^{n_0-s}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}\alpha_j. Every entry is 00, 11, βj\beta_j, or 1−βj1-\beta_j for some jj, so the matrix depends continuously on 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta. Taking all βj=β\beta_j=\beta gives the matrix in the first assertion.

Proof of Theorem 5.3

Proof. We first construct the family A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) and compute its characteristic polynomial. Taking all parameters equal will then give the eigenvalues in the first assertion.

A directed graph specifies the matrix entries. Its vertices index both the rows and the columns, and an arrow from uu to vv carries a nonnegative number wew_e, called its weight, which contributes wew_e to row uu, column vv: Auv=∑arrows e:u→vwe.A_{uv}=\sum_{\text{arrows }e:u\to v}w_e. An empty sum is zero. If two arrows have the same starting and ending vertices, their weights are added in that one matrix entry. We will choose the weights leaving each vertex to sum to one. Thus each row distributes a total of one among its destination columns, and AuvA_{uv} can be read as the probability of moving from uu to vv in one step.

For each j=0,…,m−1j=0,\ldots,m-1, create a block of vertices vj,0,…,vj,q−1.v_{j,0},\ldots,v_{j,q-1}. The block after m−1m-1 is block zero. Within block jj, draw the arrows vj,k→vj,k+1v_{j,k}\to v_{j,k+1} with weight one for 0≤k<q−10\le k<q-1. At its last vertex vj,q−1v_{j,q-1}, draw one arrow back to the first vertex vj,0v_{j,0} with weight βj\beta_j, and another to the first vertex of the following block with weight αj=1−βj\alpha_j=1-\beta_j. These two numbers divide the row’s unit total between the two arrows. The first arrow closes a cycle of qq steps within the block, whose weights multiply to βj\beta_j. Following the arrows labelled αj\alpha_j instead joins the blocks in the order 0,1,…,m−1,00,1,\ldots,m-1,0. We adjust only the arrow labelled αm−1\alpha_{m-1}, from the last block back to block zero, so that this latter cycle has length ss.

If s≤mqs\le mq, redirect that arrow to v0,dv_{0,d}, where d=mq−sd=mq-s, keeping its weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1}. The hypothesis s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q gives 0≤d<q0\le d<q, so this vertex exists. The graph still has mqmq vertices. The cycle through all blocks now omits the first dd vertices of block zero and therefore has length mq−d=smq-d=s.

If s>mqs>mq, replace that arrow by a path containing s−mqs-mq new vertices between vm−1,q−1v_{m-1,q-1} and v0,0v_{0,0}. Its first arrow carries weight αm−1\alpha_{m-1}, and all subsequent arrows carry weight one. This adds s−mqs-mq steps to the cycle through all blocks, giving length ss and a graph with ss vertices. Each new vertex has just one outgoing arrow of weight one.

In both cases, every row has either one outgoing weight equal to one or the two outgoing weights βj\beta_j and αj\alpha_j, whose sum is one. Adding weights with the same destination preserves that sum. All entries are nonnegative, so AA is row-stochastic of order n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. Its entries are 00, 11, βj\beta_j, or αj\alpha_j, as asserted.

If m=1m=1 and s=qs=q, the two arrows from the last vertex of the only block both end at its first vertex. They therefore give the single matrix entry Av0,q−1,v0,0=β0+α0=1.A_{v_{0,q-1},v_{0,0}}=\beta_0+\alpha_0=1. The resulting matrix moves each vertex to the next and the last back to the first: it is the cyclic permutation matrix of order qq. Its characteristic polynomial is tq−1=(tq−β0)−α0,t^q-1=(t^q-\beta_0)-\alpha_0, which is (5.11) in this case. In every other case the two arrows from the last vertex of each block have distinct destinations.

Figure 3 illustrates the two constructions for m=2m=2 and q=3q=3, with common weights βj=β\beta_j=\beta and αj=α\alpha_j=\alpha. Its label δ0=mq−s\delta_0=mq-s describes the route from the last block into block zero: if δ0≥0\delta_0\ge0, the arrow ends at v0,δ0v_{0,\delta_0}; if δ0<0\delta_0<0, the route contains −δ0-\delta_0 added vertices before reaching v0,0v_{0,0}.

Source diagram.

Graphs of the realizing matrices for m=2m=2 and q=3q=3, with common weights βj=β\beta_j=\beta and αj=α=1−β\alpha_j=\alpha=1-\beta. Each arrow’s label contributes that amount to the matrix entry with its starting vertex as row and its ending vertex as column; unlabelled arrows contribute one. In (a)(a), the arrow from v1,2v_{1,2} labelled α\alpha ends at v0,1v_{0,1}, giving a cycle of five steps through both blocks in a graph with six vertices. In (b)(b), this route passes through the added vertex ww, giving a cycle of seven steps in a graph with seven vertices. The arrows labelled β\beta close the two three-step cycles within the blocks. The original drawing is available in the supplied manuscript PDF.

For the remaining cases, we compute the determinant by listing the possible simple directed cycles: closed paths following the arrows, with no repeated vertex except the start at the end. The product of the arrow weights along a cycle is the product of the corresponding matrix entries in the determinant expansion.

Every such cycle contains the last vertex of a block. If it uses the arrow from that vertex back to the first vertex of the same block, the arrows within the block bring it back to the same last vertex. It is therefore exactly that block’s qq-cycle, whose weights multiply to βj\beta_j. If it uses none of these arrows back to first vertices, it follows the paths joining successive blocks and is the single ss-cycle, whose weights multiply to ∏jαj\prod_j\alpha_j. The mm cycles within blocks have no vertices in common, while the ss-cycle contains the last vertex of every block and hence meets each of them. This also covers q=1q=1, when the cycles within blocks are loops, and m=1m=1, s<qs<q, when the arrow labelled α0\alpha_0 closes a shorter cycle inside the only block.

In the Leibniz expansion of det⁡(tI−A)\det(tI-A), select a collection of directed cycles with no vertices in common. A cycle of length ℓ\ell contributes ℓ\ell negative matrix entries and has permutation sign (−1)ℓ−1(-1)^{\ell-1}, giving one minus sign per cycle. A loop is selected by taking the term −Auu-A_{uu} from t−Auut-A_{uu}, so it has the same sign. Every vertex outside the selected cycles contributes tt. Hence a collection of kk cycles covering vv vertices contributes (−1)ktn0−v(-1)^k t^{n_0-v} times the product of its arrow weights.

Any subset JJ of the cycles within blocks can be selected, giving the total contribution ∑J⊆{0,…,m−1}(−1)|J|tn0−q|J|∏j∈Jβj=tn0−mq∏j=0m−1(tq−βj).\sum_{J\subseteq\{0,\ldots,m-1\}} (-1)^{|J|}t^{n_0-q|J|}\prod_{j\in J}\beta_j =t^{n_0-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(t^q-\beta_j). The ss-cycle meets every cycle within a block, so it can only be selected alone. Its contribution is −tn0−s∏jαj-t^{n_0-s}\prod_j\alpha_j. Adding these contributions gives (5.11). Zero arrow weights make the corresponding contributions vanish, so the formula holds for every parameter tuple in [0,1]m[0,1]^m. It is the full characteristic polynomial, including zero roots and their algebraic multiplicities.

Finally, take all βj=β∈(0,1)\beta_j=\beta\in(0,1) and denote the resulting matrix by AβA_\beta. For a nonzero solution λ\lambda of (5.10), multiplying the characteristic polynomial at λ\lambda by λmq+s−n0\lambda^{mq+s-n_0} gives λmq+s−n0det⁡(λI−Aβ)=λs(λq−β)m−(1−β)mλmq=0.\lambda^{mq+s-n_0}\det(\lambda I-A_\beta) =\lambda^s(\lambda^q-\beta)^m-(1-\beta)^m\lambda^{mq}=0. Since λ≠0\lambda\ne0, this implies det⁡(λI−Aβ)=0\det(\lambda I-A_\beta)=0. The matrix λI−Aβ\lambda I-A_\beta is therefore singular, so there is a vector x∈ℂn0x\in\mathbb C^{n_0}, x≠0x\ne0, with (λI−Aβ)x=0(\lambda I-A_\beta)x=0, or equivalently Aβx=λxA_\beta x=\lambda x. Thus λ\lambda is an eigenvalue of AβA_\beta, proving the first assertion. ◻

For n≥4n\ge4, consider the Farey interval used above, with m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor. Farey adjacency gives q+s>nq+s>n, while mq≤nmq\le n and q,s≤nq,s\le n. Therefore s>n−q≥(m−1)q,n0=max⁡{mq,s}≤n.s>n-q\ge(m-1)q,\qquad n_0=\max\{mq,s\}\le n. The realization theorem thus applies. With the weights in (5.7), equation (5.9) makes ω=Kn(θ)e2πiy≠0\omega=K_n(\theta)e^{2\pi i y}\ne0 an eigenvalue of a real row-stochastic matrix of order n0n_0. If y=xy=x, then ω=Kn(θ)eiθ\omega=K_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}. If y=1−xy=1-x, its conjugate has that value and is also an eigenvalue because the matrix is real. Adjoining an identity block if necessary gives order nn and retains this eigenvalue. The endpoint roots of unity are realized by cyclic permutation matrices of orders qq and ss, extended to order nn in the same way. Consequently Kn(θ)eiθ∈ΘnK_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_n on every ray for n≥4n\ge4.

Consider a radial maximum z=ρeiθ∈Θnz=\rho e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_n with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and 0<θ<π0<\theta<\pi. Let N≥4N\ge4 be the least order of a stochastic matrix having zz as an eigenvalue. Since ΘN⊆Θn\Theta_N\subseteq\Theta_n, zz is also maximal on its ray in ΘN\Theta_N. Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 give ρ≤KN(θ)\rho\le K_N(\theta). Theorem 5.3 realizes KN(θ)eiθK_N(\theta)e^{i\theta} in ΘN\Theta_N, giving the reverse inequality. Hence ρ=KN(θ)\rho=K_N(\theta), and the equality condition forces all coefficients βj\beta_j in the geometric product to agree. To identify the boundary at the prescribed order nn, it remains to prove KN(θ)≤Kn(θ)K_N(\theta)\le K_n(\theta) for N≤nN\le n directly from the scalar equations.

Comparing the candidates without assuming the theorem

Keep the ray through e5πi/7e^{5\pi i/7} fixed and allow one more state. Its angular fraction 5/145/14 lies between 1/31/3 and 2/52/5 at order seven. At order eight a new fraction 3/83/8 lies between them. Thus the two equations for the radius use different endpoints. How can we be sure the new equation places its point at least as far from zero?

We can certainly keep a seven-state eigenvalue by adjoining an eighth, absorbing state. That argument concerns eigenvalues of matrices. We still have to compare the two numbers computed by the scalar equations.

Write Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) for the actual largest eigenvalue radius on the ray, and let k≤nk\le n be the least order of a matrix with eigenvalue Rn(θ)eiθR_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}. For k≥4k\ge4, the final proof needs the chain

Rn(θ)≤Kk(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤Rn(θ). R_n(\theta)\le K_k(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le R_n(\theta).

Inequality What we use to prove it
Rn≤KkR_n\le K_k A matrix of least order kk gives the product in Topic VII. Topic IX bounds its radius.
Kk≤KnK_k\le K_n Compare the roots of the two radius equations. We do this below.

The middle inequality is the one we shall establish. If the least order is three, Topic XII uses the triangle description for the initial comparison with K4K_4.

Closing the gap between the candidate and the boundary

Fix an order n≥4n\ge4 and an angle θ\theta. On this ray Topic X constructed a stochastic matrix with eigenvalue Kn(θ)eiθK_n(\theta)e^{i\theta}. Could a different matrix of the same order put an eigenvalue farther along the ray? Write Rn(θ)R_n(\theta) for the greatest radius any such matrix achieves. The construction gives Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n. To prove the other inequality we start at the farthest point itself.

There is a small catch in choosing a matrix for that point. Adjoining a 1×11\times1 identity block turns a three-state example into a four-state example with the very same eigenvalue. The polygon proof uses the smallest order at which the farthest point occurs. We shall find the first three regions directly, then bring the bound at this smallest order back to the order nn with which we began.

Recall that Θn\Theta_n is the set of individual eigenvalues of real row-stochastic n×nn\times n matrices. Such a matrix has nonnegative entries and row sums one. Its action cannot increase the largest absolute coordinate of a vector, so every eigenvalue has modulus at most one. Why does a farthest eigenvalue exist? Take eigenvalues approaching the supremum on a ray, and choose a stochastic matrix for each. All entries lie in [0,1][0,1], so a subsequence of the matrices converges to a matrix AA. The row sums are still one and the entries are still nonnegative. If zz is the limit of the eigenvalues, continuity gives det⁡(zI−A)=0\det(zI-A)=0. Thus AA has the eigenvalue at the end of the ray.

The first three orders

The single entry of a stochastic matrix of order one has to be 11, so Θ1={1}\Theta_1=\{1\}. With two states we can choose the first entry in each row freely. The row sums determine the other entries, giving

A=(a1−ab1−b),a,b∈[0,1]. A=\begin{pmatrix}a&1-a\\b&1-b\end{pmatrix},\qquad a,b\in[0,1].

The column of ones gives the eigenvalue 11. The trace a+1−ba+1-b is the sum of the two eigenvalues, so the other is a−ba-b. This difference lies between −1-1 and 11. For any t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], the choices (a,b)=(t,0)(a,b)=(t,0) and (0,t)(0,t) give tt and −t-t, respectively. Thus Θ2=[−1,1]\Theta_2=[-1,1].

Three states allow a rotation through a third of a turn. Write ξ=e2πi/3\xi=e^{2\pi i/3}. The three points 1,ξ,ξ‾1,\xi,\bar\xi are the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The region consists of this triangle together with one more segment on the real axis. In symbols,

Θ3=conv⁡{1,ξ,ξ‾}∪[−1,−1/2]. \Theta_3=\operatorname{conv}\{1,\xi,\bar\xi\}\ \cup\ [-1,-1/2].

Here conv\operatorname{conv} means all convex combinations. To obtain the upper restriction, let λ=u+iv\lambda=u+iv, v≠0v\ne0, be an eigenvalue. The three eigenvalues are 1,λ,λ‾1,\lambda,\bar\lambda. Nonnegative diagonal entries give 1+2u=tr⁡A≥01+2u=\operatorname{tr}A\ge0. For the two sloping sides we need one more restriction. Each entry (A2)ii(A^2)_{ii} contains aii2a_{ii}^2 and a sum of nonnegative terms aijajia_{ij}a_{ji}. Together with Cauchy–Schwarz for the three diagonal entries, this gives

tr⁡(A2)≥∑iaii2,(tr⁡A)2≤3∑iaii2. \operatorname{tr}(A^2)\ge\sum_i a_{ii}^2,\qquad (\operatorname{tr}A)^2\le3\sum_i a_{ii}^2.

Substituting the eigenvalues gives (1+2u)2≤3(1+2u2−2v2)(1+2u)^2\le3(1+2u^2-2v^2), or 3v2≤(1−u)23v^2\le(1-u)^2. Since u≤1u\le1, the sloping lines are v=±(1−u)/3v=\pm(1-u)/\sqrt3. The trace condition u≥−1/2u\ge-1/2 cuts off their left ends.

Can we reach every point allowed by these inequalities? Take a cyclic permutation matrix C3C_3 and an eigenvector vv for ξ\xi. The same vector satisfies Iv=vIv=v and C32v=ξ2v=ξ‾vC_3^2v=\xi^2v=\bar\xi v. Choose any point a+bξ+cξ‾a+b\xi+c\bar\xi in the triangle, where a,b,c≥0a,b,c\ge0 and a+b+c=1a+b+c=1. With these same coefficients the matrix aI+bC3+cC32aI+bC_3+cC_3^2 is stochastic, and multiplying it by vv gives the chosen point times vv. On the real line we already have all of [−1,1][-1,1] from order two. Adjoining one absorbing state keeps these eigenvalues at order three.

On the vertical side from ξ\xi to −1/2-1/2, the real coordinate of ρeiθ\rho e^{i\theta} is ρcos⁡θ=−1/2\rho\cos\theta=-1/2. Therefore

R3(θ)=−12cos⁡θ(2π/3≤θ<π). R_3(\theta)=-\frac1{2\cos\theta}\qquad(2\pi/3\le\theta<\pi).

At θ=5π/6\theta=5\pi/6 the radius is 1/3≈0.577351/\sqrt3\approx0.57735. Increasing the angle to 11π/1211\pi/12 reduces it to about 0.517640.51764. The radii approach 1/21/2, while the extra real segment gives R3(π)=1R_3(\pi)=1. In the left panel the red segment extends the triangle along the real axis. In the right panel this jump appears as a discontinuity in the radius at π\pi.

Why do we need the scalar radii for this triangle? The order comparison in Topic XI concerns the solutions KnK_n of an equation. To start that comparison at order three, we have to check which solution gives the intersection with a triangle side.

Identify the two triangle sides in the scalar equation

Topic X expresses the boundary equation in terms of equal weights when A,B>0A,B>0 and A+B<πA+B<\pi. These inequalities hold on both open intervals at order three.

On the arc 0<x=θ/(2π)<1/30<x=\theta/(2\pi)<1/3 the smaller denominator is q=1q=1, and s=m=3s=m=3. The two angles in the scalar equation are A=θA=\theta and B=2π/3−θB=2\pi/3-\theta. Both are positive and their sum is 2π/32\pi/3, so we obtain a unique positive root ρ<1\rho<1 and weights α,β>0\alpha,\beta>0 with α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1. Put z=ρeiθz=\rho e^{i\theta}. The product simplifies to (z−β)3=α3(z-\beta)^3=\alpha^3. Which cube root do we take? The factor z−βz-\beta has argument A+B=2π/3A+B=2\pi/3, so z=β+αξz=\beta+\alpha\xi. This is precisely a point on the side joining 11 to ξ\xi.

On the arc 1/3<x<1/21/3<x<1/2 the smaller denominator is on the right. Reflect the ray, taking ϑ=2π−θ\vartheta=2\pi-\theta and w=ρeiϑw=\rho e^{i\vartheta}. Its fraction of a turn, 1−x1-x, now lies between 1/21/2 and 2/32/3. Thus q=2q=2, s=3s=3 and m=1m=1. Substitution gives A=2π−2θA=2\pi-2\theta, B=3θ−2πB=3\theta-2\pi. Both angles are positive for 2π/3<θ<π2\pi/3<\theta<\pi, and their sum is θ<π\theta<\pi. For the root ρ\rho and weights α,β\alpha,\beta obtained here, the product is w(w2−β)=αw(w^2-\beta)=\alpha. Since α+β=1\alpha+\beta=1, the polynomial has a root at one and factors as

w3−βw−α=(w−1)(w2+w+α)=0. w^3-\beta w-\alpha=(w-1)(w^2+w+\alpha)=0.

The nonreal root ww solves w2+w+α=0w^2+w+\alpha=0. A nonreal quadratic root requires 4α−1>04\alpha-1>0, hence 1/4<α<11/4<\alpha<1. Its real part is −1/2-1/2. Conjugating back gives z=−1/2+(i/2)4α−1z=-1/2+(i/2)\sqrt{4\alpha-1}, strictly between −1/2-1/2 and ξ\xi on the vertical side. The selected factor argument and the scalar root’s uniqueness identify the radius in both ranges with the ray’s intersection with the corresponding triangle side.

Now add a fourth state. On (0,1/3)(0,1/3) the new fraction 1/41/4 divides the arc in two. The comparison for a split interval in Topic XI applies on either side because the old angle sum was 2π/32\pi/3. At 1/41/4 itself the new radius is one, while the same ray at order three meets the triangle strictly between two vertices. On (1/3,1/2)(1/3,1/2) the endpoints stay in place and the count rises from one to two. Here we can use the comparison for an extra factor since the old angle sum was θ<π\theta<\pi.

At x=0,1/3,1/2x=0,1/3,1/2 the numbers 1,ξ,−11,\xi,-1 occur already at order three and also at order four. This last endpoint accounts for the tip of the extra real segment. We have now proved R3(θ)≤K4(θ)R_3(\theta)\le K_4(\theta) everywhere in the upper half-plane.

Exactly which points lie on the unit circle?

Every root of unity of order ℓ≤n\ell\le n is an eigenvalue of an ℓ\ell-cycle permutation matrix enlarged to order nn. To prove the converse, suppose Av=λvAv=\lambda v, v≠0v\ne0, and |λ|=1|\lambda|=1. Let M=max⁡j|vj|M=\max_j|v_j| and let SS be the indices attaining this positive maximum. For i∈Si\in S,

M=|∑jaijvj|≤∑jaij|vj|≤M. M=\left|\sum_j a_{ij}v_j\right| \le\sum_j a_{ij}|v_j|\le M.

Why does equality determine the direction of each destination? Divide row ii by its target λvi\lambda v_i, which has modulus M>0M>0. Write wj=vj/(λvi)w_j=v_j/(\lambda v_i). All the wjw_j lie in the unit disk, and their weighted average is the point 11. Taking real parts gives

∑jaij(1−Re⁡wj)=0. \sum_j a_{ij}(1-\operatorname{Re}w_j)=0.

Each summand is nonnegative. A destination with aij>0a_{ij}>0 therefore has real part one. The only point of the unit disk on that vertical line is 11 itself. Thus vj=λviv_j=\lambda v_i at every such destination, even when several different states share this coordinate.

Start at any index of SS and choose an outgoing arrow of positive weight. Its destination is again in SS, since |λvi|=M|\lambda v_i|=M. We can keep going. Stop at the first repeated index and count the ℓ\ell steps since its previous visit. These steps form a cycle with ℓ≤n\ell\le n. Each multiplies the coordinate by λ\lambda. The repeated coordinate is nonzero, so returning to it gives λℓ=1\lambda^\ell=1.

The two inequalities meet

Return to order n≥4n\ge4 and the upper ray chosen at the start. At Farey angles the unit-circle classification gives Rn=Kn=1R_n=K_n=1. At any other angle Topic X gives Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n.

Choose z=Rn(θ)eiθz=R_n(\theta)e^{i\theta} on this non-Farey ray and let k≤nk\le n be its least realising order. The construction gives a positive radius, and the unit-circle classification excludes radius one. Since zz is nonreal, k≥3k\ge3. It lies as far out on the ray in Θk\Theta_k as it does in Θn\Theta_n. A point farther out at order kk would also occur at order nn by adjoining an identity block.

If k=3k=3, the point zz lies in Θ3\Theta_3. We have just compared its outer radius with K4K_4, and Topic XI compares K4K_4 with every subsequent radius up to KnK_n. Starting and ending at the radius we chose gives

|z|≤R3(θ)≤K4(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|. |z|\le R_3(\theta)\le K_4(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le |z|.

If k≥4k\ge4, work at this least order. Topics III–VI choose and arrange a kk-vertex polygon with as few open sides receiving a contact as possible. Topic VII follows the returns on that polygon. Its product and real phase give |z|≤Kk(θ)|z|\le K_k(\theta) by Topic IX. Topic XI then gives

|z|≤Kk(θ)≤Kn(θ)≤|z|. |z|\le K_k(\theta)\le K_n(\theta)\le|z|.

In either case the inequalities start and finish at the same number. Every intermediate value therefore equals |z||z|, in particular Kn(θ)=Rn(θ)K_n(\theta)=R_n(\theta). Since the matrices have real entries, conjugating an eigenvector and its eigenvalue gives another eigenvector and eigenvalue of the same matrix. Reflecting the upper rays now gives the entire lower half of the region.

Read the next diagram from the two ends of the argument. On one side we begin with an unknown matrix reaching the outermost point. On the other, we know every row of a matrix that reaches the candidate radius. The order comparison is what lets these conclusions meet at the same nn.

Retrieval checkpoint. In the main case k≥4k\ge4, identify the ingredient behind each link of Rn≤Kk≤Kn≤RnR_n\le K_k\le K_n\le R_n. Which link uses an explicit stochastic matrix?

Hint

Match the three links with “upper bound”, “independent order comparison”, and “attainment”. Which link requires a matrix having the proposed point as an eigenvalue?

Solution

Topics VII and IX give the least-order upper bound Rn≤KkR_n\le K_k. Topic XI gives Kk≤KnK_k\le K_n. Topic X constructs an eigenvalue at the candidate, giving Kn≤RnK_n\le R_n. The order-three case replaces the first bound by the explicit triangle calculation and the comparison R3≤K4R_3\le K_4.

Finding a point on a reflected arc

For an order-four example, draw the ray at 105∘105^\circ, or 7/247/24 of a turn. Its Farey neighbours are 1/41/4 and 1/31/3. The radius formula of Topic VIII takes the smaller denominator on the left. Complex conjugation sends the two endpoints to 3/43/4 and 2/32/3, respectively. Reading the reflected arc in increasing angle therefore gives

23<1724<34. \frac23<\frac{17}{24}<\frac34.

Use ϑ=2π(17/24)=17π/12\vartheta=2\pi(17/24)=17\pi/12 for this calculation. With p/q=2/3p/q=2/3, r/s=3/4r/s=3/4 and m=1m=1, we get A=3ϑ−4π=π/4A=3\vartheta-4\pi=\pi/4 and B=6π−4ϑ=π/3B=6\pi-4\vartheta=\pi/3. The radius is the unique positive solution of

ρ4sin⁡(π/4)+ρ3sin⁡(π/3)=sin⁡(7π/12). \rho^4\sin(\pi/4)+\rho^3\sin(\pi/3)=\sin(7\pi/12).

Both terms on the left increase with ρ\rho. Solving gives ρ≈0.86752\rho\approx0.86752. Reflection back puts the boundary point at ρe7πi/12\rho e^{7\pi i/12} on the original ray. Real matrix entries ensure that the same matrix has the conjugate pair of eigenvalues, so the radius belongs to both rays.

Filling the region and a check

Every segment from zero to an attainable point is attainable for n≥2n\ge2. One matrix explanation uses a stationary probability row πT\pi^T, satisfying πTA=πT\pi^TA=\pi^T, and the column 𝟏\mathbf1 of ones. If Av=λvAv=\lambda v, multiply by πT\pi^T to obtain πTv=πTAv=λπTv\pi^Tv=\pi^TAv=\lambda\pi^Tv. Thus πTv=0\pi^Tv=0 whenever λ≠1\lambda\ne1. When λ≠1\lambda\ne1 and 0≤t≤10\le t\le1, multiplying this eigenvector by tA+(1−t)𝟏πTtA+(1-t)\mathbf1\pi^T gives tλvt\lambda v. Each row of this matrix is a convex combination of probability rows. The segment [0,1][0,1] is already realised at order two, covering λ=1\lambda=1.

The added matrix 𝟏πT\mathbf1\pi^T resets every row to the same probability distribution. It annihilates this eigenvector because its weighted mean πTv\pi^Tv is zero. For a small exact check, take A=(1/54/54/51/5)A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1/5&4/5\\4/5&1/5\end{smallmatrix}\right), whose vector (1,−1)T(1,-1)^T has eigenvalue −3/5-3/5 and whose stationary row is (1/2,1/2)(1/2,1/2). We know the last point on each ray, and we can reach every point between it and zero. Putting the rays together gives, for n≥4n\ge4,

Θn={reiθ:−π≤θ≤π,0≤r≤Kn(θ)}. \Theta_n=\{re^{i\theta}:-\pi\le\theta\le\pi,\ 0\le r\le K_n(\theta)\}.

Take a nonzero point strictly below the outer radius. Since KnK_n is continuous, the gap stays positive under a sufficiently small change of angle and radius. Thus the point has a neighbourhood in Θn\Theta_n. The origin is interior as well. The positive continuous function KnK_n has a positive minimum on the circle, and the disk of that radius lies in the region.

At the outer radius we have an actual eigenvalue, and arbitrarily close points farther out on its ray lie outside Θn\Theta_n. These and only these outer points therefore form the boundary. The equal-weight matrices of Topic X describe each arc between successive roots of unity. At the real endpoints 11 and −1-1 the upper and lower boundaries meet.

Continue with Topic XIV to follow the eight-state example from return paths through its actual invariant polygon. Topic XIII uses the boundary radius to choose a polygon for measuring contraction.

Measuring a rotation with a polygon

Draw a square centred at the origin, with a horizontal top side. A quarter turn takes it onto itself. An eighth of a turn puts one of its corners above the middle of its top side. The two rotations preserve every Euclidean length, yet the square measures them differently. If we can choose the polygon, how much of this dependence on direction can we remove?

For a fixed rotation and dilation, we can answer the question with the boundary radius from Topic XII. The shape used in Topic XIV gives a concrete example at eight vertices.

Let N≥4N\ge4, take 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, let RθR_\theta denote rotation through θ\theta, and set T=ρRθT=\rho R_\theta with ρ>0\rho>0. Reflection covers the other directions. Choose a polygon PP with at most NN vertices and zero in its interior. Define its gauge by

VP(x)=inf⁡{a>0:x∈aP},x∈ℝ2. V_P(x)=\inf\{a>0:x\in aP\},\qquad x\in\mathbb R^2.

Imagine enlarging a copy of PP from the origin until it first contains xx. Its scale at that instant is VP(x)V_P(x). Multiplying xx by a≥0a\ge0 multiplies the required scale by aa.

For example, take the asymmetric rectangle P=[−1,2]×[−1,1]P=[-1,2]\times[-1,1] and e1=(1,0)e_1=(1,0). Containing e1e_1 requires scale 1/21/2, but containing −e1-e_1 requires scale one. Thus VP(e1)=1/2V_P(e_1)=1/2 and VP(−e1)=1V_P(-e_1)=1. This asymmetry is possible for a gauge. For contraction we seek one factor that controls every vector measured by this gauge.

A factor γ>0\gamma>0 satisfies

TP⊆γP⇔VP(Tx)≤γVP(x)for every x. TP\subseteq\gamma P \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_P(Tx)\le\gamma V_P(x)\quad\text{for every }x.

To see both directions, first note that PP is the unit sublevel set {x:VP(x)≤1}\{x:V_P(x)\le1\}. For x≠0x\ne0, the gauge is positive because PP is bounded. The polygon is closed, so the least scale is attained and x/VP(x)∈Px/V_P(x)\in P. If TP⊆γPTP\subseteq\gamma P, apply the inclusion to this rescaled vector and use homogeneity to obtain the gauge inequality. At x=0x=0 both sides are zero. Conversely, if the inequality holds for every vector, then every x∈Px\in P has VP(x)≤1V_P(x)\le1, so VP(Tx)≤γV_P(Tx)\le\gamma and Tx∈γPTx\in\gamma P.

Identify the plane with ℂ\mathbb C. Dividing TP⊆γPTP\subseteq\gamma P by γ\gamma asks whether multiplication by z=(ρ/γ)eiθz=(\rho/\gamma)e^{i\theta} takes PP into itself. Topic I turns this inclusion into an eigenvalue of a stochastic matrix with at most NN states. We can add absorbing states to reach order NN. On the ray of angle θ\theta, Topic XII gives |z|=ρ/γ≤KN(θ)|z|=\rho/\gamma\le K_N(\theta). Thus every possible choice of PP requires γ≥ρ/KN(θ)\gamma\ge\rho/K_N(\theta).

This bound is attained. A nonreal boundary point inside the unit disk supplies an invariant polygon with zero in its interior. A nonreal unit-circle boundary point is a root of unity of order at most NN. Its orbit gives a regular invariant polygon. At angles zero and π\pi, a centred square works. Thus, if ΓN(T)\Gamma_N(T) denotes the smallest factor over allowed polygons,

ΓN(ρRθ)=ρKN(θ). \Gamma_N(\rho R_\theta)=\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}.

Strict contraction in some such gauge is possible exactly when ρ<KN(θ)\rho<K_N(\theta). At angle π\pi the bound N≥4N\ge4 lets us choose the square. A triangle containing zero in its interior cannot be invariant under −1-1, since central symmetry pairs up the vertices.

The worst angle and a numerical check

Let QQ be the convex hull of the NNth roots of unity. For z∈Qz\in Q, express zz as a convex combination of those roots. Multiplying by any vertex of QQ permutes the roots, so every image vertex under multiplication by zz is again in QQ. Thus zQ⊆QzQ\subseteq Q, and the polygon criterion gives Q⊆ΘNQ\subseteq\Theta_N. Its inscribed disk has radius cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N), so KN(θ)≥cos⁡(π/N)K_N(\theta)\ge\cos(\pi/N) at every angle.

Where can equality occur in this bound? On the first Farey interval the endpoints are 0/10/1 and 1/N1/N. There q=1q=1 and s=m=Ns=m=N, and the boundary is the segment joining 11 to e2πi/Ne^{2\pi i/N}, as in Topic XI. The perpendicular from the origin to this segment points in direction π/N\pi/N and has length cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N). Project the boundary point KN(θ)eiθK_N(\theta)e^{i\theta} onto this direction to obtain

KN(θ)=cos⁡(π/N)cos⁡(θ−π/N). K_N(\theta)=\frac{\cos(\pi/N)}{\cos(\theta-\pi/N)}.

At θ=π/N\theta=\pi/N the radius equals cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N). The largest value of ΓN(ρRθ)/ρ\Gamma_N(\rho R_\theta)/\rho over the angles is therefore sec⁡(π/N)\sec(\pi/N).

What if we have to draw the polygon before learning the angle? Our polygon QQ has circumradius one. Let DD be the closed unit disk. Every rotated copy of QQ lies in DD. Distance from the origin to each side of QQ is cos⁡(π/N)\cos(\pi/N), so enlarging QQ by sec⁡(π/N)\sec(\pi/N) makes it contain DD. We have proved

RθQ⊆D⊆sec⁡(π/N)Q R_\theta Q\subseteq D\subseteq\sec(\pi/N)Q

for every θ\theta, with one fixed polygon. At θ=π/N\theta=\pi/N even the best polygon for that particular rotation needs the factor sec⁡(π/N)\sec(\pi/N). Thus QQ attains the smallest possible worst-case factor.

For a square and an eighth of a turn the formula gives K4(π/4)=1/2K_4(\pi/4)=1/\sqrt2. A dilation by 0.70.7 combined with this rotation has smallest possible factor 0.72≈0.989950.7\sqrt2\approx0.98995, so we can make all vectors contract. Increasing the dilation to 0.80.8 still shortens every Euclidean length, but 0.82>10.8\sqrt2>1. With only four vertices no choice of polygon then gives strict contraction for all vectors.

Try the square P=[−1,1]2P=[-1,1]^2 itself. The least scale that contains (x1,x2)(x_1,x_2) is max⁡{|x1|,|x2|}\max\{|x_1|,|x_2|\}. Take its corner (1,1)(1,1), which has gauge one. The rotation sends it to (0,2)(0,\sqrt2), and the dilation takes it to (0,ρ2)(0,\rho\sqrt2). The other three corners give the same gauge by symmetry. Since the image of the square is their convex hull, ρ2P\rho\sqrt2 P contains it. Any smaller copy misses the first corner image. This square therefore attains the factor predicted by the theorem.

The angle 5π/75\pi/7 of the worked octagon gives a different answer to the same practical question. For dilation 0.950.95, its optimal eight-vertex factor is 0.95/K8(5π/7)≈0.978760.95/K_8(5\pi/7)\approx0.97876, below one. Now suppose we know only the dilation. For eight vertices the best guarantee over all rotations is 0.95/cos⁡(π/8)≈1.028270.95/\cos(\pi/8)\approx1.02827. To guarantee strict contraction we need cos⁡(π/N)>0.95\cos(\pi/N)>0.95. Nine vertices give about 0.939690.93969 for the cosine and ten give 0.951060.95106. A regular decagon therefore suffices for every angle, and ten is the least possible vertex budget for that guarantee.

The gap near the unit circle

For a given number NN of vertices we would like to estimate the distance 1−KN(θ)1-K_N(\theta) from the boundary point on our ray to the unit circle. Take an angle strictly between two Farey endpoints. Write yy for its fraction of a turn, reflecting to 1−θ/(2π)1-\theta/(2\pi) if necessary to place the smaller denominator on the left. In these coordinates p/q<y<r/sp/q<y<r/s and q<sq<s. Let tt be the fraction of the interval width between its left endpoint and yy. With the factor count mm of Topic VIII this gives

m=⌊N/q⌋,t=y−p/qr/s−p/q,A=2πts,B=2π(1−t)mq. m=\lfloor N/q\rfloor,\qquad t=\frac{y-p/q}{r/s-p/q},\qquad A=\frac{2\pi t}{s},\qquad B=\frac{2\pi(1-t)}{mq}.

Here 0<t<10<t<1 measures position within the interval. The gap is small for two reasons. The endpoint angles differ by only 2π/(qs)2\pi/(qs), and the sines in the radius equation are nearly linear at this scale. The first nonzero term is

1−KN(θ)=2π2t(1−t)qs(ts+1−tmq)(1+O(N−2)). 1-K_N(\theta)= \frac{2\pi^2t(1-t)}{qs} \left(\frac ts+\frac{1-t}{mq}\right) \bigl(1+O(N^{-2})\bigr).

Write LN(θ)L_N(\theta) for the product preceding 1+O(N−2)1+O(N^{-2}). There are constants C>0C>0 and N0N_0, independent of the interval and tt, such that for every N≥N0N\ge N_0 and every angle strictly inside an order-NN Farey interval,

|(1−KN(θ))−LN(θ)|≤CN2LN(θ). \left|(1-K_N(\theta))-L_N(\theta)\right| \le\frac{C}{N^2}L_N(\theta).

A single relative bound covers positions arbitrarily close to either endpoint, where the gap itself is especially small. To put a scale on the formula, take the eight-state ray y=5/14y=5/14. Between 1/31/3 and 3/83/8 its relative position is t=5/14−1/33/8−1/3=47. t=\frac{5/14-1/3}{3/8-1/3}=\frac47. Here q=3q=3, s=8s=8 and m=2m=2. The two terms t/st/s and (1−t)/(mq)(1-t)/(mq) are both 1/141/14, giving L8=π2/343≈0.02877L_8=\pi^2/343\approx0.02877. The radius equation gives an actual gap of about 1−0.970613=0.029391-0.970613=0.02939. The relative error in using the leading term is about two per cent in this example. The uniform estimate states how the error behaves as NN grows.

Where does the leading term come from?

To estimate how far the scalar root lies below one, compare the function at the root and at one. Set H(u)=us/msin⁡A+uqsin⁡BH(u)=u^{s/m}\sin A+u^q\sin B and K=KN(θ)K=K_N(\theta). Since q+s>Nq+s>N and q<sq<s, we have s>N/2s>N/2. Also (m+1)q>N(m+1)q>N and m≥1m\ge1, so mq>N/2mq>N/2. Thus A+B=O(N−1)A+B=O(N^{-1}). The scalar equation gives H(K)=sin⁡(A+B)H(K)=\sin(A+B), while

Measuring contraction with polygons

Invariant polyhedra and functions that measure vector size by scaling them are standard tools in stability and control [Bitsoris], [FarinaBenvenuti], [Blanchini]. Hennet and Lasserre describe when a rotation followed by a dilation leaves a centered regular polygon invariant [HennetLasserre], Lemma 2. Regular polygons also appear in constructions of polyhedral Lyapunov functions for planar systems with nonreal eigenvalues [RossiColaneriShorten]. Kousoulidis and Forni study such constructions with a fixed number of vertices or defining linear inequalities [KousoulidisForni]. Here the boundary theorem gives the best possible contraction factor when vector size is measured by scaling a polygon with a prescribed maximum number of vertices. The polygon need not be regular or symmetric.

Let RθR_\theta denote planar rotation through the real angle θ\theta, and put Tρ,θ=ρRθT_{\rho,\theta}=\rho R_\theta, where ρ>0\rho>0. Fix N≥4N\ge4. We allow any convex polygon PP with at most NN vertices and 0∈int⁡P0\in\operatorname{int}P.

Measure the size of x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb R^2 by VP(x)=inf⁡{a>0:x∈aP}.V_P(x)=\inf\{a>0:x\in aP\}. This measures how much we must scale PP to contain xx. We impose no symmetry on PP; in particular, VP(−x)V_P(-x) may differ from VP(x)V_P(x), so VPV_P need not be a norm. For γ>0\gamma>0, the inclusion Tρ,θP⊆γPT_{\rho,\theta}P\subseteq\gamma P is equivalent to VP(Tρ,θx)≤γVP(x)(x∈ℝ2).V_P(T_{\rho,\theta}x)\le\gamma V_P(x) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R^2). A factor γ<1\gamma<1 therefore means contraction in this measurement. Define the best possible factor over all the allowed polygons by ΓN(Tρ,θ)=inf⁡{γ>0:Tρ,θP⊆γP for some such P}.\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta}) =\inf\{\gamma>0:T_{\rho,\theta}P\subseteq\gamma P \text{ for some such }P\}. For 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, Theorem 1.1 gives the exact boundary radius KN(θ)=max⁡{r≥0:reiθ∈ΘN}.K_N(\theta)=\max\{r\ge0:re^{i\theta}\in\Theta_N\}. The next theorem expresses the optimal factor in terms of this radius.

Theorem 7.1 (Optimal contraction factor). For N≥4N\ge4, ρ>0\rho>0, and 0≤θ≤π0\le\theta\le\pi, (7.1)ΓN(Tρ,θ)=ρKN(θ).\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})=\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}. Proof of Theorem 7.1

Proof. Suppose an allowed polygon PP satisfies ρRθP⊆γP\rho R_\theta P\subseteq\gamma P. Dividing this inclusion by γ\gamma gives (ρ/γ)RθP⊆P.(\rho/\gamma)R_\theta P\subseteq P. The invariant-polygon criterion (2.1) therefore gives (ρ/γ)eiθ∈ΘN(\rho/\gamma)e^{i\theta}\in\Theta_N, and hence ρ/γ≤KN(θ),γ≥ρKN(θ).\rho/\gamma\le K_N(\theta),\qquad \gamma\ge\frac{\rho}{K_N(\theta)}. Taking the infimum over all allowed polygons and factors proves the lower bound in (7.1).

If λ\lambda is nonreal and |λ|<1|\lambda|<1, the criterion supplies a polygon with at most NN vertices. The observation following (2.1) shows that it has zero in its interior. If λ\lambda is nonreal and |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, the unit-circle classification makes it a root of unity of order d≤Nd\le N. To bound the radius for every angle, let QNQ_N be the regular polygon whose vertices are the NNth roots of unity. Since ΓN(Tρ,θ)/ρ=1/KN(θ)\Gamma_N(T_{\rho,\theta})/\rho=1/K_N(\theta), the largest optimal factor relative to ρ\rho is 1/cos⁡(π/N)1/\cos(\pi/N), attained at the same angle. ◻

A planar polygon has as many sides as vertices. If it has L≤NL\le N sides and zero in its interior, write its defining inequalities as ℓj(x)≤1\ell_j(x)\le1, where each ℓj\ell_j is linear. Then VP(x)=max1≤j≤Lℓj(x).V_P(x)=\max_{1\le j\le L}\ell_j(x). Thus the vertex bound also limits the number of linear functions needed to represent VPV_P. By the theorem, such a polygon can be chosen to give a contraction factor smaller than one exactly when ρ<KN(θ).\rho<K_N(\theta). If the polygon may depend on the angle, strict contraction with at most NN vertices is possible for every angle exactly when ρ<cos⁡(π/N)\rho<\cos(\pi/N). The assumption N≥4N\ge4 is needed in the negative real direction. Although −1∈Θ3-1\in\Theta_3, the inclusion −P⊆P-P\subseteq P also gives P⊆−PP\subseteq-P, so P=−PP=-P. Its vertices then occur in opposite pairs, which is impossible for a triangle with zero in its interior.

Farey asymptotics and vertex complexity

The formulas above give the boundary radius and optimal contraction factor at each order. We now estimate their behavior as N→∞N\to\infty and determine how many polygon vertices are needed for a given accuracy. These estimates follow from the completed boundary theorem.

oković used polygons generated by powers of a complex number to simplify the description of the stochastic eigenvalue region [Djokovic]. Dubuc and Malik connected these convex hulls with Farey sequences and trinomial equations, that is, polynomial equations with three nonzero terms [DubucMalik]. Dubuc and Zaoui studied the fractal dimension of unions of the resulting arcs [DubucZaoui]. For points zz on a trinomial Farey arc associated with p/q<r/sp/q<r/s and s>q>2s>q>2, Dubuc and Malik prove the lower bound |z|s≥1−π2qs|z|^s\ge1-\frac{\pi^2}{qs} [DubucMalik], Theorem 13.1. Kirkland, Laffey, and Šmigoc later characterized the boundary at a fixed argument [KirklandLaffeySmigoc]. Here the matrix order NN varies. The resulting equation gives a leading term for the gap 1−KN(θ)1-K_N(\theta) with relative error O(N−2)O(N^{-2}): the error divided by the leading term is O(N−2)O(N^{-2}). This term depends on both endpoint denominators and the argument’s position between them, and the error bound remains valid arbitrarily close to either endpoint. The estimate refines the lower bound in the trinomial case and also applies to products with several factors.

Let N≥4N\ge4 and suppose x=θ/(2π)x=\theta/(2\pi) lies strictly between consecutive fractions f<gf<g in FN∩[0,1/2]F_N\cap[0,1/2]. If ff has the smaller denominator, take y=xy=x and keep the interval (f,g)(f,g). Otherwise reflect it to (1−g,1−f)(1-g,1-f) and take y=1−xy=1-x. Write the chosen interval as (p/q,r/s)(p/q,r/s), so its lower endpoint p/qp/q has the smaller denominator: pq<y<rs,q<s,rq−ps=1.\frac pq<y<\frac rs,\qquad q<s,\qquad rq-ps=1. Set m=⌊N/q⌋m=\lfloor N/q\rfloor, the number of factors in the product. Since r/s−p/q=1/(qs)r/s-p/q=1/(qs), define t=y−p/qr/s−p/q=s(qy−p)∈(0,1).t=\frac{y-p/q}{r/s-p/q}=s(qy-p)\in(0,1). Thus tt measures the distance from p/qp/q to yy as a proportion of the interval length, and y−pq=tqs,rs−y=1−tqs.y-\frac pq=\frac{t}{qs},\qquad \frac rs-y=\frac{1-t}{qs}. Theorem 8.1 (Uniform asymptotic estimate). For the interval data defined above, (8.1)1−KN(θ)=2π2t(1−t)qs(ts+1−tmq)(1+O(N−2))(N→∞).1-K_N(\theta)= \frac{2\pi^2t(1-t)}{qs} \left(\frac{t}{s}+\frac{1-t}{mq}\right) \bigl(1+O(N^{-2})\bigr) \qquad(N\to\infty). The relative error statement concerns only open Farey intervals: at an endpoint, both the gap 1−KN(θ)1-K_N(\theta) and the leading term are zero. For an irrational x=θ/(2π)x=\theta/(2\pi), both endpoint denominators and the position within the interval vary with NN. For badly approximable xx, the following corollary gives a simpler rate. Recall that xx is badly approximable if some cx>0c_x>0 satisfies |x−ab|≥cxb2for every rational a/b with b≥1.\left|x-\frac ab\right|\ge\frac{c_x}{b^2} \qquad\text{for every rational }a/b\text{ with }b\ge1. For positive sequences, we write aN≍xbNa_N\asymp_x b_N when aN/bNa_N/b_N is bounded above and below by positive constants depending only on xx.

Near equality and products with different exponents

Theorem 5.2 uses Jensen’s inequality to bound the modulus, with equality when all coefficients βj\beta_j agree. We now quantify this equality condition: a small nonnegative difference between the two sides of Jensen’s inequality bounds how far the factor arguments, and hence the coefficients, can differ. We then allow factors with different exponents. Their arguments have different allowed ranges, so we optimize the product by choosing these arguments within their individual ranges while keeping their sum fixed.

Since (log⁡sin⁡t)′=cot⁡t(\log\sin t)'=\cot t and (log⁡sin⁡t)″=−1/sin⁡2t(\log\sin t)''=-1/\sin^2t, Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives Φ(v)−Φ(v*)=∑jcot⁡(vj*)Δj−∑jΔj2∫011−tsin⁡2(vj*+tΔj)dt≤∑jcot⁡(vj*)Δj−12∑jΔj2.\begin{aligned} \Phi(v)-\Phi(v^*) &=\sum_j\cot(v_j^*)\Delta_j -\sum_j\Delta_j^2\int_0^1 \frac{1-t}{\sin^2(v_j^*+t\Delta_j)}\,dt\\ &\le\sum_j\cot(v_j^*)\Delta_j -\frac12\sum_j\Delta_j^2. \end{aligned} Each segment vj*+tΔjv_j^*+t\Delta_j lies in (0,π)(0,\pi). The inequality follows from 1/sin⁡2t≥11/\sin^2t\ge1 and ∫01(1−t)dt=1/2\int_0^1(1-t)\,dt=1/2. Because vv and v*v^* both have sum SS, ∑jΔj=0\sum_j\Delta_j=0. Subtracting cot⁡c∑jΔj\cot c\sum_j\Delta_j therefore leaves the linear term unchanged and gives ∑jcot⁡(vj*)Δj=∑j(cot⁡(vj*)−cot⁡c)Δj=∑Uj<c(cot⁡Uj−cot⁡c)(vj−Uj)≤0.\begin{aligned} \sum_j\cot(v_j^*)\Delta_j &=\sum_j\bigl(\cot(v_j^*)-\cot c\bigr)\Delta_j\\ &=\sum_{U_j<c}(\cot U_j-\cot c)(v_j-U_j)\le0. \end{aligned} Only indices with Uj<cU_j<c contribute, since otherwise vj*=cv_j^*=c. For each contributing index, cot⁡Uj−cot⁡c>0\cot U_j-\cot c>0 because cotangent decreases on (0,π)(0,\pi), whereas vj−Uj≤0v_j-U_j\le0 by the upper bound. Consequently, Φ(v*)−Φ(v)≥12∑j(vj−vj*)2.\Phi(v^*)-\Phi(v)\ge\frac12\sum_j(v_j-v_j^*)^2. This proves the unique maximum: every v≠v*v\ne v^* gives a strictly smaller value of Φ\Phi, and hence of the sine product. For the original factor arguments, the product identity proved above turns the left-hand side into log⁡∏jsin⁡vj*ρe∏jsin⁡Mj,\log\frac{\prod_j\sin v_j^*}{\rho^e\prod_j\sin M_j}, proving (A.6). Exponentiation gives the product bound and its equality condition. Finally, if S/m≤min⁡jUjS/m\le\min_jU_j, the choice c=S/mc=S/m gives vj*=S/mv_j^*=S/m for every jj, yielding the last assertion. ◻

To recover the equal-exponent case of Theorem 5.2, take qj=qq_j=q, z=ωz=\omega, θ=ϑ\theta=\vartheta, e=s−mqe=s-mq and L=r−mpL=r-mp. Then Mj=MM_j=M, Uj=M−AU_j=M-A, and the real argument identity gives S=m(M−A−B).S=m(M-A-B). Since B>0B>0, the common value S/m=M−A−BS/m=M-A-B is smaller than every upper bound Uj=M−AU_j=M-A. Thus equality requires vj=M−A−Bv_j=M-A-B, or equivalently uj=A+Bu_j=A+B, for every jj. The strict increase of Arg⁡(ωq−β)\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-\beta) with β\beta makes this equivalent to equal coefficients. With different exponents, it is the differences Mj−ujM_j-u_j that share the common maximizing value cc, except where an upper bound UjU_j forces a smaller value. The theorem bounds the product under the stated product and real argument identities. To determine the largest eigenvalue modulus at a fixed argument and matrix order, one would also need a stochastic matrix of that order attaining the proposed bound and a proof that no matrix of that order has an eigenvalue at the same argument with a larger modulus.

Matrices with independently varying parameters

Theorem 5.3 constructs a row-stochastic family A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta), with 𝛃=(β0,…,βm−1)∈[0,1]m\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m-1})\in[0,1]^m, and gives its full characteristic polynomial. Its directed graph is illustrated in Figure 3. Here we count the positive entries, show when every vertex can be reached from every other, and determine when a matrix power has all entries positive. We then examine the choices βj=0\beta_j=0 and βj=1\beta_j=1 for all jj. Finally, for the order-nn Farey data and 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1, consider a root ω=ρeiϑ\omega=\rho e^{i\vartheta} with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1 and argument inside the chosen interval. If it satisfies the real argument identity (5.4), we show that ρ≤Kn(θ)\rho\le K_n(\theta), where θ=min⁡{ϑ,2π−ϑ}\theta=\min\{\vartheta,2\pi-\vartheta\}. Its modulus reaches Kn(θ)K_n(\theta) exactly when all parameters βj\beta_j are equal.

Proposition B.1. Let A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) be the family constructed in Theorem 5.3, with positive integers m,q,sm,q,s satisfying s>(m−1)qs>(m-1)q and q<sq<s. Put n0=max⁡{mq,s}n_0=\max\{mq,s\}. If 0<βj<10<\beta_j<1 for every j=0,…,m−1j=0,\ldots,m-1, then A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta) is irreducible: every vertex can reach every other along a directed path whose arrow weights are positive. It has exactly n0+mn_0+m positive entries: mm rows have two each, and the remaining n0−mn_0-m rows have one each. If also gcd⁡(q,s)=1\gcd(q,s)=1, the matrix is primitive: some positive integer kk makes every entry of A(𝛃)kA(\boldsymbol\beta)^k strictly positive.

For any 𝛃∈[0,1]m\boldsymbol\beta\in[0,1]^m and integer n≥n0n\ge n_0, the block diagonal matrix A(𝛃)⊕In−n0=(A(𝛃)00In−n0)A(\boldsymbol\beta)\oplus I_{n-n_0} =\begin{pmatrix} A(\boldsymbol\beta)&0\\ 0&I_{n-n_0} \end{pmatrix} is row-stochastic of order nn and retains every eigenvalue of A(𝛃)A(\boldsymbol\beta). Here In−n0I_{n-n_0} is the identity matrix of order n−n0n-n_0; when n=n0n=n_0, no block is added.

Proof of Proposition B.1

Proof. Suppose 0<βj<10<\beta_j<1 for every jj, so both βj\beta_j and 1−βj1-\beta_j are positive. From any vertex in a block, the arrows of weight one lead to its last vertex. The arrow of weight βj\beta_j leads back to the first vertex, allowing every vertex of that block to be reached. The arrows of weight 1−βj1-\beta_j lead through all blocks in cyclic order, including any vertices inserted between the last block and block zero. Thus every vertex can reach every other by arrows of positive weight, proving irreducibility.

At the last vertex of each block, the two outgoing arrows have distinct destinations. For m≥2m\ge2, the arrow of weight βj\beta_j stays in its block, while the other leads to a different block or an inserted vertex. For m=1m=1, the inequality q<sq<s requires inserted vertices, so the destinations are again distinct. These mm rows therefore have two positive entries each. All other n0−mn_0-m rows have one, giving 2m+(n0−m)=n0+m2m+(n_0-m)=n_0+m positive entries.

Now assume gcd⁡(q,s)=1\gcd(q,s)=1. The vertex v0,q−1v_{0,q-1} lies on both the cycle of length qq within block zero and the cycle of length ss through all blocks. Every integer L≥(q−1)sL\ge(q-1)s can be written as L=aq+bsL=aq+bs with nonnegative integers a,ba,b. Indeed, coprimality allows a choice b∈{0,…,q−1}b\in\{0,\ldots,q-1\} with bs≡L(mod⁡q)bs\equiv L\pmod q; then a=(L−bs)/qa=(L-bs)/q is an integer and is nonnegative because bs≤(q−1)s≤Lbs\le(q-1)s\le L.

For any vertices u,vu,v, choose paths from uu to v0,q−1v_{0,q-1} and from there to vv, and let their total length be ℓuv\ell_{uv}. Repeating the two cycles aa and bb times between these paths gives a walk from uu to vv of length ℓuv+aq+bs\ell_{uv}+aq+bs; a walk may revisit vertices. Thus there is such a walk of every length k≥ℓuv+(q−1)sk\ge\ell_{uv}+(q-1)s. Its arrow weights are positive, so their product contributes a positive term to (Ak)uv(A^k)_{uv}. There are finitely many vertex pairs, so one common threshold works for all of them. Every sufficiently high power of AA therefore has all entries positive, proving primitivity.

For every parameter tuple in [0,1]m[0,1]^m, the construction gives a row-stochastic matrix AA. Adding an identity block preserves nonnegative entries and row sums of one. Moreover, det⁡(tIn−(A⊕In−n0))=(t−1)n−n0det⁡(tIn0−A),\det\bigl(tI_n-(A\oplus I_{n-n_0})\bigr) =(t-1)^{n-n_0}\det(tI_{n_0}-A), so every eigenvalue of AA is retained, including when n=n0n=n_0 and no block is added. ◻

Let p/q<r/sp/q<r/s be consecutive fractions in FnF_n, with q<sq<s, and put m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor. Farey adjacency gives q+s>nq+s>n and rq−ps=1rq-ps=1. Since mq≤nmq\le n and q,s≤nq,s\le n, s>n−q≥(m−1)q,n0=max⁡{mq,s}≤n.s>n-q\ge(m-1)q,\qquad n_0=\max\{mq,s\}\le n. Thus the realization theorem applies and its matrices can be extended to order nn. The identity rq−ps=1rq-ps=1 implies gcd⁡(q,s)=1\gcd(q,s)=1, so the preceding proposition also gives primitivity whenever every βj\beta_j lies in (0,1)(0,1).

If all βj=β\beta_j=\beta and α=1−β\alpha=1-\beta, substituting into (5.11) gives det⁡(tI−A)={(tq−β)m−αmtmq−s,s≤mq,ts−mq(tq−β)m−αm,s>mq.\det(tI-A)= \begin{cases} (t^q-\beta)^m-\alpha^m t^{mq-s},&s\le mq,\\ t^{s-mq}(t^q-\beta)^m-\alpha^m,&s>mq. \end{cases} For 𝛃=𝟏=(1,…,1)\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf1=(1,\ldots,1) and 𝛃=𝟎=(0,…,0)\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf0=(0,\ldots,0), respectively, this becomes det⁡(tI−A(𝟏))=tn0−mq(tq−1)m,det⁡(tI−A(𝟎))=tn0−s(ts−1).\begin{aligned} \det(tI-A(\mathbf1))&=t^{n_0-mq}(t^q-1)^m,\\ \det(tI-A(\mathbf0))&=t^{n_0-s}(t^s-1). \end{aligned} The nonzero eigenvalues are therefore precisely the qqth roots of unity for A(𝟏)A(\mathbf1) and the ssth roots of unity for A(𝟎)A(\mathbf0). The powers of tt give the multiplicities of zero. Since the entries vary continuously with 𝛃\boldsymbol\beta, these endpoint matrices belong to the same continuous family. The characteristic formula remains valid when some parameters are zero or one and others lie in (0,1)(0,1). The irreducibility assertion above requires every parameter to lie in (0,1)(0,1).

The following corollary identifies the parameter choices whose eigenvalue modulus reaches Kn(θ)K_n(\theta). For 0≤βj<10\le\beta_j<1, the characteristic equation (5.11) determines the sum of arguments only modulo 2π2\pi. We therefore also require the real argument identity (5.4), with the specific value 2π(r−mp)2\pi(r-mp) on its right-hand side.

Corollary B.2. Let n≥4n\ge4, and let f<gf<g be consecutive fractions in Fn+F_n^+. If the smaller denominator belongs to ff, put p/q=fp/q=f and r/s=gr/s=g. Otherwise put p/q=1−gp/q=1-g and r/s=1−fr/s=1-f, corresponding to reflection of the arc in the real axis. In either case, p/q<r/sp/q<r/s and q<sq<s. Put m=⌊n/q⌋m=\lfloor n/q\rfloor and let 𝛃=(β0,…,βm−1)∈[0,1)m.\boldsymbol\beta=(\beta_0,\ldots,\beta_{m-1})\in[0,1)^m. Let ω=ρeiϑ\omega=\rho e^{i\vartheta}, with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, be a root of the characteristic polynomial (5.11), with pq<ϑ2π<rs.\frac pq<\frac{\vartheta}{2\pi}<\frac rs. Define A=qϑ−2πp,B=2πr−sϑm,θ=min⁡{ϑ,2π−ϑ},A=q\vartheta-2\pi p,\qquad B=\frac{2\pi r-s\vartheta}{m},\qquad \theta=\min\{\vartheta,2\pi-\vartheta\}, and use arguments in (0,π)(0,\pi) to set M=Arg⁡(ωq−1),uj=Arg⁡(ωq−βj)(0≤j<m).M=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-1),\qquad u_j=\operatorname{Arg}(\omega^q-\beta_j)\quad(0\le j<m). These satisfy A≤uj<MA\le u_j<M. Assume the following identity holds as an equality of real numbers: (s−mq)ϑ+∑j=0m−1uj=2π(r−mp).(s-mq)\vartheta+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}u_j=2\pi(r-mp). Then ρ≤Kn(θ),\rho\le K_n(\theta), and ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) if and only if β0=⋯=βm−1\beta_0=\cdots=\beta_{m-1}. Proof of Corollary B.2

Proof. Since ω≠0\omega\ne0, dividing the characteristic equation (5.11) at t=ωt=\omega by ωn0−s\omega^{n_0-s} gives ωs−mq∏j=0m−1(ωq−βj)=∏j=0m−1(1−βj).\omega^{s-mq}\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(\omega^q-\beta_j) =\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-\beta_j). The angle identities (5.2) give A,B>0A,B>0 and A+B<πA+B<\pi. Together with the assumed real argument identity, these verify the hypotheses of Theorem 5.2. It yields ρs/msin⁡A+ρqsin⁡B≤sin⁡(A+B),\rho^{s/m}\sin A+\rho^q\sin B\le\sin(A+B), with equality exactly when all βj\beta_j agree. The left-hand side is strictly increasing in ρ\rho and equals the right-hand side at ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) by (5.3). Hence ρ≤Kn(θ)\rho\le K_n(\theta), with ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta) exactly when all parameters agree.

In that case, write β\beta for their common value and uu for their common factor argument. The assumed real identity gives u=2π(r−mp)−(s−mq)ϑm=A+B.u=\frac{2\pi(r-mp)-(s-mq)\vartheta}{m}=A+B. Put R=|ωq−β|>0R=|\omega^q-\beta|>0, so ωq−β=Rei(A+B)\omega^q-\beta=Re^{i(A+B)}. Taking real and imaginary parts, as in (5.8), gives R=ρqsin⁡Asin⁡(A+B),β=ρqcos⁡A−Rcos⁡(A+B)=ρqsin⁡Bsin⁡(A+B).\begin{aligned} R&=\frac{\rho^q\sin A}{\sin(A+B)},\\ \beta&=\rho^q\cos A-R\cos(A+B) =\frac{\rho^q\sin B}{\sin(A+B)}. \end{aligned} The last equality uses cos⁡Asin⁡(A+B)−sin⁡Acos⁡(A+B)=sin⁡B\cos A\sin(A+B)-\sin A\cos(A+B)=\sin B. Conversely, (5.7), (5.8) and (5.9), evaluated at ρ=Kn(θ)\rho=K_n(\theta), give this tuple with coefficients in (0,1)(0,1) satisfying both the product relation and the real argument identity. Following one complete eight-state example

On the ray of angle 5π/75\pi/7, how far can an eigenvalue of an eight-state stochastic matrix lie from zero? We will find the point, write down a matrix that reaches it and draw the eight coordinates of an eigenvector. A state will therefore have two pictures. In the transition graph it has a label and arrows to its successors. In the complex plane it is a point, and its successors tell us where multiplication by the eigenvalue sends that point.

We first work out what the proposed contacts would force. Once we have a value of zz, we can check the contacts by constructing the polygon.

Suppose an invariant polygon has eight vertices v0,…,v7v_0,\ldots,v_7 in counterclockwise order. Multiplication by z=ρeiθz=\rho e^{i\theta} sends each vertex into the assigned side (vi+2,vi+3](v_{i+2},v_{i+3}], with indices modulo eight. Two images fall strictly between the endpoints of a side, namely c1∈(v0,v1)c_1\in(v_0,v_1) and c2∈(v1,v2)c_2\in(v_1,v_2). Thus the order is N=8N=8, the cyclic shift is κ=3\kappa=3, and the number of interior contacts is two.

Where do the fractions come from in this example? The ray makes 5/145/14 of a turn. With denominators at most eight, its neighbours are 1/31/3 below and 3/83/8 above. Indeed 3⋅3−1⋅8=13\cdot3-1\cdot8=1 and their denominator sum is 11>811>8, so no fraction of order eight fits between them. In the notation p/q<r/sp/q<r/s we have q=3q=3, s=8s=8 and m=⌊8/3⌋=2m=\lfloor8/3\rfloor=2. There is room for two blocks of three steps and two steps left over. We shall find all eight in the following paths.

The return paths and the real turn count

Starting at v1v_1 or v2v_2, each image that lands on a vertex advances its index by three modulo eight. Following the images from the two starting points gives

v1→v4→v7→c2, v_1\longrightarrow v_4\longrightarrow v_7\longrightarrow c_2,
